Electricity service is expected to begin in 2028, with Microsoft agreeing t...

NiSource Inc. (NYSE:NI) has entered into a 20-year energy agreement with Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) to supply approximately 1,100 megawatts (MW) of generation resources to a data centre campus in northwest Indiana. Electricity service is expected to begin in 2028, with Microsoft agreeing to fund the generation and transmission infrastructure required to meet the facility's power requirements. The agreement will be implemented through NiSource Generation Company LLC (GenCo), a generation subsidiary of NiSource, and is structured to prevent the additional infrastructure costs from being passed on to existing Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (NIPSCO) electricity customers. NiSource also increased its projected customer savings associated with its data centre agreements to approximately $1.75 billion over the life of the contracts, compared with a previously announced estimate of $1.4 billion. Under the agreement, Microsoft will be responsible for funding all generation and transmission infrastructure required to serve its data centre campus. The arrangement is intended to ensure that the costs associated with supplying the additional electricity demand are borne by Microsoft rather than existing NIPSCO customers. The infrastructure will be developed through NiSource's GenCo subsidiary, which provides generation resources for large electricity customers. The agreement covers approximately 1,100 MW of generation resources over a 20-year period. The scale of the commitment reflects the substantial electricity requirements associated with large data centre operations, particularly facilities supporting cloud computing and artificial intelligence workloads. NiSource has not yet disclosed the total capital expenditure associated with the agreement or the detailed composition of the generation resources. Further financial and operational information is expected during the company's third-quarter earnings call. NiSource said the Microsoft agreement increases its projected savings for existing NIPSCO electricity customers to approximately $1.75 billion over the life of its data centre contracts. The revised figure compares with the company's previously disclosed estimate of $1.4 billion. The increase of approximately $350 million reflects the additional benefits NiSource expects from its arrangements with large electricity users. According to the company, the savings could amount to as much as $140 annually for each existing electricity customer.

The agreement is expected to expand customer savings while supporting economic growth across the region, reflecting NiSource's continued focus on aligning economic development with customer affordability. Through NiSource Generation Company LLC (GenCo), the company is serving new large-load customers under a structure designed to protect existing Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (NIPSCO) electric customers from incremental costs and return value from large-load customers' use of the existing electric system. "Our priority remains clear: protect existing customers, support safe and reliable service, and ensure that new growth contributes tangible benefits to the communities we serve. Microsoft's Business Software Proposed to Receive Increased UK Regulatory Scrutiny

No summary available

Microsoft (MSFT) business software is on verge of being designated with UK strategic market status that would subject it to greater scrutiny and regulation, the country's Competition and Markets Authority said Friday. The regulator has also published a roadmap outlining possible future intervention...

Microsoft (MSFT) business software is on verge of being designated with UK strategic market status that would subject it to greater scrutiny and regulation, the country's Competition and Markets Authority said Friday. The regulator has also published a roadmap outlining possible future interventions in the business software ecosystem, including how Microsoft bundles its business software like Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, Teams and Copilot, the company said. The regulator wants to increase Microsoft products' compatibility to "mix and match software and AI services from a broad range of competing suppliers," the regulator said. "The ability to choose, switch and combine digital services (especially AI), without being overly dependent on a single technology provider, is also increasingly important for resilience and strategic autonomy," the regulator said. The regulator is also in discussions with Microsoft as well as Amazon (AMZN) Web Services to increase competition in the cloud services realm, the regulator said. Microsoft did not immediately reply to MT Newswires' request for comment.

It will rely much more on its custom-designed silicon than on leading graphics processing units (GPUs) like those from Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA). It's already made significant progress in expanding workloads for its Maia 200 chips, and it expects its next-generation Maia 300 chips to deliver significant improvements when it starts deploying them next year. "Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services," CEO Satya Nadella said. That's great news for its custom chip partner, Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL), and bad news for Nvidia. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia's extreme dominance of the data center GPU space during the first few years of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom left its market share with nowhere to go but down. Its biggest customers, including the hyperscalers and leading AI frontier labs, have developed custom solutions that can handle AI workloads, and that can deliver better price performance on specific tasks than Nvidia's GPUs. That said, GPUs offer far greater flexibility in terms of the types of tasks they can perform, making them particularly valuable for companies deploying servers to sell compute capacity to third parties with dynamic demands. Notice that Microsoft is starting its Maia expansion by focusing on its own products and services, not on leasing Maia compute capacity to third parties looking to cut costs on their OpenAI GPT-based applications. Their use, though, could expand over the long run. Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), which has been building its own custom AI chips for longer than any of its competitors, has seen strong adoption of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) by its Google Cloud customers for training and inference. Apple used TPUs to train Apple Intelligence, and Anthropic is using gigawatts worth of TPUs to develop its large language models. While Nvidia can continue to grow sales extremely quickly, other chipmakers' growth rates are likely to outpace it. That's reflected in its P/E valuation, which now sits below those of its biggest rivals.

Tucuvi brings a differentiated clinical approach to conversational AI within the Microsoft Pegasus Program, extending voice AI beyond administrative interactions into clinically governed care management. BOSTON, Oct. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tucuvi, an AI care management company, today announced it is joining the Microsoft for Startups Pegasus Program, which connects companies to Microsoft's enterprise customer ecosystem and go-to-market channels. For Tucuvi, the selection comes at a pivotal moment as the company scales its platform across health systems. Through Pegasus, Tucuvi will be able to bring its clinically-governed approach to AI care management to more organizations, helping them move beyond point solutions and deploy patient-facing AI across both administrative and clinical workflows on a single platform. Health systems and life sciences companies can contract Tucuvi directly through Microsoft Marketplace or apply that spend against the Microsoft Azure commitment they have already made to Microsoft, turning a new vendor evaluation into a purchase against budget that is already allocated, through a procurement path their organization has already approved. The Challenge Health systems evaluating patient-facing AI increasingly need one platform that can support both patient access, such as scheduling, navigation and referral routing, and clinical enablement, like care-gap closure, medication adherence, transitions of care, monitoring and follow-up. These are fundamentally different problems. In access, success means getting patients to the right service. In clinical care, AI must reliably follow protocols, capture clinically relevant information, and escalate the right cases to clinicians. Tucuvi was built from the clinical side and expanded into access. Today, more than 80 health settings run 50+ workflow types on the platform. LOLA®, clinical voice AI, and the platform behind it Tucuvi Health Manager is Tucuvi's AI care management platform. At its core is LOLA®, a clinical voice AI agent that holds inbound and outbound phone conversations with patients in natural language. LOLA follows configurable clinical and administrative protocols, captures structured information, and escalates cases when human intervention is required. The platform is omnichannel, extending the same workflows to text when needed. LOLA® integrates with Microsoft Foundry as the platform layer for deploying and monitoring the models behind LOLA's conversational capabilities in addition to Azure Speech for the voice layer of patient conversations.

UBS has raised its price target for Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), the software and cloud computing company, to $675 from $525, arguing that strong demand for artificial intelligence services supports higher growth expectations ahead of its 28 October results. The bank reiterated its 'buy' rating, saying Microsoft's valuation remains reasonable at 23 times estimated 2027 adjusted earnings despite a 39% rally since its June-quarter results. UBS expects investors to focus on Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing business, where the market now anticipates revenue growth of 47% for the September quarter, representing a potential two-percentage-point beat against previous expectations. The bank believes this target is achievable, citing solid enterprise demand, increased artificial intelligence infrastructure spending and potential benefits from higher OpenAI revenues flowing through to Azure. Microsoft could also benefit from rising prices for hosted graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips used to power artificial intelligence workloads. UBS expects Microsoft 365, the company's productivity software suite, to offer another source of upside as the company expands usage-based pricing for its Copilot artificial intelligence tools and increases adoption of its security products. However, investor expectations have risen alongside the share price, leaving Microsoft a widely held favourite among investors betting on further artificial intelligence growth. UBS believes the company can meet those higher expectations through strong demand, disciplined cost management and continued improvements in operating profit margins and earnings per share. The bank also sees potential for further positive sentiment from Microsoft's leadership meetings at the Ignite conference in mid-November. UBS has increased its valuation assumption for Microsoft to 25 times the estimated 2028 adjusted earnings, up from 19 times previously, reflecting what it considers a justified premium to peers. The revised target reflects growing confidence in the company's ability to monetise artificial intelligence while maintaining profitability, although the higher expectations leave less room for disappointment in its upcoming results.

Morgan Stanley finds a new twist in Microsoft's AI story

In a note shared with TheStreet on Oct. 12, Morgan Sta...

Everyone has been watching the wrong race. While the AI world obsesses over which lab builds the best model, a fresh CIO survey from Morgan Stanley points to a quieter fight playing out beneath the surface, one Microsoft may already be winning. In a note shared with TheStreet on Oct. 12, Morgan Stanley published findings from its third-quarter 2026 AlphaWise CIO survey. The bank maintained its Overweight rating and $600 price target on Microsoft, against a closing price of $541.15 that day. But the more telling data was not about the stock. It was about where enterprise IT chiefs think AI money is actually heading. Also read: Wall Street doubles down on Microsoft stock for investors One of the more interesting questions Morgan Stanley threw into this survey was about AI orchestration. Not which model do you use, but who sits above the models, directing traffic, managing data permissions, keeping an eye on costs. Microsoft pulled 20% of responses on that one. LLM providers collectively were right behind at 17%. Google got 5%, Amazon 4%. That finding runs counter to the popular narrative. The assumption has been that whoever wins the model race wins the enterprise AI race. But a growing number of companies are spreading workloads across multiple models rather than committing to one. The moment a business is running different models for different tasks, it needs something above the models to keep things organized. That is the orchestration layer, and right now Microsoft is where most CIOs say they'd go for it. Microsoft's setup for this is Azure at the infrastructure level, Fabric for enterprise data, Foundry to select and route AI tasks, and Copilot to surface the results inside everyday applications. A company could run a competitor's model through that stack and Microsoft still collects on the infrastructure, the data layer, and the software. Three revenue opportunities from one AI workflow. Thirty percent of CIOs named Microsoft as the vendor most likely to capture the biggest share of generative AI spending in 2026, up from 27% the prior quarter, according to the survey. LLM providers came in at 16%, Google at 8%, Amazon at 7%. Pull back to a three-year horizon and things get messier. Microsoft is at 28%, which was 30% just last quarter. LLM providers climbed from 17% to 21% in that same window. The vendor consolidation story that once looked inevitable hasn't materialized.

Why Wall Street Is Comfortable With Microsoft Stock Even as AI Trade Pressured

Microsoft’s CEO is still haunted by staying silent in a meeting with Bill Gates. Years later, his boss Steve Ballmer taught him how to speak up

No summary available

Satya Nadella spent more than two decades climbing the ladder at Microsoft before becoming CEO in 2014. But looking back, the billionaire recently admitted that he once failed to speak up when he believed the company was making the wrong call—and is still haunted by the memory today. Nadella recall...

Satya Nadella spent more than two decades climbing the ladder at Microsoft before becoming CEO in 2014. But looking back, the billionaire recently admitted that he once failed to speak up when he believed the company was making the wrong call—and is still haunted by the memory today. Nadella recalled a meeting around 2008–09, convened by then-chairman Bill Gates, to review a potential acquisition involving a team working on parallel data warehousing. Nadella, who was leading Microsoft's search engine team at the time, thought the deal made little sense. "I looked at it [and thought], 'It is completely architecturally stupid in that time to go buy that,'" Nadella said on an episode of the Confession With Ali Partovi podcast released this week. But rather than challenge the proposal, he sat through the review without voicing his concerns. "It haunts me to think that I may be in a review where there's somebody in that meeting who sees the future a lot more clearly than I do and the other person presenting—but does not really advocate for it," Nadella said. "And so that's what I did." He left the meeting thinking it had been a "waste of time." In hindsight, however, the experience became a reminder of how easy it can be to stay quiet rather than challenge a decision—even when you believe speaking up could lead to a better outcome. Nadella admitted that voicing dissent can be difficult at any company, especially one as large as Microsoft. But a conversation with then–Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer helped shape his view of leadership: Employees should think beyond their individual responsibilities and take an "owner mindset," considering what's best for the company as a whole. "Life's not lived by just being so transactional about everything," Nadella said. "Because at the end of the day, we all perish, and nobody's going to look at any balance sheet or income statement. It's going to be like, 'Hey, how do you live your life?'" In other words, career success isn't just about checking off boxes or avoiding conflict. It's about having the courage to stand up for what you believe is right and helping the company make better decisions—even when that means challenging your colleagues. The key, Nadella said, is learning how to push for the right outcome without putting others on the defensive. And now that he's leading the $4 trillion giant, Nadella is building a culture where employees can consistently speak up and push for the best possible outcome.

Preorders for Apple's (AAPL) $1,999 foldable iPhone Duo sold out in minutes after opening Friday, with delivery dates jumping from Oct. 23 to late January. Apple's most ambitious iPhone yet, the passport-sized Duo features a 5.4-inch front display and a 7.6-inch foldable inner screen, with a nano-texture finish that helps prevent glare while making the panel's center crease all but invisible. The book-style foldable is a first for Apple, which has sat out of the folding-phone market for years, leaving rivals Samsung (005930.KS) and Google (GOOG, GOOGL) to grab market share and iterate on their designs. But Apple is notorious for letting other companies do the legwork to develop a new market, only to swoop in and grab its own piece of the pie. That's exactly what the iPhone maker did with the AirPods and Apple Watch, which have become bestselling devices in their respective categories. The iPhone Duo brings a number of new features to Apple's all-important product line, including the ability to run two apps side by side or two windows of the same app simultaneously. Apps seamlessly transition from the front screen to the main display and back. You can also take advantage of the Duo's foldable design by positioning it like an open laptop on your desk and viewing content on the top of the screen while navigating on the bottom half. In standing mode, you can position the Duo like a tent on a flat surface to watch shows and movies or use the phone as a high-powered clock for your nightstand. Apple has also thrown in some extras on the camera. When you unfold the phone and open the camera app, the front screen will provide your subject with a preview of your shot. The idea is to spare friends, couples, and everyone in between the awful experience of having someone take your picture, only to immediately look at the result and demand a redo. The Duo gets ultrawide-angle and wide-angle rear cameras, but no telephoto option. Up front, the phone gets Apple's Center Stage camera, which helps keep the user in view even if they move side to side. There's also a FaceTime camera hidden beneath the main folding screen. Foldable phones are still a relatively niche market segment. According to market research firm IDC, manufacturers were projected to ship 1.25 billion units in 2025. Foldables were expected to make up just 20.6 million of those. But the company said it anticipates foldable smartphones will account for roughly 10% of the market by 2029. It hit a major cumulative milestone in 2026 with total lifetime units set to surpass 100 million by the end of the year, according to Counterpoint Research's latest Foldable Smartphone Market Forecast. But Apple said when it announced the new Duo that pre-orders would open on 16 October, with the device going on sale and arriving with the first customers on 23 October. Pre-orders opened at 1pm in the UK or 5am local pacific time – and, just half an hour later, Apple's website said that any orders would not ship until January. At 1.30pm UK time, for instance, customers on both the US and UK stores were told that an order placed now would not arrive until 22 January, almost exactly three months after the device goes on sale. That is likely to continue to slip back even further as more orders are placed and Apple works to fulfil them. The high demand is despite a steep price for the iPhone. The Duo starts at $1,999, or the same in pounds, and additional storage options can take the price up to $3,199. What Apple’s hand-embroidered product launch reveals about advertising in the age of AI slop

No summary available

To promote its latest product launch, Apple—one of the world's biggest technology companies—picked up a needle and thread. In this era of AI food slop, AI agents behind plush toys with eerie smiles, and deepfakes that make it harder to trust what's real, the human touch could become a selling point...

To promote its latest product launch, Apple—one of the world's biggest technology companies—picked up a needle and thread. In this era of AI food slop, AI agents behind plush toys with eerie smiles, and deepfakes that make it harder to trust what's real, the human touch could become a selling point on its own. Showing that someone took the time to make something by hand gives brands a way to signal care, creativity, and attention to detail. The effort—along with the small imperfections that reveal a human hand—can become part of the appeal, potentially making a brand feel worth paying more for. There's early evidence it works. An Ipsos study with Syracuse University tested 20 advertisements with 3,000 U.S. consumers and found that human-made ads scored, on average, 14% higher on predicted short-term sales effectiveness and 17% higher on long-term brand health than AI-generated alternatives. "Human-made might become more of a luxury over time," Stijn van Osselaer, a Cornell University marketing professor who studies how consumers connect with the people behind products, told Fortune. For Apple's Oct. 13 "Welcome Home" launch, that human touch took the form of its iconic 1977 rainbow Apple logo embroidered by Sydney-based twin sisters Maricor/Maricar. The company didn't share just a photo of the finished design. Instead, they released a video showing hands stitching the familiar shape, from the bite to the leaf. Apple's advertising hasn't always shown such a delicate touch. In 2024, the company promoted its thin new iPad Pro by crushing musical instruments, cameras, and other creative tools beneath a hydraulic press, prompting a backlash and an apology. That year, it also pulled an ad filmed in Thailand after criticism that it portrayed the country through outdated stereotypes. Then in 2025, Apple removed "The Parent Presentation," a video teaching students how to persuade their parents to buy them a Mac, though the company's reason for removing it was unclear. Rather than the AI-generated imagery spreading across sidewalks and Instagram feeds, its recent campaigns have put human handiwork on display. The embroidery follows Apple's use of stop-motion animation campaigns for the Mac mini and Apple Games, which also followed the route of showing the humans at work behind the animation. Apple and Maricor/Maricar did not respond to Fortune's requests for comment. The appeal of human craftsmanship goes beyond appreciating how many hours something took.

Amazon Web Services ("AWS") opened a preview of Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents powered by OpenAI in late September and, on Oct. 1, 2026, previewed the AWS Well-Architected Agent to help customers optimize cost, security and performance. This month, Bedrock also added Claude Haiku 5.5 at roughly 75% lower cost than its predecessor for most tasks. Cheaper inference and production-ready agent tools should widen enterprise adoption and deepen AWS consumption. Fundamentals firmly back this momentum. In the second quarter of 2026, both AWS' AI business and Amazon's chips business, spanning Trainium and Graviton, crossed a $25 billion annual revenue run rate, each growing at triple-digit percentages. Anthropic and OpenAI have made multi-year, multi-gigawatt Trainium commitments, Graviton revenue commitments rose nearly 3x sequentially, and Bedrock customers spent more in the quarter than in all prior quarters combined. Such contracted demand enhances revenue visibility. For the third quarter of 2026, Amazon expects net sales of $197-$202 billion, up 9-12% year over year, with growth nearly 400 basis points higher excluding the Prime Day timing shift. Operating income is projected at $22.5-$26.5 billion, up from $17.4 billion a year ago. Second-quarter AWS sales jumped 37% to $42.2 billion, the fastest pace in 18 quarters, and segment operating margin widened to 39.4% from 32.9%. Trailing-12-month operating cash flow rose 33% to $161.4 billion. However, Amazon raised its 2026 cash capital expenditure outlook to about $220 billion from $200 billion on higher memory costs, and trailing-12-month free cash flow swung to an outflow of $7.6 billion from an inflow of $18.2 billion. Management also expects capacity to fall short of demand through 2027, which could cap near-term AI revenues. Still, with a deep backlog and expanding AWS margins, Amazon appears well-placed to turn its AI spending into stronger cash generation over time. Microsoft MSFT and Alphabet GOOGL are also balancing AI-driven growth against heavy spending. In fourth-quarter fiscal 2026, Microsoft's Azure revenues grew 43%, while operating cash flow rose 30% to $55.4 billion. However, Microsoft's capital expenditures of $41 billion reduced free cash flow by 23% to $19.6 billion, and fiscal 2027 capex is expected to be near $175 billion. Alphabet's Google Cloud revenues jumped 82% to $24.8 billion in the second quarter, with backlog reaching $514 billion. Yet Alphabet's capex doubled to $44.9 billion, turning quarterly free cash flow negative at $5.9 billion, and Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to up to $205 billion.

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. HANGZHOU, China, Oct. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Geely Holding Group (ZGH) today announced a global strategic partnership with Google to bring built-in Google Automotive Services to digital cockpits in all eligible ZGH portfolio brand vehicles in overseas markets where Google services are available. At roll-out, eligible ZGH overseas vehicles will come with built-in Google services including Google Gemini, Play, Maps and more. This fully integrated system delivers a comprehensive set of capabilities featuring a multimodal intelligent voice large model, global smart navigation, seamless cross-device connectivity, and an extensive portfolio of in-vehicle applications to elevate everyday journeys by making them easier and more convenient while keeping drivers' attention where it belongs: on the road. This partnership builds on other ZGH portfolio brands' long-standing partnerships with Google, including the Polestar 2 which has featured the built-in services beginning in 2020. The next roll out of Google services will be included in ZGH passenger vehicles from Geely, Lynk & Co., Proton, Riddara, and smart among others. "People increasingly expect the same level of convenience and connectivity in their cars as they enjoy in their everyday lives," said Dr. Shen Yuan, Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer, ZGH. "Through our partnership with Google, we are bringing digital services directly into our vehicles to create a more seamless, intuitive and enjoyable driving experience." For ZGH, meeting customers where they are means recognizing that digital habits and service ecosystems differ by market. The partnership is intended to connect customers to eligible ZGH portfolio brand vehicles through the familiar and global-leading Google digital ecosystem, helping deliver an improved customer experience. "With this collaboration, we're transforming the in-car experience for ZGH customers by providing drivers with their favorite apps, intuitive navigation and a personal AI assistant right from their dashboard." Additional information on supported models, markets, features and timing will be announced as the rollout progresses. Customers should refer to their local ZGH portfolio brand websites and authorized retail channels for the latest information.

Today's top news: Crypto majors rebound despite hot PPI; BTC at $82.7k MSCI finalized index rules putting Strategy at risk of removal (MSTR -3%) White House has no crypto lead after Patrick Witt announces departure Binance US tries to raise $100M at $1B valuation Jupiter rolls out Papertrade-like perps product, does $1B volume first day Eight days ago an Ethereum researcher told large holders to move their coins. Today Google published a result that makes him look less paranoid and more early. Google Quantum AI cut a critical class of quantum errors roughly 40-fold on its Willow chip, per a new paper in Science. The technique attacks what may be quantum computing's single biggest tax - producing the clean, single-use resources certain operations need, which by some estimates eats up to 95% of a machine's capacity. Instead of building dedicated qubit factories to purify them, Google filters: inject a rough state, run it through a gauntlet of checks, throw out the 92% that fail. What survives hits 99.99% fidelity. Nobody is draining wallets with this. Breaking an RSA-2048 key needs errors around one in 10 billion - about a million times cleaner than what Google just showed. But researchers are moving closely. In 2019, cracking RSA-2048 was estimated to need 20 million noisy qubits. By 2025 that was under one million. A March 2026 Google whitepaper put Bitcoin's elliptic curve cryptography at under 500,000 physical qubits. Willow has 105. Google Says It Just Cracked One of Quantum Computing's Biggest Bottlenecks The irony this week is that Justin Drake's actual fear wasn't quantum at all. He thinks AI-driven mathematics breaks elliptic curves first, on ordinary hardware, in "months not years." His advice: big holders should move funds to fresh addresses that have never signed a transaction, because signing exposes your public key. So crypto is being "attacked" on two fronts: quantum advancement and AI advancement. With that said, key players are making moves and starting serious preparations. Coinbase spent this week arguing the migration has to start now. Sui is already running quantum-safe transactions on a test network. Ethereum, Zcash and Near all have plans to be quantum-resistant.

Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut. Google Quantum AI published "Magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor" in the journal Science on October 15, 2026. The paper is the first hardware demonstration of a technique that cut errors 40-fold compared with states prepared without it. Class A shares of Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) rose 0.45% that day to close at $349.22, which valued the company at $4.27 trillion. The small move reflects how a stock this large trades on search, cloud, and AI, and investors treated the paper as good science with a distant return. A lab result like this changes very little. It strengthens a long-term research effort that Alphabet can fund with its own profits. The experiment ran on Google's Willow processor. It produced T-states, a type of magic state, at 99.99% logical fidelity, which means an error rate of 0.0001 or less. Google researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones developed the method in 2024. It places an imperfect state in a small chip region. It checks the state with measurements, discards failures, and extends the survivors into a larger error-correcting code. Only 8% of attempts passed the filter. Throwing away most attempts is how the method works, because it gives up volume to get quality. ------ Free Report, Just Released Why Didn't GOOG Make The Top 10 List? 24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now. This makes it a Dividend King, or a company that has raised its payout for 50 consecutive years or more. Regulated utilities have historically been a sleepy part of the stock market because of their low volatility and stable cash flows, but lately they have been making headlines for long-term agreements with major technology companies. On Oct. 6, Black Hills announced multiple agreements with Alphabet's Google to provide energy infrastructure and services for its hyperscale data center campus in Cheyenne, Wyoming. The agreement runs through 2048 and builds on Black Hills' position as the region's top energy provider for hyperscalers. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Here's what investors need to know. As part of its arrangement with Google, Black Hills will deliver 2.7 gigawatts (GW) of power for Google's data center campus. This includes 590 megawatts (MW) of utility grid-connected service and another 2.1 GW of privately managed, third-party-contracted resources operating as an off-grid microgrid, and boosts Black Hills' position in the region. Energy services are projected to begin in late 2027 and ramp up to peak operational load by 2030. At that point, Black Hills projects the deal will deliver $150 million in annual net income and $2.4 billion in unlevered free cash flow through 2048. Under the deal, Black Hills will invest $1.8 billion in capital expenditures to build 564 MW of natural gas power generation between 2027 and 2029. Google provided $399 million in refundable advances for long-lead equipment procurement, which Black Hills plans to reimburse by next year. The move helps Black Hills build on its strong regional position. It operates across eight states, including Wyoming, Colorado, Montana, and South Dakota. Cheyenne, Wyoming, has emerged as a data center hub thanks to favorable regulatory policies, a cool climate, and major grid investments. Wyoming Electric has seen peak electric loads grow over two decades since Black Hills acquired the utility, and its system peak reached a record of 439 MW in July 2026, up 16% from 2025. Black Hills has partnered with Microsoft in Cheyenne for over a decade and continues to build on that collaboration. In April, Microsoft announced it would acquire 3,200 acres in the area for a new data center capacity under the state's Large Power Contract Service (LPCS) tariff. In addition, Meta Platforms is another hyperscaler building a data center in the region, which is scheduled to open in 2027.

The smartwatch business has spent years figuring out what more consumers can accomplish with their wrists. Now, Google is wagering that some customers would want to do less. The new $179.99 Fitbit Edge from Alphabet (GOOGL) subsidiary Google is positioned purposefully between the company's screenless Fitbit Air and its more powerful Pixel Watch 5. Google hasn't gone so far as to make it a complete smartwatch, but it does include a bigger screen, health sensors, integrated GPS tracking, and phone alerts. That compromise is the company's objective. Google says many consumers are looking for something between an advanced smartwatch and the simplicity of a fitness band. The Edge is its answer, offering up to seven days of battery life while still putting workout and health information on a screen. The tracker opened for preorders Oct. 12 and is scheduled to reach stores Oct. 27. However, there are trade-offs associated with Google's middle ground. The Verge claims that the Edge does not include the near-field communication chip required for contactless payments, nor does it have a speaker or microphone for receiving calls from the wrist. Google is essentially asking customers to spend $179.99 for a wearable that is purposefully less competent than a smartwatch. It's a wager that some consumers will see it as a feature rather than a limit. Read more: Google set to challenge Meta Muse in the Agentic AI race With its mechanical side button and 1.34-inch color display, the Edge provides consumers with additional information at a glance without having the Pixel Watch's more extensive software. The device's hardware includes built-in GPS tracking, an altimeter, heart-rate monitoring, blood-oxygen sensors, skin-temperature sensors, and electrical sensors that work with the ECG app, according to Google Store. Battery life could be the more significant differential, but health is still the major concern. The Edge is rated by Google for a maximum of seven days in between charges. A full charge takes around 90 minutes, however, five minutes of charging may extend the battery's useful life by up to one more day. According to The Verge, that estimate drops to around two days when the always-on display is turned on. The Verge states that GPS tracking is around 40% more accurate than automated activity monitoring, which Google claims is twice as precise and covers over 100 activities. These figures contribute to the explanation of why Google did not just convert the Edge into a less expensive Pixel Watch.

Meta’s Two-Track Strategy Is Now Explicit – and the Gap Is the Moat

No summary available

With the October 15, 2026, release of Muse Spark Open, Meta has effectively abandoned the pretense of a singular open-weights philosophy. This move follows the company's earlier shift toward proprietary dominance. The strategy is now explicit: the frontier remains locked behind the closed-source Mus...

With the October 15, 2026, release of Muse Spark Open, Meta has effectively abandoned the pretense of a singular open-weights philosophy. This move follows the company's earlier shift toward proprietary dominance. The strategy is now explicit: the frontier remains locked behind the closed-source Muse Wonder, while the open-weights track is reserved for agent-native and coding-specific workflows. By segmenting its portfolio, Meta is attempting to capture the developer ecosystem without compromising the competitive advantage of its most capable systems. Standardized monetization is becoming the industry norm, as evidenced by the licensing for Spark Open. The Muse Model License imposes a $20M MaaS (Model-as-a-Service) gate over any consecutive 12-month period. This $20M threshold signals a clear industry convergence, aligning Meta with the revenue-gating structures seen in StepFun Model License 1.0 and Mistral's revenue-gated models. Unlike StepFun, however, Meta has omitted a hardware OEM gate, providing slightly more flexibility for cloud-based deployment. The requirement to include the attribution "Built with Muse Spark Open" serves as a persistent marketing tether for the model's usage, reflecting a broader trend in deployment restrictions. Performance defines the strategic moat. Muse Wonder, the closed-source flagship, scores 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. In contrast, Spark Open scores 39. This 17-point gap is the structural barrier that protects Meta's proprietary interests. While Meta's blog describes Spark Open as "the most capable US open-weight model to date," that claim is carefully scoped to the domestic market. When measured against international competitors, the model's limitations become apparent; despite its 816B total parameters, it trails GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44), and Qwen3.8 (40) on the same index, highlighting how pricing and ecosystem have become the primary competitive levers. Data suggests that Spark Open is not a general-purpose intelligence powerhouse. Its architecture – a natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 42B active parameters – is optimized for specific agentic and coding tasks rather than broad reasoning. For enterprise deployers, the question is whether the model's 1M context window and specialized tuning justify its underperformance on general intelligence benchmarks. The reality is that Spark Open is a tool for specific operational pipelines, not a replacement for frontier-grade reasoning.

This story was originally published on Social Media Today. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Social Media Today newsletter. Meta announced three ad updates at its brand building summit on Oct. 15, including Ads Super Burst, which is designed to maximize campaign awareness. In addition, the company launched a new way to measure cumulative brand exposure over time and First Impression Ads, which offers expanded options for Reels trending ads. First, the Ads Super Burst option lets advertisers make the most of their campaign exposure within a short period, allowing brands to get a targeted awareness boost. As explained by Meta: "Most brands have a few moments a year that matter more than the rest. This can be the window around a product launch, timing a campaign to an external event, such as an awards night, or the first weekend of a new sports season. Ads Super Burst lets you book a window of 3 to 24 hours and reach your audience at TV-like scale inside that window, and with category exclusivity available, no other advertiser in your category can book the same window." Essentially, advertisers will be able to secure priority ad placement and get a lot of exposure within their chosen time period. It's a higher-end ad option that comes with higher costs. But it could be a valuable option for brands looking to boost promotions tied into events. Meta is also experimenting with First Impression Ads, which will ensure that advertisers' promotions are in the first ad position in user feeds. "Advertisers have asked us for the first ad position in Feed for years, and we are now testing it in the United States," Meta said. "The first ad someone sees when they open their Feed comes with a kind of prominence no other placement offers. This is an early test, with just one brand per day, but we have heard feedback from advertisers that there is appetite for a product like this." LinkedIn, Snapchat and TikTok offer similar priority exposure options, enabling brands to book prime placement in the feed each day. Meta is also continuing to build out its Reels Trending Ads offering, which allows brands to display their promotions alongside trending Reels content. Meta said there are now 15 standard topics an advertiser can choose from for Reels Trending Ads, "including new categories around Home & Garden and Spanish language content, as well as seasonal lineups built around the moments that pull people together." Meta said it's also expanding its targeting capabilities for this option.

Meta's new teen limits have a loophole parents can't ignore

Every parent learns the same lesson sooner or later: Lock the door, and your teenager finds a window. That has been the quiet weakness of every screen-time fix so far. A limit on one app pushes the scrolling onto the next one, and your family's evenings go with it. For most households, that next a...

Every parent learns the same lesson sooner or later: Lock the door, and your teenager finds a window. That has been the quiet weakness of every screen-time fix so far. A limit on one app pushes the scrolling onto the next one, and your family's evenings go with it. For most households, that next app is easy to name. Roughly nine in 10 U.S. teens use YouTube, and 61% are on TikTok every day, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 1,458 teens published Dec. 9, 2025. In August, Meta Platforms (META) agreed to the toughest teen rules any major social platform has accepted. Facebook and Instagram are set to carry a default two-hour daily cap for users under 18 and a block on the apps between midnight and 6 a.m. Meta itself has said teens who hit a limit on one app simply move to another. Now a group of family advocates wants the window closed too. The American Principles Project (APP), a national pro-family advocacy group, sent a coalition letter urging TikTok, Snapchat, and Alphabet's (GOOGL) YouTube to match Meta's protections, according to a statement from the group obtained by FOX Business. The letter asks the three platforms to voluntarily adopt the same safeguards Meta accepted, at least until broader federal protections arrive, FOX Business reported on Oct. 13. That list covers daily time limits, quiet hours during school and overnight, parental control over algorithmic feeds and autoplay, hidden likes by default and age verification. The group's pitch is about leakage. If Instagram cuts your teen off at two hours, nothing stops the next two hours from landing on TikTok. Read more: Zuckerberg says Meta's AI bet only fails if all AI fails "A standard has been set, and the challenge issued. The stakes could not be higher," the APP letter states. The signers argue that "an industry-wide standard will do far more for our children than adjustments to a handful of apps." APP said the letter was signed by leaders including: Penny Nance, CEO and president of Concerned Women for America LAC Craig DeRoche, president and CEO of Family Policy Alliance Jordan Sekulow, president and CEO of ACLJ Action Casey Stefanski, executive director of Digital Childhood Alliance Matthew Mehan, associate dean at Hillsdale College's Van Andel Graduate School of Government 88 other signers APP President Terry Schilling, a father of eight, framed it as a parent's problem first. "I am playing serious defense here, and we need a lot more help," he told FOX Business.

(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc. made one of its new artificial intelligence models available for developers to download and modify, while keeping its most advanced technology closed in an effort to convert its AI investments into revenue. Most Read from Bloomberg CoreWeave's Big Dream Crashes I...

(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc. made one of its new artificial intelligence models available for developers to download and modify, while keeping its most advanced technology closed in an effort to convert its AI investments into revenue. Most Read from Bloomberg CoreWeave's Big Dream Crashes Into Reality as Yields Top 15% S&P 500 Bounces as Traders Buy Non-Chip Stocks: Markets Wrap China's Unloading of US Bonds Gets Fresh Look as Skeptics Grow Anduril in Talks to Sell Insider Shares at Roughly $90 Billion Valuation Anthropic Revenue Jumps to $16.8 Billion in Quarter Before IPO On Thursday, Meta announced it's releasing the "weights" — the settings that allow developers to run and adapt a model themselves — to Muse Spark Open. According to Meta, this model, which is designed for coding and to support AI agents, is less advanced than Muse Wonder, which it debuted earlier this week. Releasing a less-advanced open-weight model fulfills a prior Meta commitment to make its technology widely available. "Because of both safety and capabilities, we will generally not open-source our most powerful models," Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang said in an interview. "But we do think it is important over time to keep open-sourcing great models and we intend to keep doing so." Chinese companies, including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and DeepSeek, have had great success in developing open-source AI models that developers can tweak. Their fast adoption, including in the US, has further intensified the technological rivalry between the two countries. Meta Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg had long championed making AI models and their building blocks open to the developer community. But last year, after the company's open-weight Llama models disappointed Silicon Valley, Zuckerberg overhauled Meta's AI organization and brought in Wang, who has since helped develop a series of more capable but closed models. Wang said he believes it's important for American companies to release open-weight models to ensure their dominance over China in the fast-moving AI race. "Most of the world's AI will run on open models," he said. "They should be American." At the same time, he said he expects Chinese-based AI developers to learn from and build upon Muse Spark Open. "It might even be good if Chinese models adopt some of our principals into their models," he said. The release of Muse Spark Open also comes as Meta works to stand up its own cloud business, where it would sell access to AI models and computing infrastructure. Wang said giving Muse Spark Open away for free won't undercut that effort. Instead, he sees it as a funnel where developers can experiment on their own, and then pay Meta for additional tools when they need more computing power.

Meta Platforms' (META) advanced personal artificial intelligence assistant Muse has seen positive reception, and investors look forward to understanding its return on interest, Oppenheimer said in a Wednesday note. As of Oct. 13, Muse reached around 10.8 million cumulative downloads, with US downlo...

Meta Platforms' (META) advanced personal artificial intelligence assistant Muse has seen positive reception, and investors look forward to understanding its return on interest, Oppenheimer said in a Wednesday note. As of Oct. 13, Muse reached around 10.8 million cumulative downloads, with US downloads steady at 350,000 per day since the start of the month, UBS analysts said. They added that the AI assistant has also held down the top spot on the iOS App Store since Sept. 28, citing Apptopia. However, the analysts estimate that Muse has an annual cost of $14 to $35 per user, citing data from SemiAnalysis, meaning roughly $30 billion per year for 100 million users at the midpoint. To add 15% to the 2028 consensus estimate for earnings before interest and taxes, Muse should generate around $960 billion of gross merchandise value at a 5% take rate, or attain 96 million paying subscribers at an 80% margin, according to the note. Muse usage would also provide data for targeted advertising, but the upside is hard to quantify, the analysts said. Although Meta gives formal guidance on expenses in Q4, the analysts expect detailed commentary on Muse expenses in the upcoming earnings call, which should lead to an EPS estimate reset. Meta will release its Q3 financial results after market-close on Oct. 21. Oppenheimer's rating on the company's stock is perform.

After a two-week delay, the Tesla (TSLA) Roadster event went off with a massive bang — a flying one. The wedge-shaped, cyberpunk-looking Roadster EV appeared in front of an inverted half roller coaster ramp erected at SpaceX's facility in Waco, Texas. The Roadster cruised halfway up — glued to the ramp using a vacuum fan system — then launched off the ramp upside down and performed flips in the air, using air thrusters to right itself and land on the tarmac. Tesla stock rose as much as 5.4% during premarket trading on Friday following the Roadster event. Then the Roadster performed a similar stunt, jumping over several Teslas (including a semi), inverted itself, and then used its thrusters to land — an automaker first. "Well, it worked," CEO Elon Musk deadpanned. The Roadster also went 0-60 mph in less than 1 second (0.81 seconds) during a test Tesla conducted at the event. While Tesla claimed the car could hit a top speed of 230 mph, Musk boasted that the production version could target half the speed of sound, or Mach 0.5 (383 mph). So when can you expect to get one? "We enter production in 2028," Musk said. Tesla said the car comes in three configurations: Performance: road-ready, seats 2, with multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off track; Thrust: race-ready, seats 2, with multi-mode suction system and rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable 0–60 in <1 second Rocket: air-ready, seats 1, with multi-mode suction system, plus perimeter-mounted cold-gas thrusters for forward, upward acceleration and lateral rotational movement. So ... yes, it can fly. Tesla said the three versions had a range exceeding 300 miles, with a top speed of up to 230 mph for the Rocket version. Officially, in terms of performance, 0- 60 mph across the range is <1.6 seconds for Performance, <0.9 seconds for Thrust, and <0.59 seconds for Rocket. No word yet on how the Rocket version, with its thrusters that allow short flights, would be allowed on public roads. The event came two weeks after the initial Oct. 1 reveal date. Tesla said the reveal was pushed back due to weather conditions at the demo site, SpaceX's (SPCX) Rocket Development and Testing facility in Waco, Texas. Tesla is asking prospective buyers to put down a $5,000 deposit, followed by a $45,000 wire transfer due within 10 days of the initial deposit. Tesla has not said how much the new Roadster will cost, though it is expected to exceed $250,000. Tesla bull Gene Munster of Deepwater Management had two big takeaways from tonight's Roadster event. "1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can't wait to bring Tesla and SpaceX together," he posted on X.com.

Happy Friday! We have flying cars now. Here's a closer look at Tesla's SpaceX-powered Roadster.

Will SpaceX merge with Tesla? Speculation resurfaces it could happen before the end of 2026.

No summary available

The steady drip of Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) merger talk is increasing, and this time it's coming from a Wall Street bank. In a note to clients on Wednesday, Barclays analyst Dan Levy said a tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." He pointed to media reports and to Elon Mus...

The steady drip of Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) merger talk is increasing, and this time it's coming from a Wall Street bank. In a note to clients on Wednesday, Barclays analyst Dan Levy said a tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." He pointed to media reports and to Elon Musk's own public hints. For now, though, it's still speculation. Tesla and SpaceX stock were both higher in Friday's premarket trading. Timing was the most notable part of Levy's note. Tesla must hold its annual general meeting [AGM] by Dec. 6, per SEC rules, and Levy and Barclays believe that this would be the appropriate avenue for shareholders to vote on a proposal. Levy said a merger announcement that slips later into October or early November "may increasingly challenge merger approval as part of the AGM." In that case, a deal wouldn't be dead, but may come instead in the next six to 12 months, since investors see an advantage in closing any deal under the Trump administration's friendly M&A environment. Levy argues AI vertical integration would be a key component of the merger. Tesla's physical AI, such as Robotaxi and Optimus, would be paired with SpaceX's virtual AI, such as Grok, all supplied by the companies' planned Terafab chip plant. Right now, Terafab decisions need approval from both boards, a process Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said would take "a while." Musk's shareholding in the two companies illustrates how a merger would unfold. Musk owns around 20% of Tesla, compared with about 48% of SpaceX. SpaceX super-voting Class B shares give him around 82% of the vote. SpaceX is worth about $2.1 trillion and Tesla about $1.5 trillion. If SpaceX bought Tesla at those values, Musk would own about 37% of the combined company and control 56% of the vote, Levy said. That's well above the 25% Tesla stake he has long said he wants. Warren Buffett spent nearly 60 years at Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) buying businesses with durable competitive advantages, strong cash flow, and capable management teams. Now, Berkshire is doubling down on an unfamiliar technology company that went public just three months ago. On Oct. 14, a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) revealed that Berkshire is investing $330 million in Bending Spoons (NASDAQ: BSP). This follows a $600 million investment during the company's initial public offering (IPO) in July. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Continue » What makes this investment interesting isn't simply Berkshire's involvement. It's how closely Bending Spoons' business model resembles Buffett's own investment philosophy. Despite its unconventional name, Bending Spoons operates a straightforward business. The company acquires other businesses, improves their operations, and uses the resulting profits to fund additional acquisitions. Its portfolio includes AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite, and Airtable. I like to think of Bending Spoons as a technology-focused version of Berkshire Hathaway. Instead of buying insurance companies, railroads, and utilities, Bending Spoons acquires software platforms, digital media properties, and subscription businesses. Although these businesses serve different markets than Berkshire's portfolio, they share several characteristics: recognizable brands, established customer bases, recurring revenue, and opportunities to improve profitability. Over time, this strategy can create a powerful compounding cycle. Unlike traditional private equity firms, which typically acquire businesses intending to sell them, Bending Spoons has never sold a material business. That philosophy should resonate with Berkshire shareholders. Buffett favors businesses he can understand, particularly those generating reliable cash flow without requiring constant product reinvention. Although Berkshire eventually became a major shareholder in Apple and Alphabet, its portfolio has historically been less focused on technology companies than that of other institutional investors. Bending Spoons offers a unique value proposition. Rather than speculating that one software product will become the next blockbuster, Berkshire is investing in a management team that specializes in capital allocation. This is financial jargon for the process of deciding where a company's money should go to generate the highest long-term returns. It's also one of the defining characteristics of Berkshire's track record.

If you've been a longtime fan and follower of Berkshire Hathaway's (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) former chief stock-picker Warren Buffett, then you know he's steered clear of technology stocks, arguing they're too difficult to understand. That is, until somewhat recently. Berkshire took on a small (now-exited) position in Amazon back in 2019, and of course, Apple has grown to become the conglomerate's single-biggest equity holding since first stepping into it back in 2016. It's not clear to what extent these were Buffett-directed trades, and to be fair, both companies are as much consumer-oriented as they are technology names, making their businesses at least somewhat easier to understand. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. Continue » If there was any doubt that Warren Buffett has officially warmed up to tech stocks, though, it's been wiped away this year by Berkshire's entry into a sizable stake in Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL). It wasn't clear to what extent Warren Buffett had a hand in the matter when Berkshire first scooped up 17.8 million A shares of Alphabet in Q3 of 2025. By then, the Oracle of Omaha had already announced his then-impending retirement as CEO at the end of that same year, and seemed more interested in cleaning up some loose ends rather than adding new stocks to the company's portfolio. Besides, it was only about a $5 billion stake at the time, suggesting perhaps that he'd merely allowed one of his lieutenants to take on a token position. That changed dramatically in the first quarter of this year, however, when Berkshire bought another 36.4 million A shares of Alphabet, and then 24.5 million in Q2. Paired with the 27.2 million C shares of Alphabet purchased this year, this $37.4 billion (combined) holding accounts for a little over 10% of Berkshire Hathaway's $358 billion stock portfolio, making it the conglomerate's third-biggest holding. The kicker: This was largely Buffett's idea after all. Although he still consults with current CEO Greg Abel on such matters, in an interview with CNBC this July, Warren Buffett plainly explained: "I initiated it." This still doesn't mean Berkshire is embracing all technology stocks. As Buffett said in the very same interview, "I would say that I don't like it as well as at least four or five other businesses that we own."

Most Read from Bloomberg Stock Buyers Step In to Power Wall Street Rebound: Markets Wrap China's Unloading of US Bonds Gets Fresh Look as Skeptics Grow CoreWeave's Big Dream Crashes Into Reality as Yields Top 15% Anduril in Talks to Sell Insider Shares at Roughly $90 Billion Valuation Anthropic Revenue Jumps to $16.8 Billion in Quarter Before IPO The banks have been marketing the offering for Volta, an AI cloud startup, since last week and sold it on Thursday at 6.5 percentage points above the benchmark rate and a discounted price of 95 cents on the dollar, according to people with knowledge of the matter. That price point pushed yields up past the 11% that banks had earlier floated, rivaling the highest rates paid so far to finance the AI buildout. Click here for Bloomberg News' AI Debt Tracker The deal also offered greater investor protections, and included structural changes that would require the borrower to pay a penalty if the debt is repaid early, one of the people said, asking not to be identified because they're not authorized to speak publicly. A representative for JPMorgan declined to comment, while those for Goldman Sachs and Volta didn't respond to requests for comment. Volta is among a group of AI companies known as neoclouds, which rent access to chips and other AI infrastructure. The company's deal will be used to finance a data center complex in Norway that will be managed by Volta Infrastructure in partnership with Bitdeer Technologies Group, a Bitcoin miner that operates data centers. Anthropic PBC has already signed a six-year agreement for compute capacity at the site, Bloomberg previously reported, citing people familiar with the agreement. The loan sale immediately rankled managers of collateralized loan obligations — the biggest buyers of leveraged loans — for a number of reasons. For one, it's unrated, which makes it harder for CLOs to buy the debt. But on top of that, it's a large transaction from a debut borrower tapping the market at a volatile time. Among other changes, the interest rate on the debt will change if Volta gets certain ratings, the person added. The debt is split into two parts: a $1.3 billion term loan and a $3.7 billion chip loan. The transaction was initially pitched at spreads in the range of 6.25 to 6.5 percentage points above the benchmark rate, and a discounted price of 97 to 98 cents on the dollar.

‘You don’t want rogue agents’: Jamie Dimon bars outside AI agents like Meta’s Muse from JPMorgan accounts

On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank is blocking outside AI agents from logging in to or acting on customer accounts, citing security...

Just as Big Tech is rolling out agents meant to help with your finances, banks are drawing a line at AI agents accessing your account information. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank is blocking outside AI agents from logging in to or acting on customer accounts, citing security risks from "rogue agents." "We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon said during the bank's third-quarter earnings call. "You don't want rogue agents." He warned that AI tools create new risks for banks and their customers, particularly when more people turn to these agents capable of performing tasks on their behalf. "Protecting our customers is our top priority," a JPMorgan spokesperson told Fortune. "When we detect a third-party agent attempting to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials, we do not allow it. We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers." The bank's concerns come in the wake of several security incidents involving "rogue" AI agents. Dimon's remarks keep JPMorgan's massive balance sheet in mind. According to its third-quarter earnings release filed with the SEC, the bank reported $15.3 billion in net income—with $1.6 trillion in average loans and $1.5 trillion in cash and marketable securities. It had $5.1 trillion in total assets as of Sept. 30. "We have to make sure we protect our customer in the right kind of way," Dimon said. "So we're building tools to do that, too." A Cloud Security Alliance research note last month found that the risks of AI agents extend beyond controlled testing. The note summarized a cybercrime campaign in which three open-source AI agents allegedly worked together to breach at least 27 organizations and take more than 600,000 credit card records from two of them. "Enterprises should incorporate agentic AI attack scenarios into their threat models for retail and payment infrastructure specifically," the note read, "rather than treating agentic AI risk as a generic or future-facing concern, given that this campaign demonstrates the capability is already commoditized and in active use against the retail sector." But AI agents managing user finances isn't new. In August, the German bank Scalable Capital opened its platform to AI models like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, letting users analyze portfolios, set up savings plans, and place trades through prompts. Users had to approve trades, and the assistants couldn't make payments or withdraw money.

This story was originally published on Banking Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Banking Dive newsletter. Really, let's keep debanking in the news. Hours before the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency published a 47-page report detailing nine banks' missteps with regard to alleged wrongful account closures, the largest of those banks urged a federal court to throw out a lawsuit brought by the debanked-in-chief. Lawyers for JPMorgan Chase argued Tuesday that President Donald Trump's claims against the bank would "fail – multiple times over – and should be dismissed with prejudice." Trump sued JPMorgan and its CEO, Jamie Dimon, in a Florida court in January, accusing the bank of trade libel and breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Trump also accused Dimon of violating Florida's unfair and deceptive trade practices act by directing JPMorgan to put the plaintiffs on a "blacklist," which allegedly was "published" to other, unnamed banks. JPMorgan's lawyers in February argued the plaintiffs "do not explain what this 'blacklist' entails, when it was created, to whom it was supposedly circulated, or any other detail describing it. "If and when Plaintiffs explain what they mean by this 'blacklist,' JPMorgan will respond accordingly," the bank's lawyers wrote at the time. Now that the case has moved to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, JPMorgan's lawyers are amplifying their stance. "Plaintiffs' allegations regarding the alleged 'blacklist' are so bare that it is impossible to determine what JPMorgan allegedly stated, when, or to whom," the bank's lawyers wrote Tuesday. JPMorgan's lawyers explicitly denied allegations that the bank closed Trump-tied accounts for political reasons or placed them on such a list. One of Trump's personal accounts with JPMorgan remains, the bank argued, adding that several plaintiffs have opened new accounts with JPMorgan. "Moreover, as far as Defendants can tell, no 'blacklist' matching the Complaint's description exists, which is why Plaintiffs cannot identify one," JPMorgan's lawyers wrote. "However, at this stage, the Court need not weigh the veracity of Plaintiffs' allegations, nor accept Plaintiffs' invitation to engage in a policy debate on access to banking. Under well-settled law, even treating Plaintiffs' allegations as true, those allegations fail to state any claim cognizable at law." The bank acknowledged the account agreements the plaintiffs signed "expressly allowed the Bank to close their accounts for any reason (or no reason at all)."

Wall Street’s earnings split: Goldman’s $18.7 billion blowout quarter—and why JPMorgan and BofA fell short

For Wall Street banks reporting earnings this week, it was largely a hit—or, for two big names, a stunning miss. Goldman Sachs gave investors exactly what they wanted, while JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America gave them reason to flinch. JPMorgan set the tone early Tuesday morning. For the first tim...

For Wall Street banks reporting earnings this week, it was largely a hit—or, for two big names, a stunning miss. Goldman Sachs gave investors exactly what they wanted, while JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America gave them reason to flinch. JPMorgan set the tone early Tuesday morning. For the first time in nearly three years, the nation's largest bank by assets and market capitalization—about $888.1 billion—fell short of expectations on both profit and revenue. JPMorgan reported $50.17 billion in net revenue, below the $51.22 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share came in at $5.57 versus $5.90, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. The company's earnings were weighed down by a slump in fixed-income trading and higher expenses. Fixed-income trading revenue fell 4% year over year to $5.4 billion—about $550 million below expectations. JPMorgan's noninterest expenses were $90 million higher than estimates as costs jumped 12% over the past year. All in, revenue rose by only 8%, a significant decline from the 27% increase in the second quarter. Still, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said in a statement that the bank reported "another quarter of strong results." He did not directly address the earnings miss, but said investment banking activity "moderate[d] somewhat during the quarter." On a call with reporters, JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum described the bank's dealmaking pipeline as "very, very strong." JPMorgan was not the only bank to disappoint investors, though. Bank of America missed earnings expectations on Wednesday, snapping a six-quarter beat streak. Profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents per share, in the third quarter. Revenue was also below analysts' estimates by roughly $570 million. The results came just a day after regulators announced a $1.2 billion penalty on Bank of America, alleging that management failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions. The penalty added to the pressure of an already lackluster quarter. One other laggard—albeit less surprising than JPMorgan or Bank of America—was Wells Fargo. The bank missed on revenue despite surpassing earnings estimates, reporting revenue of $21.87 billion, below the $22.31 billion consensus. It was the third time in the past four quarters that Wells came up short on the top line. Then there was Goldman Sachs' blowout quarter. No summary available

While companies across the world are embracing artificial intelligence (AI) at a rapid pace, JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon has issued a blunt warning on AI agents. Dimon said he won't allow "rogue" AI agents from outside to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf. Related...

While companies across the world are embracing artificial intelligence (AI) at a rapid pace, JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon has issued a blunt warning on AI agents. Dimon said he won't allow "rogue" AI agents from outside to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf. Related: JPMorgan issues stark warning on 2026's most crowded trade Unlike AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT, an AI agent can make decisions, pursue goals, and take actions on a user's behalf. For instance, Muse, the AI agent developed by Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms (Nasdaq: META), can not only browse the web and generate documents and images, but it can also shop on the user's behalf. But Dimon told analysts on the bank's Q3 earnings call yesterday that the Wall Street giant won't allow any outside agent because it's "just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan." "You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," Dimon said. "If data is being misused, they should understand it's being misused." If the bank's customers allow outside AI agents to act on their behalf, they should appreciate the risks and understand there's a liability transfer, Dimon said. In short, the world's largest bank by market capitalization, is against letting outside AI agents transfer funds or pay a bill on a customer's behalf. It doesn't mean the bank isn't exploring the technology at all. In fact, Dimon revealed that JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing apps. The Wall Street bank has recently begun a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, CFO Jeremy Barnum said during the earnings call yesterday. The approach isn't pro or anti-AI agents but about ensuring safe customer service, Dimon said. AI agents are tools that can be used for customers but they shouldn't hurt the bank's customers, he added. Morgan Stanley's new lab to test Wall Street's future IMF ranks Ondo among largest tokenized asset issuers JPMorgan says one asset class could soon beat gold This isn't the first time Dimon has stuck his neck out. He is among the banking industry titans who opposed the provision regarding stablecoin rewards in the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. The most comprehensive regulatory legislation for cryptocurrencies in the U.S. so far, the CLARITY Act aims to resolve jurisdictional disputes between the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

National Cybersecurity Awareness Month event equips consumers, students and small business owners with practical steps to spot AI-enabled scams and protect their money and personal information WASHINGTON, October 14, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Chase today brought practical fraud and cybersecurity guidance to communities nationwide through a live event streamed to approximately 700 branches, helping individuals, families, students and small business owners recognize increasingly convincing AI-enabled scams and take immediate steps to protect themselves. The event reflects Chase's continued expansion of in-branch and digital education and builds on the firm's longstanding work to help consumers navigate fraud and scams through education, awareness and community-based programming. Through its financial health initiatives, the firm has served more than 1 million customers and continues to host more than 1,000 fraud and scam prevention workshops annually across the country. Hosted at JPMorganChase's Mid-Atlantic Regional Headquarters in Washington, D.C., the event focused on three priorities: spotting AI-enabled impersonation and money-movement scams, strengthening everyday cyber defenses, and protecting personal and financial information when using AI tools. The panel brought together Michelle Singletary, personal finance columnist for The Washington Post; Pat Opet, Global Chief Information Security Officer at JPMorganChase; and Brett Leatherman, FBI Assistant Director, Cyber Division; and was moderated by Darius Kingsley, Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention at Chase. "AI is making scams harder to spot, but the best response is still simple: slow down, verify the request using a contact you trust and report anything suspicious," Kingsley said. Raising The Stakes for American Households and Businesses Scams are hitting Americans at record levels, affecting more than 15 million people last year and driving at least $68 billion in reported losses. Because these crimes are chronically underreported, the true toll may be as high as $200 billion. Chase Consumer Bank CEO Jennifer Roberts has called for a coordinated response across government, industry, nonprofits and law enforcement at every stage of the scam lifecycle. The discussion was designed to support that full lifecycle approach, pairing law enforcement perspective on criminal tactics with industry expertise on prevention — so consumers can recognize red flags earlier and stop scams before money moves.
