Visa Direct moves stablecoin payments into commercial deployment

No summary available

Visa has moved its stablecoin-enabled money movement service from pilot testing to commercial deployment through Visa Direct. As part of the initial rollout, payments infrastructure provider Inyo Global became the first enabler to launch the service for eligible Visa Direct clients and partners. I...

Visa has moved its stablecoin-enabled money movement service from pilot testing to commercial deployment through Visa Direct. As part of the initial rollout, payments infrastructure provider Inyo Global became the first enabler to launch the service for eligible Visa Direct clients and partners. In a statement, Visa described the move as an "important step" toward bringing stablecoin-enabled money movement into commercial operations. The rollout follows a year of work by Visa Direct with clients and partners to assess how stablecoins could support the funding and movement of money across borders. Through the new service, businesses using Inyo Global's platform can prefund cross-border payouts through Visa Direct with USDC in near real time. The capability provides an alternative to traditional funding windows. Inyo Global provides payments infrastructure for money transmitters, fintech companies, banks, and other payment businesses. Its platform will support user onboarding, fraud management, compliance, payment acceptance, and domestic and international payouts across more than 180 countries through Visa Direct. Visa Direct global head Vira Platonova said: "Over the last several years, we've worked with several partners and clients to explore how these technologies can improve money movement. "We're now seeing those efforts translate into live implementations, helping businesses access more flexible and efficient ways to fund and move money globally through Visa Direct, starting with Inyo Global as our first enabler." Inyo Global co-founder and chief product and technology officer Robson Dantas said: "Innovation in money movement is ultimately about creating a better experience for customers, and that's exactly our focus at Inyo. "By integrating Visa Direct's stablecoin-enabled prefunding into the Inyo platform, we're giving the money transmitters, fintechs and payment companies we serve a new way to fund their payouts, one that is available around the clock and runs through the same Inyo APIs they already use." The partnership forms part of Visa's broader initiative to connect traditional payment rails with blockchain-based networks. Earlier this month, digital asset platform Gate partnered with Visa to introduce a cryptocurrency-linked payment card across more than 40 countries. "Visa Direct moves stablecoin payments into commercial deployment" was originally created and published by Electronic Payments International, a GlobalData owned brand.

It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma. The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting. The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management. Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass, a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization's employees build so others can take advantage of the company's collective knowledge and skills. Barclaycard Payments has integrated Visa's Unified Checkout technology into its Smartpay Fuse payment gateway. According to Visa, the rollout simplifies payment acceptance for merchants in the UK and help them "improve ecommerce conversion." Through the integration, merchants can accept payments from credit and debit cards, Click to Pay, and digital wallets. The interface also supports non-card alternatives, including Pay by Link and digital invoicing. Built on a modular application programming interface (API) architecture, the low-code deployment allows businesses to add payment methods without extensive changes to their underlying technical infrastructure. The setup is also designed to deliver "more consistent customer journeys" across sales channels and reduce checkout friction. The agreement builds on a long-term partnership between Visa and Barclaycard covering payment processing and merchant acquiring services. Commenting on the rollout, Visa UK & Ireland Value Added Services head Dan Parsons said: "As payments evolve, we want to make it easier for merchants to tap into new innovation without having to rebuild their checkout each time. "Our Unified Checkout solution helps acquirers and their merchants offer payments to everyone, everywhere with ease. Together with Barclaycard Payments, we're supporting merchants to futureproof their checkout by giving them access to what's next as it happens." Barclaycard Payments Mid-Corporate head Ben Stagg said: "By bringing Visa's Unified Checkout solution into Smartpay Fuse, we're helping merchants through streamlined processes to simplify payment acceptance through a single, future-ready integration that strengthens security, improves visibility and adapts to evolving customer expectations. "By combining multiple payment experiences into one solution, we're enabling businesses to deliver more seamless customer journeys, unlock growth opportunities and focus on what matters most, while reinforcing Barclaycard Payments' commitment to being a trusted partner that helps merchants grow with confidence." The integration follows broader digital asset and payment pilots across Visa's UK network. Recently, Lloyds Banking Group, in partnership with Visa, completed a live pilot testing stablecoin-based settlement for cross-border transactions. The Limit Is Moving Into the Credential. The Liability Isn’t.

No summary available

Two weeks of competing architectures in agentic commerce now share one move: putting the spending limit inside the payment instrument itself. American Express's Intent Intelligence Framework, unveiled at TechCrunch Disrupt, issues a scoped payment credential derived from an intent token that carries...

Two weeks of competing architectures in agentic commerce now share one move: putting the spending limit inside the payment instrument itself. American Express's Intent Intelligence Framework, unveiled at TechCrunch Disrupt, issues a scoped payment credential derived from an intent token that carries the buyer's merchant, maximum budget, and preferences. If the agent deviates, the credential fails to validate before the transaction reaches the rails. Crossmint's Agent Commerce Toolkit, announced a week earlier, runs the same instinct one layer down: for eligible cards, it issues "scoped virtual cards with expiration dates and spend limits" through Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay. Spend limit, enforced in the instrument, at the card network rather than the issuer. That is two of the three legs. Ripple and Privy's programmable wallets on the XRP Ledger, announced the same day as the Amex framework, offer agents their own accounts and their own funds. The idea is the furthest of the three from the merchant-of-record model: if agents hold their own wallets, they do not need permission from any checkout surface. But the specific capability the other two have shipped, "policy controls for spend limits and gas sponsorship," the Privy blog calls "in development but not yet generally available." On the spend-limit question, the L1 position is a roadmap item, not a shipped control. The credential-layer approach is real control. A limit that lives inside the instrument rather than in terms of service has a mechanical advantage: it fails closed rather than relying on someone reading a policy afterward. Crossmint's own account puts it plainly: the credential layer is real control, a spend limit enforced in the instrument. That is the same instinct as Amex's budget-carrying intent token, enforced one layer down, at the card network rather than the issuer. But the control is scoped to the credential that carries it. Crossmint's toolkit runs three mechanisms and the one that does the least is the fallback for cards that are not eligible for network tokenization: a PCI-compliant vault where the purchase completes without the spend-limit scoping. Amex's framework is explicit that it shifts evidence for dispute adjudication, not the underlying loss default: issuers can "evaluate subsequent disputes against the intent confirmed by the cardholder." The limit covers what the limit covers and nothing else.

Can American Express Turn AI Commerce Into a New Growth Driver?

No summary available

American Express Company AXP is advancing its AI-powered payment strategy with its new Intent Intelligence framework. The framework captures and authenticates customers' purchase instructions and spending limits before AI agents complete transactions, helping ensure purchases align with customer aut...

American Express Company AXP is advancing its AI-powered payment strategy with its new Intent Intelligence framework. The framework captures and authenticates customers' purchase instructions and spending limits before AI agents complete transactions, helping ensure purchases align with customer authorization. The framework uses an Intent ID and a Proof of Intent Token to preserve purchase intent throughout the transaction process. The token can also enable secure payment credentials, allowing AI agents to transact without using customers' actual card numbers. These controls could strengthen fraud prevention, improve authorization decisions and streamline dispute resolution. AmEx has made the framework available through its Agentic Commerce Experiences (ACE) Developer Kit and is collaborating with industry groups to advance common standards. The initiative comes as AI agents take on a larger role in shopping and payments. By embedding security and customer control into transactions, AmEx could strengthen cardholder trust and encourage adoption. Its position as both a card issuer and payment network could provide an advantage in connecting customers, merchants and AI platforms. However, the framework's commercial impact will depend on ecosystem adoption and transaction growth. Financially, broader adoption could support payment volumes and associated revenues while lowering fraud- and dispute-related costs. Although these benefits remain uncertain, the framework could reinforce AmEx's competitive position, strengthen customer loyalty and create incremental growth opportunities as AI-driven commerce expands. American Express faces intense competition in the payments space from Mastercard Incorporated MA and Visa Inc. V. Mastercard's Verifiable Intent framework, developed with Google, aims to establish tamper-resistant proof that AI agents act within customer-approved limits. Its planned integration into Mastercard Agent Pay's intent APIs could strengthen transaction security, improve accountability and support the expansion of AI-driven payment flows. Visa's Intelligent Commerce initiatives could help it capture additional payment volumes as AI agents handle more shopping activities. Its Trusted Agent Protocol verifies legitimate AI agents, while tokenization helps secure transactions. Wider adoption among merchants and AI platforms could strengthen Visa's position in the emerging agentic commerce market.

Visa lowers interchange fees for tens of thousands of small businesses, but new credit card fees are on the horizon

No summary available

TORONTO, Oct. 14, 2026 /CNW/ -- More small businesses will pay lower credit card processing fees when new Visa interchange rates take effect on October 24, says the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB). Small businesses pay interchange fees every time a customer pays by credit card. T...

TORONTO, Oct. 14, 2026 /CNW/ -- More small businesses will pay lower credit card processing fees when new Visa interchange rates take effect on October 24, says the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB). Small businesses pay interchange fees every time a customer pays by credit card. These fees go to the bank that issued the customer's card and are levied as a percentage of each sale. In an agreement with the federal government that took effect in 2024, Visa and Mastercard significantly lowered interchange fees for small businesses with sales under $300,000 for Visa and $175,000 for Mastercard. Visa is expanding its small merchant interchange rate to firms with up to $750,000 in annual Visa sales and lowering rates for all qualifying businesses. Mastercard is not expanding its small merchant program, and its threshold remains at $175,000. "This is a big win for many small businesses that will now qualify for Visa's special, lower interchange rate. The additional businesses that now qualify for the small merchant program will save thousands each year," said Dan Kelly, CFIB president. "Sadly, there are new credit card processing fees on the horizon as well," Kelly added. Visa has announced plans to join Mastercard in assessing a new 1.8-cent USD fee on all domestic transactions. Mastercard will expand this fee to all transactions starting this week and Visa intends to levy the exact same amount starting in April 2027. These fees are first charged to card processors but are routinely passed on to small merchants. "After reducing credit card interchange fee revenue that goes to the bank, it is disappointing to see Visa and Mastercard increase their own slice of the payment fees that may end up being paid by small businesses," noted Corinne Pohlmann, CFIB's executive vice-president of advocacy. CFIB continues to put pressure on the government and payments industry to expand the program of lower small business rates to additional credit card providers, regularly review size thresholds, and ensure that the cost savings are fully passed on to merchants. "For two decades, CFIB has been pushing for fairer credit card fees for small businesses. We're glad to see Visa include more small merchants, and we are calling on Mastercard and other card brands to do the same," said Pohlmann. For more information on CFIB's work to reduce credit card fees for small businesses, visit cfib.ca/credit-cards. About CFIB The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) is Canada's largest association of small and medium-sized businesses with 103,000 members across every industry and region. CFIB is dedicated to increasing business owners' chances of success by driving policy change at all levels of government, providing expert advice and tools, and negotiating exclusive savings. Learn more at cfib.ca. View original content to download multimedia: http://www.newswire.ca/en/releases/archive/October2026/14/c4624.html

Prove Unveils The Trust 25, Recognizing Leaders From Uber, Citi, PayPal, Visa, and 20+ Other Organizations Solving the Hardest Problems in Digital Identity

No summary available

Honorees span banking, payments, gaming, and technology, reflecting the breadth of industries now confronting AI-driven fraud, authentication, and the rise of AI agents NEW YORK, October 14, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Prove, the leader in digital identity, today announced The Trust 25, a new industry r...

Honorees span banking, payments, gaming, and technology, reflecting the breadth of industries now confronting AI-driven fraud, authentication, and the rise of AI agents NEW YORK, October 14, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Prove, the leader in digital identity, today announced The Trust 25, a new industry recognition program honoring 25 executives who are redefining how businesses establish trust in an increasingly AI-driven world. The inaugural class draws from a wide swath of the economy including global banks, payment networks, e-commerce marketplaces, gaming platforms, and technology companies, underscoring how identity, fraud, and authentication have become board-level priorities across every sector. Honorees were selected from hundreds of nominations by an independent panel of industry experts, who evaluated each leader's impact, innovation, and contributions to advancing trust in the digital economy. The final list spans five categories: Identity, Payments, Customer Experience, Agentic Commerce, and Fraud & Compliance. "These leaders are defining what trust looks like in a world where AI is changing how people interact and transact online," said Rodger Desai, Co-Founder and CEO of Prove. "As it becomes harder to know who or what is on the other side of a digital interaction, identity becomes even more foundational. The Trust 25 recognizes the people building the systems, standards, and strategies that will make trusted digital relationships possible in this next era." The Trust 25: Recognizing Leaders Across Digital Identity, Payments, Fraud, and AI The Trust 25 honorees represent organizations including Uber, Amazon, Citi, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, TD, PayPal, Visa, Stripe, eBay, FanDuel Group, Fanatics Betting and Gaming, Synchrony Financial, AvidXchange, Care.com, and others illustrating that the challenge of establishing digital trust is no longer confined to financial services alone. Across every category, honorees are addressing the identity trust challenges of the AI era: Identity executives are architecting systems where verification is not a single event but a continuous, adaptive process that persists across the customer relationship. Payments innovators are rethinking authentication as money moves faster and increasingly without a human directly initiating the transaction. Customer Experience leaders are proving that security and seamless design are not in tension, using identity signals to reduce friction for trusted users while targeting it precisely where risk exists. Agentic Commerce pioneers are building the standards and infrastructure needed to let AI agents shop, pay, and act on consumers' behalf without surrendering control, consent, or accountability. Fraud & Compliance leaders are moving beyond static rules toward real-time, layered signals that can detect AI-generated impersonation and social engineering without penalizing legitimate customers.

But the company under Buffett, and his successor, Greg Abel, isn't afraid to make big moves. Berkshire closed several positions in its portfolio this year, including selling its entire stake in credit card giants Visa and Mastercard. But it's not completely out of the credit business. It still has significant stakes in two companies that operate under different umbrellas in the credit space -- American Express (NYSE: AXP) and Moody's (NYSE: MCO). Missed Nvidia in 2009? And both are prototypical Berkshire holdings in the style of Buffett -- with reliable earnings, competitive advantages, and businesses that can grow over decades. Let's take a closer look at them both. American Express is a core Berkshire Hathaway holding. Buffett first bought shares in 1964 after a financial scandal sent the company's stock plunging, recognizing that its brand and customer relationships were worth far more than the market was valuing. That investment worked out pretty well. Today, American Express is one of Berkshire's largest stock holdings, with a stake valued at more than $47 billion. And I think there's a good reason Buffett has remained so loyal to the company. Unlike Visa and Mastercard, which primarily operate payment networks, American Express also issues cards and lends money directly to customers. That allows it to collect interest on outstanding balances, in addition to fees from merchants and cardholders, and provides another revenue stream to help beef up American Express' coffers. American Express also targets businesses and affluent consumers who are willing to pay for premium benefits. Its revamped Platinum Card carries an annual membership fee of $895 -- a hefty price, but one that customers continue to accept in exchange for travel benefits and other rewards. In the second quarter of 2026, American Express reported revenue of $19.6 billion, up 10% from a year ago. Card member spending increased 9%, while earnings per share climbed 11% to $4.53.

You might hold Visa (V) stock alongside an index fund, or perhaps you are considering it. The shares advanced 5.3% over the last five sessions, compared with a 0.4% gain for the S&P 500. Since index-tracking portfolios already capture broader equity movements, the critical test for a new position is how it behaves during market volatility. When the market has a bad day, how much of it does Visa pass on to you? Visa Passed On A Quarter Of Typical Market Drops Over the past year of daily closes, the S&P 500 fell 0.6% on its average down day. During those sessions, a $10,000 position in Visa stock lost about $15. That decline represents roughly a quarter of the broader index drop. On positive sessions Visa kept more of the move. The index rose 0.65% on its average up day, while $10,000 of Visa stock gained about $24, capturing a little over a third of the market advance. Distilled to a single figure, Visa moved about 0.31% for each 1% the index moved over the past year. This indicates that on an average day, the stock adds little to the market risk already present in a standard index fund. Yet the shares swing much more than the index on their own. The stock posted an annual volatility rate of 22.2% over the past year, compared with 13.0% for the S&P 500. Visa brings swings of its own, and those price movements are wider than the fluctuations of the broader market. If you have held Visa for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not its day-to-day swings. See how a tax-aware transition works. Does Visa's Payments Business Point To A Change? Recent disclosures point to continued operational stability. Net revenue rose 14% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026. Payments volume grew 10% in constant dollars. Management noted on the fiscal Q3 earnings call that they saw no sign of weakness among lower-spending consumers, framing an outlook that assumed stable consumer spending would continue. Visa operates a steady business rather than a large bet still to be proven. Over the past year, those movements operated largely independent of broad market direction. The stock and the S&P 500 were only loosely aligned, carrying a correlation of 0.18 on a scale where 1 indicates perfect synchronization. Investors will look to Visa's payments volume in the fiscal Q4 report, which is expected on or around October 27, 2026. Visa Trailed The S&P 500 While Moving More Over the past five years, Visa returned 12.7% a year with dividends included, trailing the 14.0% for the S&P 500. The stock also recorded an annual volatility of 22.9% over the same five-year period, compared with 17.0% for the index.

According to The Fly, Keefe Bruyette maintained its 'Outperform' rating and $430 price target on Visa following the announcement. The analyst viewed the development as a positive regulatory move that brings Visa closer to participating in China's domestic card market and narrows the gap with Mastercard (MA). Keefe noted that although the approval allows Visa to begin formal preparations for a domestic bankcard clearing institution, it does not authorize the company to start operations. In a separate note reported by The Fly, Evercore ISI called the approval "certainly a good headline for Visa and marks a milestone they have been chasing for a long time." However, the firm said it was "hard to get too excited about the extrapolation of future revenues," citing Mastercard's track record and its inability to grow a meaningful business in China. Evercore also noted that Mastercard took four years to move from initial approval to launch, while American Express (AXP) took two years. The firm maintained its 'In Line' rating on Visa shares, saying the company's domestic operations could take time to ramp up. Visa said it would continue taking the necessary steps under PBOC regulations to begin operating domestically in China. Lightbridge Letter to Shareholders Outlines Expedited Pathway to Bring Lightbridge Fuel™ to Commercial Reactors

No summary available

RESTON, Va., Sept. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today issued a letter to shareholders from Lightbridge's Chairman & Chief Executive Officer, Seth Grae, following the Company's select...

RESTON, Va., Sept. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today issued a letter to shareholders from Lightbridge's Chairman & Chief Executive Officer, Seth Grae, following the Company's selection for the U.S. Department of Energy's Launch Pad INL Program. Dear Shareholders, Recently, we announced that Lightbridge has been selected to participate in the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE's) Launch Pad program at Idaho National Laboratory (INL). This is an important milestone for our Company that can enable an accelerated pathway for the commercial deployment of Lightbridge Fuel™. In this letter, I want to provide additional context on the significance of this milestone and convey why we believe we will look back on this day as one of the most consequential milestones in Lightbridge's history. What makes this milestone so significant for Lightbridge? DOE's Launch Pad INL enables a new two-prong commercialization strategy. The Special HALEU Extrusion Demonstration (SHED) facility that will produce Lead Test Assemblies (LTAs) will be deployed under DOE authorization. The Lightbridge Expandable Fuel Facility (LEFF) will proceed separately toward U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing for commercial-scale production (see below). This two-pronged approach can accelerate our time-to-market by several years compared to our previous projections. While detailed cost estimates for SHED are still being developed, based on preliminary estimates, we currently expect our existing cash and financial resources to be sufficient to fund the construction, operation, and decommissioning of SHED. The path for SHED goes through the DOE. The path for LEFF runs through the NRC. Which one applies depends on the facility's scale and purpose. SHED, a pilot-scale facility that produces LTAs, the full-size assemblies of Lightbridge Fuel that a utility would load into the core of an operating commercial reactor, which the NRC treats as part of a testing program, does not require an NRC license. LEFF, a commercial-scale fuel fabrication facility, does. We've previously described LEFF as the world's first fuel fabrication plant designed to expand in capacity as commercial demand for our fuel grows. Our original plan was to build LEFF under an NRC license in stages, starting with pilot-scale fabrication to produce LTAs, and then expand production to commercial scale to support batch reloads. That path is well understood from a regulatory licensing standpoint but would cost substantially more and take much longer.

Lightbridge Corporation Pays Tribute to Ambassador Thomas Graham Jr., Former Executive Chairman of the Board

No summary available

RESTON, Va., Sept. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation (Nasdaq: LTBR) was deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ambassador (ret.) Thomas Graham Jr., at the age of 92. He served as Executive Chairman of the Company's Board of Directors from 2009 to 2022 and as Chairman from 2022...

RESTON, Va., Sept. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation (Nasdaq: LTBR) was deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ambassador (ret.) Thomas Graham Jr., at the age of 92. He served as Executive Chairman of the Company's Board of Directors from 2009 to 2022 and as Chairman from 2022 to 2024. A defining figure in Lightbridge's history, Ambassador Graham devoted nearly two decades to the Company and brought a career centered on American arms control and nuclear non-proliferation policy. A graduate of Princeton University and Harvard Law School, Ambassador Graham served as a senior U.S. diplomat involved in every major international arms control and non-proliferation negotiation in which the United States participated between 1970 and 1997 — including the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks, the START I and START II Treaties, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, the Conventional Armed Forces in Europe Treaty, and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty. He spent 15 years as general counsel of the U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and served as its Acting Director in 1993. Appointed by President Clinton as Special Representative of the President for Arms Control, Non-Proliferation, and Disarmament from 1994 to 1997, he led the U.S. government's effort that secured the permanent extension of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1995. Ambassador Graham joined Lightbridge as Executive Chairman in 2009 and helped shape the Company's founding proposition: that advanced nuclear fuel technology could improve the economics and safety of nuclear power while strengthening proliferation resistance. He carried creative thinking relating to non-proliferation well beyond the boardroom — as an appointee to the United Arab Emirates' International Advisory Board on nuclear energy from 2009 to 2016, as co-author of Seeing the Light: The Case for Nuclear Power in the 21st Century, and as Co-Chairman of the Atlantic Council's Nuclear Energy and National Security Coalition. Across fifteen books and more than 100 published articles, he made the case that non-proliferation and the expansion of civil nuclear energy were not competing goals. He was named Chairman Emeritus of Lightbridge in 2024 and retired from the Company the following year. Seth Grae, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Lightbridge Corporation: "Tom's name on our board did something no business plan could: it told governments, regulators, and investors that a company working on nuclear fuel took non-proliferation seriously as a first principle. He negotiated the treaties that shaped the nuclear order and spent his last two decades arguing that the same seriousness could make nuclear energy larger, not smaller. He asked hard questions at every board meeting I attended with him, and Lightbridge is a better, more credible company for it. On behalf of our Board of Directors and our entire team, I extend our deepest condolences to his family." Lightbridge Receives Notice of Allowance on New Japanese Patent Covering Multi-Zone Fuel Element and 3D Printing Method

No summary available

RESTON, Va., Sept. 01, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today announced that it has received a Notice of Allowance from the Japan Patent Office ("JPO") for Japanese Patent Application No. 20...

RESTON, Va., Sept. 01, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today announced that it has received a Notice of Allowance from the Japan Patent Office ("JPO") for Japanese Patent Application No. 2024-513980, titled "Multi-Zone Fuel Element." The allowed claims cover the fuel element design itself, a fuel assembly incorporating that design, and a method of producing the element through additive manufacturing (3D printing), extending protection for a core element of Lightbridge Fuel into a market with one of the world's largest nuclear power markets. The patent covers a fuel rod composed of three layers of different materials, with each layer varying in thickness along the rod's length. That shape can be designed to control how the fuel behaves at different points inside the reactor, improving performance and safety margins. The claims also cover the fuel assembly into which these rods go and the 3D printing method used to build them. Japan has 32 reactors classified as operable, of which 15 have received clearance from the country's Nuclear Regulation Authority and returned to service, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Japan's national energy plan targets nuclear power at approximately 20% of electricity generation by fiscal year 2040, which would require up to 30 reactors in operation. "Japan operates a significant nuclear fleet and has made nuclear power central to its energy security and decarbonization policy, which makes it an important market for us," said Seth Grae, Chairman & CEO of Lightbridge Corporation. "This decision covers the fuel rod and the assembly that holds it, and the additive manufacturing method that produces it. That three-way coverage matters commercially because it protects the fuel product, which a utility will actually load into a reactor, and the process we intend to use to produce it." Lightbridge's fuel technology is backed by an extensive worldwide patent portfolio spanning jurisdictions representing the majority of global nuclear generating capacity. Provides an Accelerated Pathway toward DOE Authorization to Manufacture Lead Test Assemblies of Lightbridge Fuel for Operation in Commercial Power Reactors RESTON, Va., Aug. 31, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fue...

Provides an Accelerated Pathway toward DOE Authorization to Manufacture Lead Test Assemblies of Lightbridge Fuel for Operation in Commercial Power Reactors RESTON, Va., Aug. 31, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today announced that it has been selected to participate in the Nuclear Energy Launch Pad INL, administered by the U.S. Department of Energy's ("DOE") National Reactor Innovation Center ("NRIC") at Idaho National Laboratory ("INL"). Selection provides an accelerated pathway toward DOE authorization for Lightbridge to design, build, and operate a dedicated facility at INL to manufacture Lead Test Assemblies ("LTAs") of Lightbridge Fuel — the Company's proprietary metallic nuclear fuel — for testing in U.S. commercial power reactors. LTAs represent the final fuel qualification stage between reactor testing and commercial fuel sales. Lightbridge now has an accelerated pathway to establishing manufacturing capability for producing LTAs. The selection marks the most significant advance to date in Lightbridge's path from fuel testing to commercial deployment. By establishing a dedicated manufacturing facility under DOE authorization, the Company expects to significantly shorten the timeline for producing LTAs for operation in a commercial U.S. reactor. "This is the most important step we have taken toward putting Lightbridge Fuel into commercial reactors, and it changes how investors should understand our timeline," said Seth Grae, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Lightbridge. "A DOE-authorized facility will let us manufacture full-scale Lightbridge Fuel assemblies that nuclear utilities will run in their plants, and can produce them years sooner than a conventional facility licensing path would allow. We have been working with a major engineering, procurement, and construction ("EPC") firm in preparation for the start of construction of the Special High-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) Extrusion Demonstration (SHED) facility as soon as next year. Our goal is for Lightbridge Fuel to become the standard fuel that produces most of the world's nuclear energy, and this is where that path begins." Launch Pad is a DOE initiative supporting the Trump administration's goal of widescale nuclear energy expansion through streamlined pathways for developers to demonstrate and accelerate commercial deployment. Facilities developed under the program are privately financed. Lightbridge continues to develop detailed cost estimates for SHED, and based on preliminary estimates, the anticipated cost to construct, operate, and decommission SHED can be funded from the Company's current cash and financial resources.

Companies to explore long-term HALEU supply arrangements supporting the commercialization of next-generation nuclear fuel technologies RESTON, Va. and BOSTON, July 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation (Nasdaq: LTBR), a leader in advanced nuclear fuel technology, and Quadrant Nuclear Industries Inc. (QNI), a developer of integrated nuclear fuel cycle capabilities, today announced they have entered into a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish a framework for collaboration on the long-term supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) fuel. The MoU reflects a shared commitment to strengthening the domestic nuclear fuel supply chain, advancing next-generation nuclear technologies, and supporting U.S. energy security and decarbonization objectives. Under the agreement, Lightbridge and QNI will engage in discussions regarding the potential supply and long-term offtake of HALEU produced at QNI's planned Vanguard facility at Idaho National Laboratory. "We are pleased to establish this Memorandum of Understanding with QNI as we continue advancing the commercialization of Lightbridge Fuel™," said Seth Grae, Chairman and CEO of Lightbridge Corporation. "As we progress in the development and regulatory licensing of Lightbridge Fuel™, it is critical that we begin solidifying a reliable domestic supply of HALEU. We look forward to working with QNI to explore opportunities that support our long-term fuel requirements and contribute to a more secure U.S. nuclear fuel supply chain." "Developing a secure, U.S.-based source of HALEU is essential to enabling the next generation of nuclear energy," said Dee Mewbourne, CEO of QNI. "Our cooperation with Lightbridge reflects the growing alignment between advanced fuel innovation and domestic fuel production. Through this collaboration, we aim to establish a framework for a long-term offtake arrangement that supports commercialization of Lightbridge's advanced fuel technology while strengthening the domestic nuclear fuel ecosystem." QNI is developing an integrated HALEU production capability in coordination with the U.S. Department of Energy and other key stakeholders. Its planned Vanguard facility at Idaho National Laboratory is designed to produce up to eighteen metric tons of HALEU annually at full capacity, supporting both commercial and government markets for advanced nuclear reactors. The companies intend to collaborate on areas including fuel supply planning, technical interface requirements, commercial structuring, regulatory coordination, and logistics considerations associated with HALEU supply arrangements.

RESTON, Va., June 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today announced that the first batch of its fuel material samples undergoing irradiation at the Idaho National Laboratory's (INL) Advanced Test Reactor (ATR) have been successfully removed and will now be cooled down over the next several months in preparation for post-irradiation examination, which is expected to begin later this year. The samples were removed on May 6, 2026, with Lightbridge's full-time fuel engineering team and senior management — 24 Lightbridge personnel in total — on site at INL for the milestone. On May 7, the Lightbridge team met with the INL personnel leading the project, including John Wagner, Laboratory Director of Idaho National Laboratory, and Jess Gehin, Associate Lab Director. Lightbridge discussed progress to date and the path forward across multiple Lightbridge projects currently underway at INL. "The data already developed at the Advanced Test Reactor is a meaningful validation of the innovation and engineering behind Lightbridge Fuel," said Seth Grae, President and Chief Executive Officer of Lightbridge. "The data to be collected during the planned post-irradiation examination are expected to support our ongoing fuel performance modeling activities and regulatory licensing efforts for commercial deployment of Lightbridge Fuel. We are grateful to Lab Director John Wagner, Associate Lab Director Jess Gehin, and the entire INL team for the operational excellence that has made this campaign possible." Image 1: The combined Lightbridge and Idaho National Laboratory Team (May 7, 2026) The fuel material samples are being tested under the Fission Accelerated Steady-state Testing (FAST) method, an accelerated irradiation technique that uses Highly Enriched Uranium to reach high burnup conditions faster than conventional test methods. The FAST method was conceived and developed at INL. Geoffrey "Boone" Beausoleil, Lightbridge's Director of Materials, played a key role on the INL team that originated the initial concept for FAST and developed the underlying testing methodology during his prior tenure at INL. Image 2: Several members of Lightbridge team looking over the ATR canal (May 6, 2026) The samples that have been removed from the ATR will undergo post-irradiation examination to collect the data on fundamental material properties under high-burnup irradiation conditions. The data developed will support the broader testing program aimed at confirming the safety, performance, and economic advantages of Lightbridge Fuel relative to conventional nuclear fuel used in commercial reactors worldwide.

Lightbridge Fuel™ is Designed to Deliver Power Uprates that Expand the Output from Both the Existing U.S. Reactor Fleet and New Reactors RESTON, Va., June 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today participated in the White House launch of the Utility Power Reactor Incremental Scaling Effort ("UPRISE"), a federal initiative to expand U.S. nuclear capacity by maximizing output from the existing reactor fleet. The Company was represented by Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Seth Grae at the event held at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in the White House complex in Washington, D.C. Image 1: Lightbridge Chairman & CEO Seth Grae at the UPRISE launch at the White House (June 17, 2026) UPRISE, launched by the U.S. Department of Energy ("DOE"), targets the addition of approximately 5 GW of nuclear capacity and advances the President's May 2025 executive orders, which direct DOE to facilitate 5 GW of power uprates at existing reactors. The initiative brings together nuclear utilities, energy off-takers, and other stakeholders to support the expansion of output from the nation's operating reactor fleet. RESTON, Va., April 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, announced its financial results for the quarter ended March 31, 2026, and provided an update on the Company's continued progress. Seth Grae, President & Chief Executive Officer of Lightbridge, commented, "The first quarter of 2026 reflects the depth and pace of Lightbridge's program execution. We received patent allowances from three major jurisdictions—Canada, the United States, and the European Patent Office—expanding the scope of patent protection for Lightbridge Fuel™ across the CANDU fleet, the U.S. domestic light water reactor market, and 39 European contracting states. We also entered into an engineering contract with Stern Laboratories to launch a multi-phase thermal-hydraulics test program to support U.S. regulatory licensing of our fuel for light water reactors. We were selected to serve on the Industry Advisory Board of a $6 million DOE-funded research initiative at Penn State. And our technical team presented proprietary uranium-zirconium alloy research at TMS2026, contributing to the scientific foundation that underpins everything we are building." "We believe this is the most promising time for the growth of nuclear power in decades. Record global generation in 2025, sweeping U.S. executive action to accelerate reactor permitting and NRC reform, and landmark procurement commitments from the world's largest technology companies have collectively shifted the industry from a question of 'if' to a question of 'when and how fast.' Lightbridge is building to be the answer to the 'how'—specifically, how the existing global reactor fleet and new-build water-cooled reactors deliver more power and further enhanced safety, with improved economics." "Our program is advancing on every front. We have grown to over two dozen in-house engineers across all of our core disciplines, including neutronics, thermal hydraulics, fuel performance, materials, fuel assembly mechanical design, licensing, high-performance computing, and program management, and we continue to add talent. The qualification pathway ahead of us is well-defined. We expect Lightbridge Fuel will enable power uprates of up to 30% or more for new-build water-cooled reactors, meaningfully more than any other approach, while operating approximately 1,000 degrees Celsius cooler. In existing light-water reactors, Lightbridge Fuel is expected to enable power uprates of up to 20% or more (depending on balance-of-plant constraints) and to extend the fuel cycle length. In addition to creating new nuclear generating capacity, the world is seeking greater power from the infrastructure it already has. That is precisely the problem we've designed Lightbridge Fuel to solve."

Lightbridge Receives Notice of Allowance for European Patent Covering Multi-Zone Fuel Element and Additive Manufacturing (3D Printing) Method

No summary available

RESTON, Va., April 15, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today announced that the European Patent Office (EPO) has issued a Notice of Allowance for European Patent Application No. 22777419.7,...

RESTON, Va., April 15, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lightbridge Corporation ("Lightbridge" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: LTBR), an advanced nuclear fuel technology company, today announced that the European Patent Office (EPO) has issued a Notice of Allowance for European Patent Application No. 22777419.7, titled "Multi-Zone Fuel Element." The allowed patent covers Lightbridge's proprietary nuclear fuel element design, featuring multiple radial zones with variable thicknesses along the axial direction, enabling precise control of neutron flux distribution throughout the fuel element's operational lifetime. The European allowance extends intellectual property protection for a core element of Lightbridge's fuel technology across 39 contracting states, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and all major European nuclear markets. The patent covers fuel elements manufactured via additive manufacturing (3D printing), a process that enables the production of complex multi-material zone architectures that are unachievable through conventional fuel fabrication techniques. Combined with Lightbridge's existing U.S. and international patent portfolio, this grant meaningfully expands the Company's IP moat in advanced nuclear fuel. The allowed claims are directed to a fuel element comprising three distinct radial zones of different materials — a first zone extending along the central axis, a second surrounding zone, and a third outermost zone — in which the thickness of both the second and third zones in the radial direction varies along the axial direction. The manufacturing method claims cover the use of additive manufacturing to produce this multi-zone architecture using metallic, ceramic, or cermet fuel systems. The variable zone thickness along the axial direction enables engineers to tailor the radial and axial neutron flux profile within a single element, supporting optimization of reactor performance, safety margin management, and fissile material efficiency throughout the fuel cycle. "Receiving this allowance from the European Patent Office is an important validation of the technical depth and novelty of Lightbridge Fuel™," said Seth Grae, President and Chief Executive Officer of Lightbridge Corporation. "Europe is home to a significant installed base of nuclear generating capacity, and the countries and utilities advancing nuclear energy as part of their clean energy programs represent a natural market for Lightbridge Fuel. This patent ensures that the fuel element design at the heart of Lightbridge Fuel, with our precise multi-zone architecture and variable radial zone configuration, is protected across those markets as we advance toward commercialization."

Initially wholly owned by Ondas and supported by Palantir's technology, Regna AI aims to help governments, defense organizations and enterprises adopt sovereign AI solutions for mission-critical operations. Ondas will become Regna AI's first customer, deploying specialized AI models to coordinate autonomous missions directly on edge devices. The venture will also serve other government agencies, businesses and institutions seeking greater control over their AI infrastructure and sensitive operational data. Palantir will provide model-training infrastructure and deployment support, while both companies collaborate on engineering solutions tailored to customer requirements. Regna AI's models are designed to operate across intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) platforms, including drones, stratospheric balloons, ground vehicles and surface vessels. They will also support command-and-control systems, enabling operations in environments with limited or disrupted connectivity. These capabilities will help personnel evaluate intelligence, assess alternatives and recommend mission adjustments, subject to human review and authorization. The initiative builds on Ondas and Palantir's existing partnership on SkyWeaver, an AI-enabled command, control, communications, computers and intelligence (C4I) platform connecting surveillance capabilities across multiple domains. On its second-quarter 2026 earnings call, Ondas highlighted successful ground and aerial testing of SkyWeaver, marking progress toward integrating AI-driven intelligence and autonomous operations across its portfolio. Regna AI will leverage Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) and open-weight models to help customers develop specialized AI capabilities without incurring the substantial costs of building foundational models independently. By allowing institutions to retain control over their models and mission data, the venture seeks to address growing concerns surrounding data sovereignty and dependence on commercial AI providers. Ondas expects to collaborate with Palantir to expand Regna AI's platform and support initial customer deployments over the coming months. While ISR applications will provide the initial focus, the company plans to extend its capabilities into additional defense missions, security, critical infrastructure and industrial markets, potentially broadening Ondas' long-term growth opportunities.

People have always found ways to prove how strongly they believe in something. Some put their money on the line, and some put their reputations up for grabs. In Silicon Valley, belief in artificial intelligence (AI) has turned into its own kind of identity. Founders talk about curing diseases, ending scarcity and building machines smarter than any person alive. Those promises have helped drive enormous investment. They have also created a culture where the boldest prediction often gets the most attention. Few companies have benefited from that wave more than Palantir. Its software helps governments and corporations put AI to work, and its stock has become a favorite of retail investors betting on the trend. Now one of Palantir's top executives says the culture around AI has gone too far. The example he chose to make his point is a strange one. Palantir Technologies (PLTR) Chief Technology Officer Shyam Sankar said on CBS's "Face the Nation" on Sunday, Oct. 11, that some AI researchers have taken up smoking. Their reasoning, he said, is that AI will cure cancer before cigarettes can hurt them. "So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," Sankar said, according to Business Insider. He described the thinking behind it in the researchers' own imagined words. "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I'm showing you my chips are all in," Sankar said. More Artificial Intelligence: Franklin Templeton CEO says AI is hiding a bigger tech story The AI buildout is on track to be the biggest bet in US history Palantir's answer to a deadly targeting failure was more AI Sankar did not name any researchers or provide evidence for the claim, Business Insider reported. The outlet noted that its own reporter had written the previous month about some people in tech taking up smoking, in an industry better known for obsessing over health. That earlier reporting captured the same mindset. "By the time you do get lung cancer, our AI robots are supposed to have cured that," Avi Schiffmann, founder of AI wearable startup Friend, told Business Insider. Sankar told the story as a criticism. He raised it while attacking what he called the "mass psychosis" and "social delusion" surrounding AI in Silicon Valley, according to Benzinga. He aimed that criticism at both ends of the debate. Warnings that AI could destroy humanity reflect a theological view more than an evidence-based one, Sankar argued, Benzinga reported.

NVDA-Led AI Boom Looks a Lot Like the Railroad Bubble of 1873, Pulitzer-Winning Historian Warns

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below. The AI boom powering Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) has entered its "manic phase," Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Liaquat Ahamed warned Friday, comparing it to the railroad frenzy that ended in the Panic of 1873. Speaking on the Prof G Markets podcast, Ahamed said competition, overbuilding and debt could undermine returns on the vast sums pouring into data centers, even if the boom continues another year or two. Railroads transformed the economy, but many of the companies financing their expansion went bankrupt. Ahamed traced the crash to Jay Cooke, a powerful banker who raised billions for the Union during the Civil War. Cooke then backed the Northern Pacific, a new transcontinental railroad. With hundreds of miles of track laid, investors assumed he could finance the rest. But in September 1873, Cooke announced he couldn't secure the necessary funding. His firm collapsed, triggering a financial panic. As Ahamed explained, if even Cooke couldn't raise the money, what chance did smaller railroad companies have? Within three months, railroad construction had ground to a halt, and roughly a quarter of U.S. railroad companies defaulted within a year. Ahamed drew a modern parallel: What if OpenAI suddenly couldn't finance its enormous AI commitments? He later identified Oracle as another company potentially vulnerable to a funding crisis. Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella has cited Ahamed's book on 1873, saying Microsoft would be careful not to overbuild. Ahamed said Nadella "got the wrong end of the stick." Individual railroad companies weren't necessarily reckless. Each kept expanding because slowing down meant surrendering business to competitors. "It's the collectivity of their decisions that leads to overbuilding," he said. Today's hyperscalers could face the same trap. Ahamed identified three warning signs before the railroad crash: excess capacity, eroding profitability and more expensive financing. He said much of today's AI borrowing remains opaque. He described Nvidia as "essentially lending to its customers," although its arrangements also involve equity investments and purchase commitments rather than conventional loans. Nvidia has invested in CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) and entered a $6.3 billion agreement to purchase qualifying unused computing capacity through 2032. Some CoreWeave bonds yielded around 16% this week amid mounting debt concerns.

Fine-tuned NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivered strongest overall performance based on Navan's internal evaluation with lowest latency and significant efficiency PALO ALTO, Calif., October 16, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Navan (NASDAQ: NAVN), the global AI-powered business travel and expense platform, today announced that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now powering several of its AI travel agents in production. Just three weeks after receiving early access and beginning its work with NVIDIA, Navan trained and deployed the model. The deployment is the latest example of Navan's open-model strategy: evaluating models for specific travel tasks, adapting them with Navan's travel expertise, and self-hosting them to maintain control over performance, cost, and reliability. Before deployment, Navan internally evaluated Nemotron 3.5 Super VL against its self-hosted production baseline and other models using consistent prompts, tools, travel scenarios and criteria. After fine-tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel VLM LoRA training recipe, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivered the strongest overall performance, beating or tying every competing model on six of seven measures, including having the lowest latency. The model is now in production and powering customer conversations at a lower cost while delivering greater value to Navan users. "Building reliable agentic travel systems involves much more than choosing a model, but continuously iterating to improve and solve real-world problems," said Ilan Twig, co-founder and CTO of Navan. "We're grateful to NVIDIA for early access to Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, which shows how open models can help us move faster, maintain control, and deliver meaningful value without compromising quality." Navan combines open and closed models to build AI travel agents that understand what travelers want, follow policies, and use the right tools to get the job done. I recently reviewed Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) latest quarterly SEC filing, and what I read persuaded me to change my call on the stock. In the recent past, I called Nvidia a buy amid its rapid revenue growth and comparatively low valuation. Today, as I look more closely at the numbers, I worry more about its near-term future. Amid that concern, I am now switching my call on Nvidia from buy to hold. Here's why. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » First, making this shift does not mean I have turned on Nvidia. I still see it as an excellent choice for the long term. The company continues to dominate the artificial intelligence (AI) accelerator market and is investing enough into research and development to stay on top of the market and pivot into cutting-edge technologies. Moreover, it currently trades at just 28 times earnings. Considering the S&P 500's average P/E ratio is 27, that looks like a reasonable valuation for a top company. Furthermore, Nvidia plans to buy back $235 billion of its stock between now and January 2028. Between its future sales growth and its dwindling outstanding share count, the stock could easily outperform the market over the longer term. A quarter-century ago, the internet industry endured the dot-com bust. A similar event is likely to hit the AI industry at some point. An AI bust would be unlikely to destroy Nvidia, but the company has a key vulnerability that makes its near-term direction less certain. Buried in Nvidia's latest quarterly filing was the revelation that five companies each make up between 10% and 22% of its accounts receivable balance, for a total of 70%. Nvidia did not reveal which specific companies they were. Still, one is likely to be OpenAI, a company that's underperforming its financial expectations. Additionally, even better-established hyperscalers like Amazon have borrowed heavily and turned free-cash-flow negative. Those factors could limit its spending over time. For now, Nvidia's growth remains exceptionally strong. In the first half of its fiscal 2027 (a period that ended July 26), its revenue was $178 billion -- a 96% increase from the prior-year period. Analysts forecast that its growth will remain in the high-double-digit percentages through at least the next fiscal year.

The deal is expected to be unveiled...

Nvidia (NVDA) is reportedly lining up another government partnership in Europe. Germany plans a wide-ranging cooperation agreement with Nvidia to push AI deeper into German industry, Reuters reported on Thursday, October 15, citing the business daily Handelsblatt. The deal is expected to be unveiled next week at the government's Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, which CEO Jensen Huang will attend. Government sources confirmed the plan to Reuters on Friday, October 16, saying Germany will announce the agreement next week with partners beyond Nvidia. The funding, the participants and the terms still rest on Handelsblatt's reporting, and nothing official has been published. Handelsblatt says the agreement has two goals. The first is to lay the groundwork for physical AI, meaning the tools used to train robots and self-driving vehicles. The second is to build high-performance AI models for industry. That work would run through SOOFI (Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models), a German project launched last year with universities, research institutes and AI companies. Berlin would put in hundreds of millions of euros for computing power and model training, and Nvidia would send engineers. About 12 German companies are expected to join. They include Siemens (SIEGY), Audi (owned by Volkswagen (VWAGY)) and the AI startup Black Forest Labs. Start with the size of the deal. Nvidia booked $302.97 billion in revenue over the last 12 months, after its revenue roughly doubled this year. Suppose Germany spent a full €1 billion and every euro went to Nvidia hardware. That would still be under 0.4% of the total. The business this deal targets is bigger than Nvidia's segment table suggests. In fiscal 2026, which ended in January, the Automotive segment made $2.35 billion, or 1.1% of total revenue, against $193.74 billion from Data Center. But CFO Colette Kress said on the February earnings call that physical AI brought in more than $6 billion that year, and Nvidia put the figure above $9 billion over the trailing 12 months when it reported in May. That puts physical AI at more than roughly 3.5% of Nvidia's sales over the same 12 months. Automotive, the one piece of it Nvidia broke out, grew 39% last fiscal year, against 68% for Data Center. For Nvidia, the money matters less than whose tools German industry trains on. Siemens is already building a joint industrial AI operating system with Nvidia, announced at CES in January. Deutsche Telekom (DTEGY) runs an industrial AI cloud with Nvidia under a €1 billion partnership, with Nvidia supplying 10,000 GPUs. That cloud already hosts SOOFI: Leibniz Universität Hannover hired Telekom to supply the project's computing infrastructure. That makes it a likely home for any new compute spending, though no allocation has been reported.

Nvidia has announced the release of three new models in its Nemotron family, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120 billion-parameter open model. The company states that this new model is designed to enable higher efficiency and accuracy for always-on AI agents performing specialised tasks, with two additional 'Bolt' models aimed at edge deployment scenarios. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB are available immediately, while the Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is expected to launch on 23 October. The Nemotron 3.5 models are intended to support a variety of agent deployments, ranging from enterprise servers to local hardware and edge devices. Nvidia said that with the new releases, organisations using its infrastructure can select models optimised for their needs without compromising between capability and deployability. The Nemotron range now comprises the new Super VL and Bolt models alongside earlier releases named Ultra and Lightning. According to Nvidia, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL achieves accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks, such as instruction following, workflow automation, and visual understanding, on par with its larger reasoning model, but at roughly one-fifth of the parameter count. The company claims that Super VL is five times faster than comparable open models in completing complex workflows, and that organisations can customise the model with their own data and deploy it on their own systems. On the edge deployment front, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB has been optimised to run on Nvidia RTX and DGX Spark hardware, using a 2-bit quantisation method to fit into a 24GB memory footprint. The company says this balancing of intelligence and speed enables a wider range of local tasks by users without relying on cloud services. The Bolt E4B 4GB model has been designed for conversational and physical agents running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and other Nvidia systems. Nvidia reported that dozens of organisations are customising and post-training the Super VL model for specific business use cases, including financial document analysis, medical claims management, and scientific discovery. Companies such as Scale AI, EY, AfterQuery, AI21, Mercor, ModelScope, Ramp, and others are named as users adapting the model for their sectors. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL's design allows it to process structured data, images, web pages, and PDFs, integrating both text and visual information for agent tasks. The model is released with open weights, datasets, and training recipes, supporting customisation through Nvidia NeMo and other developer tools.

ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) reported excellent third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 14. The semiconductor equipment maker raked in a record 11.7 billion euros in revenue, which was the high end of its guidance. ASML's gross margins came in at a whopping 57.5% -- above guidance. Management stated that customers are already looking to place orders in 2029 and 2030 to fulfill their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts. Here's why that's great news for ASML, and why ASML is arguably the best artificial intelligence (AI) growth stock for long-term investors to buy now. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » There are three main parts of ASML's business -- extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines, deep ultraviolet (DUV) and non-EUV machines, and servicing its installed base. DUV systems are mainly used for general-purpose chip manufacturing. They can be used for AI chip manufacturing through a process called multiple patterning, but that's less efficient than EUV machines, which use far shorter wavelengths of light to print ultra-precise designs on microchips. The high numerical aperture (High-NA) EUV machine -- the most advanced lithography system in the world -- can cost up to $400 million. But ASML is only shipping around one unit a quarter as it gradually scales production of this relatively new technology, purpose-built for commercial-scale production of next-generation AI chips. When ASML reported second-quarter results in July, the company forecast a 30% increase in Low-NA EUV production capacity in 2027 and possibly by 2028, as well as a 30% increase in DUV immersion capacity in 2027 and another 30% increase in 2028. CEO Christophe Fouquet said the following in ASML's Oct. 14 earnings release: With such strong visibility and an order book momentum that continues to increase quarter on quarter this year, we now expect that our supply as currently planned for both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers. Given this, we are investigating ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase we previously communicated. In addition, we continue to provide significant wafer capacity to our customers through our productivity upgrade portfolio. So in just six months, ASML's visibility shifted from probably needing to ramp production capacity through 2028 to stating that even a 30% jump could be insufficient. That sends a clear signal to investors that ASML can't keep up with order volumes, which should give it even more pricing power.

Besi's HBM prospects are also weakening, SemiAnalysis said, as Korean challengers catch up and HBM adoption of die-to-wafer bonding is expected to slip to 2029 or beyond. ASML's design differs from conventional machines, where a bond head picks each die off a diced wafer and places it. Instead, each die moves on its own holder around a track past inspection, cleaning, plasma activation and measurement stations before reaching a bonding station, where a chuck lifts the bottom wafer to meet it. SemiAnalysis said ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control, the two factors that set bonding yield, but still needs to solve challenges around feed-forward metrology, die-to-wafer contact, modifying non-bonding tools and keeping the loop clean. It expects ASML to price its tools at a premium to peers. The Elec reported in March that ASML had started architecture design of a hybrid bonder with Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG. Memory chipmakers hesitated to expand at first, but now have hundreds of billions of dollars worth of new facilities set to go into chip production starting next year. Meanwhile, the largest third-party chip manufacturer in the world, TSMC, has continuously raised its capital expenditure budget as it aims to keep up with demand. While there are multiple ways to invest in the growing demand for semiconductor production, one of the best is to move up the supply chain to silicon wafer fabrication equipment makers. Two of the biggest companies in the space are ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) and Applied Materials (NASDAQ: AMAT). Both are excellent companies with strong competitive advantages, but if you can only choose one, which stock is worth buying today? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Applied Materials holds a broad portfolio of equipment and maintains a very impressive market share across the group. Its deposition equipment (which adds conductive or insulating materials to a silicon wafer) is one of its fastest-growing businesses in 2026, even as it maintains a leading market share. The company is also seeing strong growth across etching, process diagnostics and control, and its thermals and treatments segments. The diversified approach comes with a significant benefit. Applied Materials can sell combined offerings to customers by integrating different processes into a single piece of equipment. That can save its customers up-front costs as well as floor space, increasing production capacity. Over time, Applied Materials has come to work more closely with its customers, which has given it better insight into their needs. Of course, maintaining a broad portfolio of market-leading equipment also requires significant investment in research and development (R&D). Applied Materials' R&D budget is significantly larger than its competitors' with much narrower product lines. That said, Applied Materials also earns revenue capable of supporting that R&D. Its operating margin of 31% is below that of competitors like KLA and Lam Research, but that's largely due to the lower-gross-margin profile of deposition equipment, which accounts for a larger share of Applied Materials' revenue.

ASML Says AI Chip Demand Is Stretching Into 2030. It Already Expects Supply Shortages Through 2028.

ASML said Wednesday that some customers are already looking to place orders for advanced chipmaking equipment for 2029 and 2030 as demand tied to artificial intelligence continues to stretch the company's manufacturing capacity. The Dutch semiconductor equipment maker expects its currently planned ...

ASML said Wednesday that some customers are already looking to place orders for advanced chipmaking equipment for 2029 and 2030 as demand tied to artificial intelligence continues to stretch the company's manufacturing capacity. The Dutch semiconductor equipment maker expects its currently planned production capacity for 2027 and 2028 to fall short of customer requirements, even after previously announcing plans to expand output by as much as 30% in each of those years. The outlook accompanied record third-quarter net sales of €11.66 billion and net income of €4.96 billion, according to ASML's latest financial results. ASML raised the lower end of its full-year revenue forecast to €44 billion, from €43 billion previously, while maintaining the upper end at €45 billion. The company expects fourth-quarter sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion. Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said customers were increasing their near- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts, driven primarily by expectations about the scale and duration of AI-related investments. Some customers have expressed interest in orders extending into 2029 and 2030, although the company did not identify them or disclose the value of those potential purchases. ASML supplies lithography machines used to manufacture advanced semiconductors, including processors that power AI systems. Its extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, technology enables chipmakers to produce the intricate circuit patterns required for increasingly sophisticated chips. The company's customers include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Samsung Electronics and Intel, alongside memory chipmakers such as SK Hynix and Micron. TSMC manufactures advanced processors for companies including Nvidia, while memory manufacturers are expanding production of chips used alongside AI processors in data centers. ASML had outlined plans in July to increase its 2026 production capacity for certain EUV and deep ultraviolet lithography systems by 30% in 2027, while examining another increase for 2028. In its second-quarter financial results, the company said it was planning around annual capacity of 65 low-NA EUV machines and 130 deep ultraviolet immersion systems in 2026. However, management said Wednesday that the expansion plans would not fully satisfy expected demand, prompting ASML to investigate additional capacity for 2028 beyond the previously discussed increase. The company is also expanding upgrades that allow customers to process more silicon wafers using existing equipment, reducing the need to rely entirely on deliveries of new machines.

(NASDAQ:ASML) has secured higher prices for its most critical chipmaking equipment as the artificial intelligence boom strengthens its bargaining power with semiconductor manufacturers. The Dutch company confirmed Wednesday that negotiations with customers have concluded, with the increases expected to boost revenue and profit margins starting in 2027. "We thought that we were entitled to a higher percentage," CFO Roger Dassen said during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "There was a clear acceptance that maybe the overall value in the ecosystem is shifting," CEO Christophe Fouquet said, linking the change partly to AI. Fouquet said it was one of the first times in many years ASML had held such pricing discussions with customers. ASML is the only commercial supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which chipmakers need to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors. In July, The Information reported that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (NYSE:TSM), ASML's largest customer, was resisting proposed increases. ASML has now completed negotiations, although it hasn't identified which customers agreed to higher prices or disclosed the size of the increases. Its bargaining position has strengthened as manufacturers race to expand production. ASML said its planned output for 2027 and 2028 won't fully meet customer demand, even as it expands capacity. Some customers are already seeking equipment for 2029 and 2030. Beyond today's equipment shortages, ASML's next growth cycle may depend on when chipmakers adopt its more advanced High-NA EUV machines at scale, with Samsung targeting 2028 and TSMC 2030. The increases cover ASML's most critical manufacturing equipment, with prices for productivity upgrades to existing machines expected to follow. Asked by JPMorgan analyst Sandeep Deshpande how much of the increase would become profit, Dassen said some would cover manufacturing expansion costs, but a significant portion would boost gross margins. ASML reported a 57.5% gross margin in the third quarter but expects around 57% in the fourth quarter, mainly because of production expansion costs. The new price increases have yet to take effect. Asked by Berenberg analyst Tammy Qiu whether ASML could repeat the increases annually, management said that wasn't the plan.

Qualcomm alleged that Arm withheld software patches and chip-testing tools needed to verify Qualcomm's custom Oryon CPU cores. Qualcomm also claimed Arm violated a pricing structure designed to keep Qualcomm's royalties within 10% of the lowest available design pricing. Qualcomm further alleged that Arm deliberately leaked a 2024 license-termination warning letter to Bloomberg, which Qualcomm said damaged its business reputation and cost the company approximately $170 million in a potential deal with Meta Platforms. Management said memory conditions across the global smartphone market affected handset revenue. Alongside these broader conditions, management said revenue from Android phone chips dropped 20% from a year earlier. The second issue centers on Apple. Qualcomm said on its July earnings call that it expected its share of the upcoming iPhone launch to be materially lower than its earlier estimate of 20%. The company also expected Apple revenue to drop faster starting in fiscal Q4 2026. This slowdown is already visible in Qualcomm's total revenue. After growing 10.0% and then 5.0% in the first two of the last four quarters, revenue fell 3.5% and then 4.0% in the final two periods. Reduced business from Apple also alters the seasonal shape of Qualcomm's year. The fiscal first quarter was traditionally the strongest period. Within the phone segment itself, management estimates that chip sales to Chinese phone makers reached a bottom in fiscal Q3. Qualcomm has not yet proven that this growth can replace Apple. Management expects growth outside handsets in fiscal 2027 to replace the Apple revenue of fiscal 2026.
