AUSTIN, Texas, October 13, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Lumenci today announced that Derek Aberle has joined its Advisory Board. Aberle spent nearly two decades at Qualcomm serving as President from 2014 through 2018. He led the company's technology and intellectual property licensing business, growing it into one of the largest licensing operations globally. He is currently Co-founder and Executive Vice Chairman of Virewirx, Inc., a board director at InterDigital, and a Venture Partner with Stormbreaker Ventures. His addition comes as Lumenci launched iLumOS earlier this year and is expanding its network of partner firms and advisors. The platform compresses patent portfolio analysis from months to minutes, combining AI-driven portfolio triage and claim charting with Lumenci's expert capabilities across prior art, evidence-of-use analysis, validity, damages, and other diligence required to move promising patent assets toward monetization. "Derek brings a rare combination of technology leadership, licensing experience, and a deep understanding of how intellectual property creates enterprise value," said Harish Daiya, Co-founder & CEO of Lumenci. "As we build iLumOS into the operating system for patent intelligence, we want to surround the platform with people who have helped shape the IP industry at the highest level. Derek's perspective will be invaluable as we expand iLumOS and pursue our broader vision of helping make patent assets more transparent, actionable, and investable." "Patent owners have historically had to make important portfolio and monetization decisions with fragmented data, lengthy analysis cycles, and significant upfront effort," said Aberle. "What attracted me to Lumenci and its iLumOS is the opportunity to combine AI with the practical expertise required to make that intelligence useful. Lumenci has spent years working directly on complex patent and licensing matters, and iLumOS brings that experience into a platform that can help organizations identify value faster, focus resources on the right assets, and make better-informed IP decisions. I'm excited to work with Harish and the team as they build this next generation of patent intelligence infrastructure." About iLumOS iLumOS is an AI-powered patent intelligence platform built for IP law firms, patent owners, and litigation funding teams. It analyzes portfolios of any size in minutes, evaluating patents across strength, quality, infringement signals, and validity resilience to help surface assets warranting deeper investigation.

VIENNA, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI applications increasingly extend to end devices, smart devices are evolving from basic data connectivity toward real-time interaction and intelligent experiences, creating greater demand for high-speed, stable, low-latency wireless connectivity. At NetworkX 2026, Fibocom is showcasing its SC153 5G smart module for the first time. Built on the Qualcomm Dragonwing™ Q-4390 processor, SC153 addresses next-generation smart devices' requirements for high-speed connectivity and complex applications, providing customers worldwide with a high-performance 5G connectivity solution that offers development flexibility. The product is currently undergoing debugging, with mass production planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. High-Speed 5G Connectivity Unlocks Device Potential As applications such as high-definition video transmission, industrial data acquisition and smart device connectivity continue to develop, devices face increasing requirements for high-speed data transmission and stable network connectivity. Designed with advanced 5G communications capabilities, SC153 supports 3GPP Release 16 and provides multimode connectivity across 5G NR sub-6 GHz and LTE, meeting the network performance and deployment flexibility requirements of different applications. For connectivity performance, SC153 supports both 5G standalone (SA) and non-standalone (NSA) network architectures, delivering maximum downlink speeds of 2.3 Gbps in SA mode and 2.5 Gbps in EN-DC mode. These capabilities enable stable, efficient data transmission for applications including high-definition video, industrial equipment and smart devices. Flexible Design Meets Diverse Device Requirements To support the rapid evolution of smart devices, customers need not only communications performance but also greater flexibility in hardware design and software development. SC153 uses an LGA package and provides a wide range of interfaces, including MIPI display, MIPI camera, USB 3.1, UART, I²C and SD, while flexibly supporting Wi-Fi 5, Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 configurations to meet the design requirements of different device form factors. SC153 also supports the Android operating system, providing a more flexible platform for software development, application expansion and device customization. With its high-speed connectivity and development flexibility, SC153 can help customers develop a new generation of wireless products for smart devices, industrial equipment and high-speed data applications.

Investors paying that price need a clear understanding of what they are buying, particularly as the company shifts its public priorities. Back in July 2025, executives anchored their presentations on sales targets for automotive and IoT chips, which power connected consumer and industrial devices. By the latest call, those figures had taken a back seat. So what does Qualcomm lead with now? Qualcomm Is Entering A New Chip Market Executives are now highlighting chips for data centers, a market the company is only just entering. During the fiscal Q3 2026 earnings call in July 2026, management stated that Qualcomm was "expanding into the data center with 4 unique product lines." That represents a distinct shift in messaging. During the fiscal Q3 2025 call a year earlier, leadership instead focused on a fiscal 2029 target of $22 billion in combined automotive and IoT revenue. Those alternative revenue streams remain critical because Qualcomm relies heavily on smartphones. Its chip business made up 87% of revenue in fiscal 2025, and phones generated $5.1 billion of that segment's $8.5 billion in revenue during fiscal Q3 2026. And on its July 2026 call, Qualcomm said it expected its share of the then-upcoming iPhone launch to be materially lower than its prior estimate of 20%. Management characterizes this push beyond phones as its diversification strategy. How Big Are Qualcomm's Old And New Priorities? Qualcomm already reports its automotive and IoT results, whereas the data center business remains mostly a forecast. The company posted automotive revenue of $1.6 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, marking a 61% increase from a year earlier. In the same period, IoT revenue grew 9% to $1.8 billion. The data center operation is still in its earliest stages. Wafer production has begun on Qualcomm's two custom data center chip wins, and these components are due to start generating revenue in the December quarter. Looking further out, management forecast data center revenue of $5 billion in fiscal 2027. Automotive and IoT products still represent the larger piece of management's long-term plan. Executives now expect to generate more than $24 billion from cars and IoT in fiscal 2029, compared to more than $15 billion from data centers. The total fiscal 2029 outlook for sales outside phones currently stands at $40 billion. Can Qualcomm Investors Take Comfort In This? For the automotive and IoT segments, the internal projections offer reassurance. Management maintained and even expanded its prior targets: the car and IoT portion of the fiscal 2029 outlook is now larger than the forecast provided in July 2025. The company also guided for another record automotive performance in fiscal Q4 2026, projecting revenue growth of approximately 60% from a year earlier.

The semiconductor landscape is shifting as AI demands redefine hardware requirements. Choosing between Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) and Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) requires weighing a massive manufacturing turnaround against a mobile titan's expansion. Intel is betting its future on becoming a world-class foundry for other chip designers, while Qualcomm is leveraging its 5G leadership to capture new markets in automotive and computing. Both companies are central to the technology narrative, but they offer vastly different financial profiles and risk levels for investors. Intel designs and manufactures processors, accelerators, and software, serving as a heavyweight among semiconductor stocks. It is aggressively expanding its foundry business to produce chips for other designers, recently deepening its partnership with Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT). This strategy targets the growing need for specialized hardware in a world increasingly dominated by artificial intelligence. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $52.9 billion, a slight decline of roughly 0.5% from the previous year. The company reported a net loss of approximately $267 million, which resulted in a net margin of negative 0.5%. This performance reflects the massive research and development costs associated with reclaiming its process technology leadership after several years of falling behind competitors. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Intel has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.4, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity. Its current ratio, comparing short-term assets to liabilities, is a healthy 2, but free cash flow was negative at nearly $4.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. Qualcomm develops essential wireless technologies, providing modems and processors for major smartphone brands like Samsung and Xiaomi (OTC:XIACF). It also generates significant income by licensing its massive portfolio of 5G intellectual property to other manufacturers. A high concentration of sales comes from a few massive customers like Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached roughly $44.3 billion, representing growth of nearly 13.7% from the prior year. Qualcomm achieved net income of approximately $5.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of 12.5%. This net margin indicates the percentage of total revenue that remains as profit after all expenses are paid, showing the company's ability to turn sales into actual earnings.

Is Intel's Record Sales Growth Still Improving?

No summary available

Intel Corporation (INTC) sold 25.4% more in the three months to June than it did in the same quarter a year earlier. The chipmaker has not grown faster in any quarter of the last ten years. To judge that record properly requires looking at what is normal for the company. So take a guess: in a typica...

Intel Corporation (INTC) sold 25.4% more in the three months to June than it did in the same quarter a year earlier. The chipmaker has not grown faster in any quarter of the last ten years. To judge that record properly requires looking at what is normal for the company. So take a guess: in a typical quarter, how much more does Intel sell than a year earlier? How Unusual Is This For Intel? The answer is hardly any more. Across the last forty quarters, the median rise in Intel's sales from a year earlier was 1.3%. In a typical quarter, the company sells about what it sold a year before. That makes the quarter to June far outside Intel's normal. Here is the same quarter in each of the last ten years. Quarter ended Sales growth from a year earlier Jul 2017 9.1% Jun 2018 14.9% Jun 2019 -2.7% Jun 2020 19.5% Jun 2021 -0.5% Jul 2022 -22.0% Jul 2023 -15.5% Jun 2024 -0.9% Jun 2025 0.2% Jun 2026 25.4% The previous high was 24% in the quarter ended March 28, 2020. That period is not shown in the table, but the quarter to June is the first to surpass it and set a brand new record. What Is Behind Intel's Record Sales Growth? During a July 23, 2026 call, management said Intel's businesses tied to AI, including data center chips, grew more than 70% from a year earlier. Those businesses now bring in about 70% of Intel's sales. Revenue in Intel's Data Center and Artificial Intelligence unit alone rose 59% from a year earlier. Management also noted that its outlook for server CPU demand had improved again. Intel also got more for each chip it sold. Management said selling prices rose because Intel sold more of its pricier chips and raised some prices, partly to pass rising costs on to customers. Is The Latest Quarter Still Improving? The broader trend reveals more than the June figure on its own. Intel's sales fell 4.1% from a year earlier in the quarter to December 2025. Growth then turned to 7.2% in the quarter to March, before the record in the quarter to June. Intel's growth has now sped up in each of the last two quarters. One quarter remains a short stretch to measure. Over the last twelve months, Intel's sales grew 7.5% from the twelve months before, which sits well behind the pace of the latest quarter. When The Record Is Next Tested In July, management expected sales in the quarter to September to come in about 1.2% above the quarter to June at the midpoint of its forecast range. That quarter has now ended, and Intel has yet to report the results. Management also noted that supply was very tight, with supply growth weighted toward the end of that quarter and into the next, especially for servers. For PCs, management expects PC consumption to fall by a low double-digit percent across 2026.

(ABNB) CEO Brian Chesky told Bloomberg in October 2025 that his company relies heavily on Qwen. The model, built by Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (BABA), is "fast and cheap," he said, as Fortune reported. Intel Corp. (INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan just explained why choices like that are spreading. At a panel hosted by lender DBS in Singapore on Monday, October 12, 2026, he called Chinese models like DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM "good enough." They cost less per token and are being adopted quickly, he said, according to Reuters. Tan also said quantum computing could become mainstream within three to five years. That is a strikingly short window for a technology many investors still file under someday. Read together, the remarks sound less like a CEO praising rivals and more like one describing his market. Cheaper models spread AI work across more hardware, and much of it lands on processors Intel sells. Also read: Elon Musk just handed Intel a new problem Wall Street can't ignore Lower prices rarely shrink demand for computing. When each answer from a model costs less, companies build AI into more products, and total usage climbs. Tan made a similar point in July, saying AI is driving "unprecedented demand for compute." Intel's latest results show that pull. Data center and AI revenue jumped 59% to $6.3 billion in the second quarter, according to Intel's earnings release. The release highlighted Xeon systems built for inference and agentic workloads, the everyday running of AI rather than training it. AI agents push that further. Each agent coordinates tasks, moves data and calls tools, much of it on CPUs rather than GPUs. Low-cost open models make agents cheaper to deploy, which multiplies that background work. The China angle cuts both ways. China generated about $12.7 billion of Intel's $52.9 billion in 2025 revenue, based on billing location, according to its annual report. That is nearly a quarter of sales, tied to the same market whose models Tan praised. Server processors also largely sit outside U.S. export curbs on advanced AI chips. Chinese buyers have been signing longer purchase agreements for them as prices climb. Cheap domestic models running on available server chips create a setup that plays to Intel's strengths. However, the politics are delicate. The U.S. government took a 9.9% stake in Intel for $8.9 billion in August 2025, according to Intel. Two weeks earlier, President Donald Trump called Tan "highly conflicted" over his China ties, Al Jazeera reported.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Here are three reasons the stock is a buy heading into 2027. Intel has topped its own financial expectations for seven straight quarters. Beating guidance repeatedly shows the company is executing well against its goals and managing its factories and costs, which can support a higher stock price over time as investors gain confidence. Here are the key highlights from the Q2 earnings report that point to building momentum in the business: Revenue rose 25% year over year to $16.1 billion -- the company's strongest growth in more than 15 years. Non-GAAP gross margin (the share of revenue left after production costs) reached 41.8%, more than 12 points higher than a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.42 more than doubled the guidance of $0.20, and reversed a loss of $0.10 in the year-ago quarter. Higher revenue, better manufacturing yields (more working chips per wafer), and stronger average selling prices drove the strong results, with data-center and AI sales growing 59% to $6.3 billion. AI-related businesses made up roughly 70% of Intel's total revenue in the quarter. CFO David Zinsner said the near-term goal was to get gross margins "comfortably into the 40s" every quarter -- implying the potential for more gains over its Q2 gross margin. Overall, the prospect of expanding margins is a positive for the stock heading into 2027. AI will need a massive number of central processing units (CPUs), as well as specialized accelerators and graphics processing units (GPUs). CPUs have proven more effective at handling orchestration, data movement, and storage around AI training and inference. The growing use of AI agents (software that performs tasks autonomously) will put more strain on existing compute capacity and is a long-term tailwind for Intel.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan bought about 105,000 shares near $95 as short interest reached roughly 158 million shares ahead of Intel's Oct. 29 earnings report. The artificial intelligence (AI) hardware cycle initially rewarded designers who could deliver raw training compute at nearly any price. Hyperscalers absorbed heavy infrastructure costs to build foundational models, leaving smaller data centers struggling to participate. As the industry pivots from training models to running daily inference workloads, AI economics are shifting rapidly. Power constraints, specialized liquid cooling requirements, and ballooning capital expenditures are forcing a reevaluation of how data centers physically scale. → A Silent Winner: Texas Instruments Anchors the AI Supercycle Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC) recently addressed this specific gap at the Open Compute Project Global Summit. The technology manufacturer revealed the technical specifications for its GPU D-Series, code-named Crescent Island. This new hardware targets cost-conscious enterprise buyers looking to deploy artificial intelligence without rebuilding physical infrastructure from scratch. By focusing on memory capacity and power efficiency over raw training speed, Intel is carving out a high-margin niche. This hardware launch introduces an interesting shift in market fundamentals as a highly anticipated corporate restructuring takes shape. → A Chinese Rival Just Spooked Memory Stocks—How Worried Should Micron Investors Be? Top-tier accelerators require extensive liquid cooling systems and heavy power draws, creating a high barrier to entry. Many enterprise facilities lack the specialized plumbing and grid capacity to support these environments. The GPU D-Series bypasses these physical limitations. Built on the Xe3P architecture, Crescent Island allocates its silicon entirely to inference. Operating within a 350-watt power envelope, the card utilizes a standard air-cooled PCIe form factor. This allows operators to slot the hardware directly into existing server racks.

Is AMD Stock Safer Or Riskier Than A Year Ago?

No summary available

Investors holding Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock have enjoyed a very good year: shares returned 157.8% over the past year, compared with a 17.9% gain for the S&P 500. A return of that magnitude prompts a closer look at the underlying business, and the company's financial report for the quarter e...

Investors holding Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock have enjoyed a very good year: shares returned 157.8% over the past year, compared with a 17.9% gain for the S&P 500. A return of that magnitude prompts a closer look at the underlying business, and the company's financial report for the quarter ended June 27, 2026, provides the latest view into its accounts. Has the company taken on more risk to get there? Mostly Safer, But AMD Is Spending More On Assets The balance sheet is mostly safer, because AMD holds far more cash than it did a year ago. At the end of the quarter on June 27, 2026, cash and short-term investments stood at $13.1 billion, up from $5.87 billion a year earlier. Total debt also rose during that period, climbing to $4.28 billion from $3.89 billion. Even so, AMD ended the quarter with net cash of $8.84 billion. AMD has changed in one key area: capital spending is now running above its depreciation and amortization charge. Over the twelve months to June 27, 2026, capital spending reached $1.68 billion, compared with a $1.17 billion depreciation and amortization charge. That reverses a long trend. At each of the 16 quarter ends prior to that, from June 2022 to March 2026, twelve-month capital spending stayed below the charge for the same twelve months. In the latest quarter alone, AMD spent $808 million on new assets, up from $282 million in the same quarter a year earlier. Why Is AMD Spending More Now? The company appears to be spending to keep pace with demand it did not anticipate. Server chip supply ran tight through the first half of the year because much of the demand was unforecasted, management noted on the August 4, 2026, call. AMD has also been working across its supply chain, from wafers to substrates, to raise capacity for servers. That demand is visible in the latest financial results. Data center revenue grew 107% from a year earlier to $6.7 billion in fiscal Q2 2026, management said. Helios, the system housing AMD's MI450 series GPUs, was in production at the time of the call, with Microsoft and Anthropic both planning to deploy it. First shipments were scheduled to begin later that quarter, which is the period AMD reports next, on or around November 3, 2026. What Does AMD's Spending Mean For Your Money? Free cash flow, the cash remaining after capital spending, was $1.56 billion in fiscal Q2 2026. Over the twelve months to June 27, capital spending amounted to 16.6% of the cash AMD's operations brought in. This offers a positive signal for shareholders: AMD pays for its new assets out of a small portion of its cash and keeps the rest.

Many Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) investors warily monitor Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO). And for good reason. AMD competes directly with Nvidia. Broadcom co-develops custom silicon for companies such as Alphabet's (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) Google to help them reduce their dependence on Nvidia. However, there's another chip designer that Nvidia investors should be watching closely. This company isn't even really a rival to Nvidia. But without it, Nvidia is unlikely to be successful going forward. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » I won't try to build the suspense: The chipmaker I'm referring to is Arm Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM). In some ways, Arm ranks as the most important semiconductor stock other than Nvidia itself. Arm's business model makes it unique from AMD, Broadcom, and other chipmakers. The company licenses its architecture, then collects royalties on every chip manufactured using its designs. Some have described the ongoing intense competition between semiconductor makers as the "chip wars." By that analogy, Arm is the top weapons supplier to many major combatants. Nvidia is a key customer for ARM. The Vera CPUs built to run agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are built on Arm's architecture. When Nvidia recently projected a stunning $20 billion in Vera CPU sales by the end of the current fiscal year, it was understandably great news for Arm. Arm has already made a huge inroad into the data center CPU market, though. Its customers include the big three cloud providers -- Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Google. Arm executive vice president Mohamed Awad recently told Nikkei Asia in an interview that his company has captured "over 50%" of the hyperscaler market, adding, "The tailwinds are running with us." Throughout most of this year, Arm's stock outperformed nearly every other semiconductor stock. It's still handily beating Nvidia and Broadcom, although a recent pullback now has Arm trailing behind AMD. This stock performance is backed up by strong financial growth. Arm's revenue jumped 22% year over year in the first quarter of its fiscal year 2027 to a record high of roughly $1.3 billion. Royalty revenue comprised around 55% of that total, reaching $715 million. This bodes well for Arm going forward. When royalties from chips sold that use its architecture generate more revenue than upfront licensing deals, the company's revenue stream is more predictable.

Is There A Risk Hiding In AMD Stock's Big Run?

No summary available

For investors holding Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), the pressing concern is how much of each sale actually translates into profit. AMD's operating margin, the share of sales left after all running costs, stood at 17.3% in the quarter to June 2026. Shareholders currently pay 22.6 times sales for AMD ...

For investors holding Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), the pressing concern is how much of each sale actually translates into profit. AMD's operating margin, the share of sales left after all running costs, stood at 17.3% in the quarter to June 2026. Shareholders currently pay 22.6 times sales for AMD stock, compared with 3.1 times for the S&P 500. At that valuation, the margin matters immensely. So has that margin been climbing steadily? Is AMD's Profit On Each Sale Rising Steadily? The trajectory is not steady, although the margin shows a large jump from a year earlier. In the quarter to June 2025, AMD posted an operating loss equal to 1.7% of its sales. AMD has said that quarter carried about $800 million of inventory and related charges, tied to U.S. export limits on its MI308 chip shipments to China. Much of the recent jump looks like the company climbing out of a single weak quarter. That quarter to June 2025 marked its only operating loss in the last five quarters. Following that deficit, the margin has fluctuated, hitting a low of 13.7% in the quarter to September 2025. Since the end of June, AMD has agreed to acquire Taalas, a startup producing chips for inference. The company has also agreed to buy the AI lab World Labs in an all-stock transaction. Neither deal appears in the margin yet. How each acquisition will ultimately affect the margin is not known. After Running Costs, AMD Lags The S&P 500 Over the twelve months to June 2026, AMD recorded an operating margin of 15.7%, compared with 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as a single entity. The gap between the two is mild. Over its last three twelve-month periods, AMD saw its sales grow an average of 24.4% a year, against 5.9% for the S&P 500. The company expands much faster than the overall market, yet it converts slightly less of each sale into operating profit. When measured across full twelve-month intervals, however, AMD shows a rising margin. The metric stood at 3.7% for the period from July 2023 to June 2024. It then increased to 8.3% for the next twelve months, a span that includes the loss quarter. In the twelve months since that timeframe, the margin has climbed once more. How Hard Has AMD Stock Fallen In Past Sell-Offs? The stock has dropped harder than the S&P 500 in each of the five market shocks since 2022. The deepest of these declines occurred during the 2022 inflation shock. In that event, AMD stock fell 63% while the S&P 500 ETF dropped 24%. During the 2025 tariff shock, the stock fell 32% against a 19% drop for the index.

Advanced Micro Devices vs. Arm: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

Choosing between Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Arm (NASDAQ:ARM) requires understanding two distinct paths within the chip industry. You must decide whether to favor a chip designer or an architecture licensor for 2026. Advanced Micro Devices operates as a direct provider of high-performan...

Choosing between Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Arm (NASDAQ:ARM) requires understanding two distinct paths within the chip industry. You must decide whether to favor a chip designer or an architecture licensor for 2026. Advanced Micro Devices operates as a direct provider of high-performance computing hardware, while Arm licenses the underlying architectural blueprints used by other designers. This comparison explores which business model and financial profile offers a more compelling opportunity for retail investors today. AMD is a prominent player among semiconductor stocks, designing high-performance computing products for data centers, gaming, and personal computers. The company sells CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators to major hyperscale operators and hardware manufacturers. Key commercial agreements include Sony (NYSE:SONY) for gaming consoles, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) for Xbox and operating systems, and a strategic partnership with OpenAI. AMD relies on a limited number of customers for a substantial portion of its revenue, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business. According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion. This represents growth of roughly 34.3% compared with the prior year, indicating strong demand for its AI-focused hardware. Net income for the period was approximately $4.3 billion, reflecting a net margin of nearly 12.5% as the company successfully scales its high-end computing segments. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.1, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, comparing current assets to current liabilities to assess short-term liquidity, was approximately 2.9. Free cash flow, calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, was nearly $6.7 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. Arm operates a unique business model by developing the compute platform and architecture that other semiconductor companies license. Its technology is ubiquitous, deployed in more than 350 billion chips to date and powering over 99% of the world's smartphones. While the company does not disclose major customers in its SEC filings, its reach extends across cloud AI, edge computing, and autonomous machines. Arm earns revenue through licensing fees and royalties paid by partners that build chips using its fundamental designs.

Chip behemoth Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) recently unveiled its Helion agentic artificial intelligence (AI) rack, which is powered by AMD Compute and built on an Open Compute Project (OCP) spec design. The platform's highlight is that, unlike Helios (built for frontier AI training), it comes in two configurations. The first configuration is that of a CPU-only rack that is built on its sixth-generation EPYC silicon, which is capable of scaling to 32,768 CPU cores. This can be used by hyperscalers seeking dedicated capacity to run AI agents, separate from the infrastructure used for model inference. The second configuration is an all-in-one rack that combines AMD EPYC CPU nodes with AMD Instinct MI350P GPU nodes. This version targets enterprise agentic AI deployments. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has pushed Brent crude above $106 a barrel, and diesel prices at the pump are at record highs. Markets now worry that higher fuel costs will soon reach grocery shelves. The bigger worry for investors is the core reading, which excludes food and energy. Core prices rose 0.3% in the month against expectations of 0.2%. Annual core inflation reached 2.6%, above the 2.5% forecast. Traders now put the odds of another hike at its Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 54%, and at more than 96% by year-end, per CME Group's FedWatch tool. With the mid-term elections approaching, investors face higher inflation, rising borrowing costs and geopolitical uncertainty at once. In such conditions, attention tends to move toward companies with solid earnings and reasonable valuations, which is where value stocks come in. Value investors can consider stocks such as Honda Motor, Micron Technology, Avnet, Inc., Delek US Holdings and Plains GP Holdings, L.P., which have high earnings yields. One metric widely used by value investors to identify potentially undervalued stocks is earnings yield. Calculated by dividing a company's annual earnings per share by its current stock price, earnings yield indicates the amount of earnings generated for every dollar invested in a stock. Generally, a higher earnings yield suggests a stock may be undervalued relative to its earnings potential, while a lower earnings yield can indicate a richer valuation. Earnings yield also provides a useful way to compare stocks with fixed-income investments such as bonds. When a stock's earnings yield exceeds prevailing bond yields, it may offer a more attractive return potential, making it a valuable tool for investors searching for opportunities in an uncertain market.

Micron (NASDAQ: MU) has been one of the biggest winners of the AI era. Over the last year, the stock is up roughly 400%, and over the last three years, the stock has jumped 1,250%. Like other memory stocks, Micron has benefited from a shortage in memory chips, which has driven up prices and sent sector stocks soaring across the board. Among the winners are SK Hynix, Samsung, and Sandisk. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » However, in recent months, some doubts have emerged about the memory boom. Micron stock peaked following its fiscal third-quarter earnings report and has struggled to return to that level, despite another blowout earnings report in September. Micron's recent results are about as strong as any company in history. It just reported 379% revenue growth to $54.2 billion with an operating margin of 80.7%. Operating income jumped 1,100% to 43.8%. Micron's operating income in its most recent quarter ranks above Apple, Alphabet, and Microsoft, and it's extraordinarily rare for any company to report an operating margin as high as 80%, meaning the company keeps four of every five dollars it earns in revenue, before interest and taxes. The spike in memory prices and surging demand are the primary reasons for those bumper results. However, those numbers weren't enough to please investors, as the market is wary of the history of cyclicality in the memory sector, and they are betting that Micron's profits will come down significantly once the supply crunch eases. The stock is now down 23% from its all-time high in June. Let's take a look at the stock's history to make an educated guess at what happens next. In recent history, Micron has a strong track record at bouncing back from sell-offs like the current one. As you can see from the chart below, five times in the last decade, Micron has fallen by more than 23%, and each time the stock has recovered to an all-time high or near one. MU data by YCharts Looking at that chart, you can see that it sometimes takes Micron years to recover from 30%, 40%, or 50%, but it always does. That period includes multiple cycles in the memory sector, including 2022-2023, when Micron was losing billions of dollars a year due to a glut. However, taking a longer view of history, the results are less encouraging.

Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) has had a great year. It's up around 230% so far in 2026, making it the fourth-best-performing stock in the S&P 500 this year. Normally, you're supposed to buy a stock before it makes a run like that, but even after the run-up, I've decided to open a position in Micron. Why? It seems as if some of Micron's old tendencies are a thing of the past. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Micron makes memory chips, and the industry is known to be cyclical. There isn't much that separates one memory chip manufacturer from another, so Micron has no pricing power. You can see this in action when you think about purchasing an aftermarket thumb drive or upgrading your computer's RAM. All components are about the same, but what really matters is how cheaply you can buy them. The market goes through demand cycles that go up and down, and when it's swinging up, times are good for Micron and its peers. But when it's a downturn, they're stuck with excess inventory and can't sell any new production, so the companies, and thus the stock, struggle. Right now, we're amid the biggest memory-demand wave ever seen, thanks to the intensity of the artificial intelligence build-out. All available production capacity for both types of memory chips (DRAM and NAND, both of which Micron makes) is currently consumed. Every memory chip company has said demand far exceeds capacity, causing prices to skyrocket. The fear is that this demand wave will eventually fade, leaving Micron in a much worse state than it is now. However, Micron is taking steps to reduce the severity of the eventual downturn. Micron has now signed several deals with its clients that set floor and ceiling prices for memory chips, which will stabilize the market. Furthermore, these are take-or-pay agreements, so Micron has locked in an estimated 35% of its revenue through 2030. That's a huge step toward ending the cyclicality of Micron's business, as Micron is now being treated more like a true supplier rather than just a commodity dealer. Another development is that Micron is partnering with Nvidia to create an industry-first custom memory chip for its GPUs. This will completely shift Micron's relationship with one of the biggest memory buyers in the world, which is a great thing for Micron.

While increased competition could eventually pressure memory pricing, Micron and SanDisk remain well-positioned to benefit from surging artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure demand. With earnings estimates trending higher and valuations remaining remarkably attractive, the recent pullback could present an ideal buying opportunity. Image Source: Zacks Investment Research Although both companies benefit from the AI memory boom, their exposure differs. Micron offers a more diversified portfolio, producing dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and NAND flash memory. Its HBM chips are particularly important for AI accelerators, including those from Nvidia NVDA), while its NAND products support rapidly expanding data-center storage needs. Meanwhile, SanDisk is a more concentrated play on NAND flash memory and solid-state drives (SSDs), which are increasingly essential for storing and retrieving the enormous amounts of data generated by AI applications. Notably, CXMT's latest breakthrough involves DRAM technology, making it a more direct competitive threat to Micron than SanDisk, whose primary Chinese competition comes from NAND manufacturer Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). That said, YMTC's competitive threat to SanDisk's higher-value enterprise storage business remains somewhat limited by U.S. trade restrictions and its greater concentration in China's domestic and consumer-oriented NAND markets. Most importantly to the buy-the-dip scenario is that Wall Street's earnings outlook for both companies remains encouraging despite the recent selloff. Micron's current fiscal 2027 earnings estimates have climbed more than 12% over the past month, with the Zacks Consensus now calling for EPS to surge 135% year over year to $177.73. Plus, FY28 EPS is projected to increase another 19% to $211.82, with estimates up nearly 12% in the last 30 days as well from $189.28 per share, despite a slight dip in the last week from $212.99. Image Source: Zacks Investment Research Meanwhile, the Zacks Consensus indicates SanDisk's EPS could more than triple from its FY26 levels to $213.31 per share.

With strong growth and an upbeat outlook, both seem poised to capitalize on rising AI infrastructure demand. But which stock offers a better buying opportunity? Let's explore – As AI infrastructure needs high-performance memory, demand for Micron's cutting-edge high-bandwidth memory ("HBM") chips has surged. This momentum helped the company post revenues of $54.23 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, up sharply from $11.32 billion a year ago, according to its Sept. 30 press release. For fiscal 2026, Micron's revenues were $133.19 billion, up from $37.38 billion in fiscal 2025. Its guidance remains even more encouraging, with the company expecting revenues of $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion, in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The data center business continues to be Micron's key growth engine, benefiting from an increase in AI-related demand. Additionally, Micron's profit margins are reaching exceptional levels. Its non-GAAP gross margin increased from 84.9% in the fiscal third quarter of 2026 to 87% in the fiscal fourth quarter, supported by higher selling prices, a favorable product mix, and operating leverage. Further, the company's management expects its Strategic Customer Agreements to improve earnings visibility. According to NVIDIA's Aug. 26 press release, the company's revenues climbed 106% year over year and 18% sequentially to $96 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2027. Its Data Center segment remained the primary growth driver, with revenues surging 117% year over year to $89 billion. Going forward, NVIDIA expects revenues of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, in the fiscal third quarter of 2027, signaling further sequential growth. The company also expects profitability to remain strong as its Vera Rubin platform has entered the full production stage, while NVIDIA remains well-positioned to capitalize on the next wave of AI infrastructure demand. By the way, NVIDIA's gross margin rose to 75% in the fiscal second quarter of 2027 from 72.4% a year earlier, while both GAAP and non-GAAP net income increased. NVIDIA's GAAP operating income more than doubled year over year, implying strong operating leverage. Both Micron and NVIDIA's recent strong revenue growth, expanding margins, and upbeat guidance could boost both stocks. However, U.S. chip export restrictions to China and stiff competition could limit NVIDIA's further growth, while Micron's evolution from a highly cyclical memory stock to a vital supplier of AI infrastructure could drive sustained growth.

Micron’s New Taiwan Plant Is Sold Out for 2027. Its Workers Want 15% of Profits

The Taichung facility, called AATT2, packages and tests high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the chips that sit next to AI processors. Pres...

Micron Technology (MU:NASDAQ) opened its second advanced assembly and test plant in Taiwan on Thursday, October 15, and said the site has nothing left to sell for 2027. The Taichung facility, called AATT2, packages and tests high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the chips that sit next to AI processors. President and COO Manish Bhatia said its entire planned 2027 capacity is already sold out. The ribbon-cutting came with a warning attached. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te used the event to urge Micron and its workers to negotiate sincerely ahead of a possible strike over bonuses. No strike has started. Sold out means customers have already claimed AATT2's planned 2027 output, so a walkout there could disrupt committed shipments. How much would depend on the strike's scale and duration, and on Micron's contingency measures. The Taoyuan union announced its strike authorization on October 7, after voting from October 1 to 6, and has floated a surprise walkout (no date set). The bigger Taichung union, with about 11,000 members among 12,300 employees, hasn't voted yet. It returns to mediation on October 22. AATT2 sits in Taichung. The unions want profit-sharing tied to 15% of Micron's operating profit. Their timing is no accident. Micron's operating income jumped to $99.34 billion in fiscal 2026 (ended September 3), roughly 10 times the $9.77 billion it earned a year earlier. Fifteen percent of that is about $15 billion a year. Samsung (005930.KS) settled its own strike threat in May with a bonus pool worth 10.5% of its chip division's operating profit. The same rate at Micron would be about $10 billion. The surge shows up quarter by quarter, too. Revenue climbed from $11.32 billion in the quarter ended August 2025 to $54.23 billion in the quarter ended September 2026, nearly five times higher. That's the leverage. Micron can afford a deal. Even a 15% payout would leave it about $84 billion of last year's operating profit. A prolonged walkout at AATT2 would put committed HBM deliveries at risk, though that needs Taichung's talks to fail first. How much it would cost, and whether any orders would drift to rivals such as SK Hynix (000660), is still an open question. Another one-off bonus probably won't settle this. Micron already offered Taiwan staff up to 68 months of pay for fiscal 2026, and the Taoyuan union rejected it because it wanted a permanent profit-sharing system. October 22 is the date that counts: if Taichung's mediation fails, Micron's largest Taiwan union can move to its own strike vote.

Comments from Broadcom (AVGO) CEO Hock Tan that many AI investors "have no clue" what they own added to the pressure. He was replying to a post that highlighted a bullish JPMorgan note on memory, and Futurum Equities' Shay Boloor said Micron could turn that goodwill into longer contracts and more market share, according to Benzinga. Musk has skin in the game as a big memory buyer. Micron's memory sits inside Nvidia chips used in his Colossus data centers, and in April, Musk named Micron as one of his existing suppliers while discussing his Terafab project. Micron and Musk's companies have not announced a direct deal. Memory costs are a sore spot across tech right now. AI servers are crowding out DRAM capacity, and TrendForce said in September that shortages and price increases could continue into 2027. The contract price of a popular smartphone memory setup had nearly quadrupled in a year by February, based on an earlier TrendForce estimate. Apple has already raised prices on its newest iPhone Pro models, as reported by TheStreet. Micron is leaning on long-term deals rather than squeezing buyers for every dollar. The company now has 26 strategic customer agreements, up from 16 a quarter earlier, and expects them to cover about 35% of its revenue through 2030. Those customer financial commitments have risen to $32 billion in total. The latest results show why customers are lining up. Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up from $11.32 billion a year earlier and $41.46 billion in the prior quarter, according to its earnings release. That works out to about $43 billion more than a year ago and about $12.8 billion more than three months earlier. The beat was broad. Revenue topped analyst estimates, adjusted earnings came in ahead of forecasts, and the gross margin reached 87%, above the company's own outlook.

Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock fell for a fourth straight day Thursday, continuing a rout that began with Monday's announcement that Chinese DRAM company ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, has invented "4F square" technology to increase DRAM storage density -- and may soon be coming for Micron's market share. Micron stock is down 2.8% as of 10:35 a.m. ET, and down 13.5% so far this week. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Continue » Image source: Micron. Global market intelligence company Trendforce says CXMT holds 9.5% of the global DRAM memory market, putting it in fourth place behind Samsung (39.4%), SK Hynix (24.9%), and Micron (23.3%). DRAM is the biggest part of Micron's business, providing 73% of the company's revenue. (The other 26% comes from sales of NAND flash memory.) Why is that important? KeyBanc analyst John Vinh predicts DRAM prices will rise 15% to 20% year over year in Q4 2026, while NAND prices rise 20%. That gives Micron two ways to profit from the global deficit in memory chips. High-bandwidth memory -- the most lucrative segment of this market for Micron and the area where CXMT is weakest -- could see prices rise 80% to 100% in Q1 2027. But now here's the important point: Memory companies that operate logically will emphasize production of HBM DRAM for artificial intelligence data centers -- because that's where the money is. Doing so, Vinh predicts they will cut DRAM production for cellphones and PCs by 20% to 30% next year. CXMT's DRAM, which is "two or three generations" behind Micron, will most likely go to fill this low-end gap -- leaving Micron free to reap better margins producing high-end HBM DRAM! In this case, CXMT mayn't be as big a threat as investors fear. Micron's profit margins should be safe. The facilities would help smaller suppliers that are essential to the operations of Nvidia's main production partner Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and AI server assemblers including Foxconn Technology Group to set up shop in the US, Kung said. Each complex would run between $2 billion and $4 billion to build, and the government is planning "more than one" site on US soil, Kung said in an Oct. 12 interview with Bloomberg News. The Taiwanese government is partnering with the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers' Association, which will be responsible for raising required funding to develop the complexes, he said. "We are going to establish a long-term, sustainable supply chain there that can also be joined by American firms and local workers, and not just Taiwanese companies," Kung said. Companies like TSMC, Foxconn and Wistron Corp. provide essential hardware for data centers and are critical to the success of US AI chipmakers including Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., and cloud service providers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Microsoft Corp. These Taiwanese manufacturing titans depend in turn on lesser-known partners that make a wide range of parts from chip packaging substrates to cooling modules — everything that's required in an AI data center. But while TSMC and Foxconn are capable of funding and managing their own US expansion, that's not always the case for smaller firms. That's how Taiwan is hoping the new industrial complexes in the US could help. Many of these suppliers got a boost from Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang when he cited the names of a few dozen parts makers during a keynote presentation in Taipei earlier this year, a gesture that signaled how indispensable the firms are to the global AI ecosystem.

TSMC (NYSE:TSM) posted record profit Thursday and said artificial intelligence demand still exceeds supply, even as semiconductor stocks extend a sharp selloff. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 4.3% Wednesday and is down about 11% over six sessions, according to Reuters. Semiconductor industry veteran Steve Williams, who spent more than 25 years at Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT), says investors may be applying an outdated playbook. "They're still in this fear of the old cyclical demand cycle," Williams told Benzinga. "And the current technology and AI build-out has broken the old demand cycle." TSMC's third-quarter net profit rose 69%. The company guided to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, roughly 58% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. But one number stood out to Williams. TSMC's 2-nanometer process jumped from 3% of wafer revenue in the second quarter to 8% in the third. 2nm is TSMC's newest leading-edge process, and the rapid increase likely points to strong early adoption of its latest technology. "I expected an increase, but that's a big, big jump," Williams said. He expects that share to keep rising as leading-edge customers compete for limited capacity. TSMC kept 2026 capex at $60 billion to $64 billion, but Williams said the unchanged figure does not signal weaker demand. Equipment arriving this year was ordered months ago, with some larger tools carrying lead times of six months or more. Williams told Benzinga last week that advanced packaging was TSMC's immediate bottleneck. TSMC has signed a $2 billion manufacturing agreement with GlobalFoundries to add U.S. silicon-interposer capacity for its CoWoS packaging ecosystem. But solving packaging would simply move the constraint, Williams said, most likely back to TSMC's ability to manufacture enough leading-edge 2nm chips. Push expansion further and equipment makers themselves may become the bottleneck. "They can only go so far before ASML can't make what they need," Williams said. ASML (NASDAQ:ASML) said this week its planned supply will not fully satisfy customer demand in 2027 or 2028. Williams sees chip demand persisting even if the current data-center construction wave slows. The growing installed base of data centers will still require chips as computing equipment is replaced and upgraded, he said.

"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," he said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore, according to Bloomberg. He said they "set very extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino." Broadcom supplies the hardware that frontier AI labs need to build their systems. But while Broadcom can profit from selling chips, the AI labs buying computing power must still find enough paying customers to cover the cost of developing and running their models. The challenge is to turn demand into sustainable revenue. Tan acknowledged that OpenAI's reported $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September points to a viable business model for AI labs, but said it doesn't guarantee that they will be profitable. Annualized revenue extrapolates a company's current sales pace across a year. It does not measure revenue collected over 12 months, and labs have expenses to cover. OpenAI expects to spend over $25 billion on training alone this year. "For now it's still losing money because they're spending a lot on training," Tan said. "So frankly, it doesn't tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models." The cost of developing AI also raises questions about whether investors will keep footing the bill, with some analysts predicting that AI capital expenditure growth will slow next year. Tan said a lack of capital "might be the biggest constraint" on the AI industry, more than a memory, semiconductor, or electricity shortage. There are already signs investors are questioning how much money AI infrastructure companies are asking for. The sell-off in AI-related stocks, according to Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson, is increasingly about who needs financing and what that financing costs. "I think the street is tiring of the Bank of Nvidia, the Bank of AMD and the Bank of Broadcom," Mortonson told Yahoo Finance Senior Reporter Brooke DiPalma (video above), referring to chipmakers Nvidia (NVDA), AMD (AMD), and Broadcom (AVGO). "This is very unusual in this cycle… It's not going over well with the institutional community," he added. Mortonson pointed to "a higher cost of capital" and "a lot of scrutiny now on circular finance," which he said was "coming out of the Anthropic research meeting." Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) reportedly told investors at a closed meeting that its third-quarter revenue climbed to $16.8 billion. CoreWeave stock (CRWV) fell more than 15% on Wednesday and fell again in pre-market trading on Thursday. Mortonson noted that that CoreWeave, Nebius (NBIS), and Oracle (ORCL) are "probably at the bottom" of tech on free cash flow. Read more: Oracle stock falls on more debt to fund AI chip buying, OpenAI revenue disclosure These companies are "very dependent on financing going forward," he said., adding: "That is the real issue… their free cash flow and the cost of capital [is] so elevated today that anything that has that exposure is being sold." Adding to the souring sentiment, a new Gartner forecast that most neocloud providers will "cease independent operations" by 2030. Chipmakers with strong results are getting hit, too. "Portfolio managers are selling names that have unadulterated blowout numbers, and they're not acting well," Mortonson said, pointing to Samsung (005930.KS), Micron (MU), and ASML (ASML). Read more: Global chip sell-off deepens as South Korean market plunges So is the drop a chance to buy? "That's the million dollar question," Mortonson said. The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) was up about 87% for the year as of Oct. 6, which he called "a good decade of performance." It closed Wednesday up 65% for that period. The pullback is "healthy," Mortonson said, but it also "represents that the institutional community that has been very overweight the infrastructure play [and] is going elsewhere." Where? "They're probably going to software, to be honest with you." Some money is leaving tech altogether, he added, as a lot of portfolio managers "are trying to lock in performance as they go into the end of the year." Elon Musk takes a direct swipe at Broadcom CEO and AI investors

No summary available

Elon Musk rarely passes up a chance at a one-liner. When Broadcom CEO Hock Tan compared many AI investors to casino gamblers, Musk replied on X to a post summarizing the remarks with five words: "No crying in the casino." The jab added fuel to a growing debate over how long the AI boom can last. T...

Elon Musk rarely passes up a chance at a one-liner. When Broadcom CEO Hock Tan compared many AI investors to casino gamblers, Musk replied on X to a post summarizing the remarks with five words: "No crying in the casino." The jab added fuel to a growing debate over how long the AI boom can last. The exchange landed at a touchy moment for the AI trade. The Nasdaq fell 1.25% on Oct. 8 as chip stocks, including Nvidia (NVDA) and Broadcom (AVGO), took a hit after questions surfaced about OpenAI's revenue. Also read: AT&T CEO holds firm stance on Elon Musk's SpaceX phone strategy Tan made the comments on Oct. 12 at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore, sharing the stage with Intel (INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan on a panel moderated by DBS CEO Tan Su Shan. "A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," he said, adding that some set very extreme expectations "only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino." He was just as blunt about corporate spending. "People are just wasting money, spending tokens, trying to understand (AI)," Tan said, comparing companies to a child who burns through $10 of arcade tokens in minutes and learns nothing. He added that OpenAI's annualized revenue of roughly $50 billion was "by itself, not that bad" for a startup. That OpenAI figure is exactly what rattled the market a few days earlier. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue was approaching $50 billion at the end of September, well below the nearly $70 billion figure that had been widely reported, and AI infrastructure stocks fell on Oct. 8. Musk has played both sides of this debate. In September, he said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was "right" after Amodei called for an intentional slowdown in advanced AI development. Tan brushed that push aside, saying on Sept. 14 that the debate had not changed Broadcom's AI forecasts "in the least." Tan's warning carries extra weight because few companies have gained more from AI spending than Broadcom. Broadcom reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $29.6 billion in early September, slightly ahead of analyst estimates, with AI semiconductor revenue up 221% from a year earlier, according to its SEC filing. It guided for $21.7 billion in fourth-quarter AI chip revenue, yet shares still fell after hours. The longer-term targets are even bigger. Broadcom expects AI semiconductor revenue of about $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and about $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Tan also arranged a financing partnership with Apollo and Blackstone to back more than 20 gigawatts of computing capacity, a buildout that will require hundreds of billions of dollars.

The 606-megawatt (MW) natural gas-fired combined-cycle facility is located outside Houston and operates in the ERCOT market. The transaction represents continued progress in satisfying regulatory commitments related to Constellation's acquisition of Calpine, which closed in January 2026. Constellation entered into an agreement to sell Brazos Valley to LS Power in August 2026, as reported in the Q2 earnings results. The company also previously announced an agreement to sell approximately 4.4 gigawatts of predominantly natural gas-fired generation assets in Delaware and Pennsylvania to LS Power. Those assets include the Bethlehem, York 1, York 2, Hay Road and Edge Moor facilities. The sale of the PJM assets is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. The divestitures are part of Constellation's agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice related to its acquisition of Calpine. Constellation completed the acquisition on Jan. 7, 2026, creating the world's largest private-sector power producer and significantly expanding the company's generation portfolio and competitive retail business. About Constellation Constellation Energy Corporation (Nasdaq: CEG), a Fortune 200 company headquartered in Baltimore, is the largest private-sector power producer in the world and the nation's largest producer of clean and reliable energy. With 55 gigawatts of capacity from nuclear, natural gas, oil, geothermal, hydro, wind and solar facilities, our fleet has the generating capacity to power the equivalent of 27 million homes, providing about 10% of the nation's clean energy and delivering the around-the-clock reliability needed to power America's growing economy. We are also the largest nuclear energy company in the U.S. and a leading competitive retail supplier, serving approximately 2.5 million customer accounts nationwide, including 80% of the Fortune 100. We are committed to investing in innovation and new technologies to drive the transition to a reliable, sustainable and secure energy future. Follow Constellation on LinkedIn and X. The technology sector's commitment to nuclear energy continues to strengthen. Just last week, Google's parent company Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) agreed to purchase nuclear-generated electricity from utility company Constellation Energy's (NASDAQ: CEG) existing nuclear power plants for 15 years, in addition to making a 20-year agreement to purchase 890 megawatts' worth of power from nuclear power production facilities that Constellation will build in the future. Alphabet's long-term commitment will enable Constellation Energy to confidently invest $4.3 billion in new nuclear energy capacity, adding to its already-extensive nuclear power portfolio. Constellation shares jumped on the news, of course. But so did shares of small modular reactor (SMR) developers Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale (NYSE: SMR), despite having no involvement in Constellation's agreement with Google. What gives? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » NuScale and Oklo may be positioned to enter the nuclear energy business. However, they're not like Constellation. Constellation Energy's typical nuclear power facility is built to serve hundreds of thousands of utility customers. NuScale and Oklo, on the other hand, are working on small-scale reactors designed to power facilities such as refineries, smelters, and desalination plants, built where the electricity is consumed. The two approaches to providing power are obviously very different -- different enough that investors seemingly shouldn't conflate the two. Yet, they did. Why? Because there's a more philosophical message being delivered here. That's the general recognition that nuclear energy is a far more practical solution to the growing power shortage that renewables were expected to shore up by now. Alphabet's management may not be interested in small modular nuclear reactors (yet). Other companies could be, given the broader reacceptance of this once-waning energy source. Investors are simply connecting the dots, and reasonably so. SMRs will never account for the lion's share of the planet's nuclear power generation, to be clear. Their fiscal math just doesn't make sense at scale. Nevertheless, when grid independence is necessary and desirable, and the need is modest, they do have their place. That's why there are now over 70 small modular reactors already planned, if not already being built, according to estimates from the World Nuclear Association, compared to none in true commercial operation.

After all -- Vistra uses nuclear fuel; Centrus produces (or more commonly, buys and resells) nuclear fuel. It seems logical that more power generation at Vistra should translate directly into Vistra buying more nuclear fuel from Centrus. And yet, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, at least, there's no indication that Vistra is a customer of Centrus -- and no solid reason to believe that Vistra's expansion will in fact benefit Centrus stock. That's not to say othercompanies won't buy more fuel from Centrus, of course. If the DOE loan is the start of a string of similar loans expanding nuclear power production across the U.S., for example, this could very well happen. It's just not a given. And "given" that Centrus stock is currently free cash flow-negative, and costs 83.5 times earnings today, I'm not convinced it's a great idea to bid up Centrus shares even more, on news that might not relate to it at all. Meanwhile, next-generation small modular reactors (SMRs) could begin arriving in the 2030s. Many of these advanced reactors require a specialized fuel that remains in short supply. That's where Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU) sees its opportunity. The company already supplies low-enriched uranium (LEU) to nuclear power operators, but its biggest growth opportunity could come from high-assay, low-enriched uranium (HALEU). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Becoming a leading U.S. producer of this next-generation fuel could make Centrus the ultimate pick-and-shovel play on the nuclear technology boom. Here's what investors need to know. Centrus is an important player in the U.S. nuclear fuel supply chain. Currently, the company generates most of its revenue from supplying LEU to utilities operating traditional nuclear reactors in the U.S. and abroad. The company has manufacturing capabilities, but over the last decade, it has sourced this fuel globally, making it an established middleman. However, this is all changing. In 2023, Congress passed the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, which blocks the import of natural uranium and LEU produced in Russia or by a Russian entity. Some operators have been given limited waivers to import from Russia, but these waivers are set to expire on Jan. 1, 2028. The restrictions will remain in place until Dec. 31, 2040. Centrus relies heavily on TENEX, a Russian state-owned entity, for its LEU. Over half of the LEU it delivers to customers in 2027 is expected to come from TENEX. Russia holds roughly 43% of global enrichment capacity, so Congress' act creates an urgent need to develop domestic nuclear fuel production. The company is pivoting from being an intermediary to becoming a U.S. producer of these fuels. It is making a multibillion-dollar investment in its Ohio and Tennessee facilities to expand domestic enrichment capacity. In Oak Ridge, Tennessee, management is investing over $560 million to produce thousands of centrifuges. Meanwhile, it's expanding its Piketon, Ohio, centrifuge and enrichment plant to develop LEU and HALEU at scale.

Although financial terms were not disclosed, the deal includes prepayments from Antares to help fund Centrus' expanded HALEU capacity. The deal holds strategic importance as Antares is developing compact microreactors for critical missions on Earth and in space. The company was also recently selected for the U.S. Army's Janus Program, a $2.2 billion initiative to build and operate tiny nuclear reactors on military bases, with the hope that they will one day power remote installations. Amir Vexler, President and CEO of Centrus Energy, commented: "This contract is another sign that demand for HALEU is real and it is accelerating, and Centrus is in prime position to meet this need. Binding orders from Antares and others are supporting our expansion to commercial-scale production – an expansion that is now well underway. We look forward to supporting Antares' continued growth and success." dan-meyers-xXbQIrWH2_A-unsplash The Antares deal provides additional evidence that HALEU demand is moving from a development concept toward contracted commercial demand. Centrus is well-positioned to capitalize on the opportunity, as its enrichment technology is already transitioning from demonstration to commercial-scale production. The company is pioneering HALEU production at its enrichment facility in Ohio, the only licensed HALEU production facility in the Western world. Last year, the company launched a multi-billion-dollar expansion to increase production of HALEU and conventional low-enriched uranium. As the Antares agreement includes prepayments, it will help reduce some of the financial burden associated with scaling production. The latest contract adds to Centrus Energy's backlog of $4.5 billion as of the end of the second quarter, including about $3 billion of contingent LEU and HALEU sales commitments. Notably, around $2.4 billion of these commitments are under definitive agreements, increasing confidence that portions of the backlog can eventually translate into material revenue. The financial contributions from the Antares deal remain hard to quantify, since the companies did not disclose the contract value, pricing, or specific delivery volumes. Moreover, deliveries are not scheduled to commence until before the end of the decade, meaning that the agreement does not provide any immediate boost to revenue or earnings.

Production will be "unobligated" that can support national security missions Adds another HALEU customer to Centrus' backlog and includes prepayments to advance domestic enrichment capacity buildout BETHESDA, Md. and TORRANCE, Calif., Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU) and Antares Nuclear today announced the signing of a definitive multi-year contract for Centrus to supply Antares with High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU), with deliveries commencing before the end of the decade. It ensures a reliable, domestic source of HALEU to support Antares advanced reactor projects, including for space and national security missions. The new contract includes prepayments from Antares to support the expanded HALEU capacity. "This contract is another sign that demand for HALEU is real and it is accelerating, and Centrus is in prime position to meet this need," said Amir Vexler, President and CEO of Centrus. "Binding orders from Antares and others are supporting our expansion to commercial-scale production – an expansion that is now well underway. We look forward to supporting Antares' continued growth and success." "Fuel supply is one of the practical questions every advanced reactor developer has to answer," said Jordan Bramble, CEO and Co-Founder of Antares. "This contract gives Antares a reliable, U.S.-origin source of HALEU for the reactors we're deploying for a wide variety of defense and space customers." Antares is developing compact microreactors for critical missions on Earth and in space. The company was recently selected for the U.S. Army's Janus Program at Fort Bragg, North Carolina; the Air Force's Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations program at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas; and a Space Force Strategic Breakthrough award to demonstrate a space reactor. Centrus is pioneering U.S. HALEU production at its American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio, the only licensed HALEU production facility in the western world. Last year, Centrus launched a multi-billion-dollar expansion including large-scale production of HALEU as well as Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU). The agreement reflects the unique role that both companies can play in meeting U.S. national security requirements. Because Centrus's enrichment technology and manufacturing supply chain are U.S.-origin, the arrangement can provide Antares with fuel that could be used for a variety of national security applications. Centrus' AC100 centrifuge design is the only deployment-ready enrichment technology capable of "unobligated" enrichment, meaning that it can be used for U.S. national security missions.

(NYSE: LEU) ("Centrus" or the "Company") today announced the pricing of its previously announced underwritten public offering of 500,000 shares of its Class A common stock (the "Class A Common Stock"), pre-funded warrants (the "Pre-Fu...

BETHESDA, Md., Sept. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU) ("Centrus" or the "Company") today announced the pricing of its previously announced underwritten public offering of 500,000 shares of its Class A common stock (the "Class A Common Stock"), pre-funded warrants (the "Pre-Funded Warrants") to purchase an aggregate of 2,005,513 shares of Class A Common Stock and common warrants (the "Common Warrants") to purchase up to an aggregate of 6,992,382 shares of Class A Common Stock. The offering is priced at a combined public offering price of $199.64 per share of Class A Common Stock and accompanying Common Warrants and $199.54 per Pre-Funded Warrant and accompanying Common Warrants. The purchase price of each Pre-Funded Warrant is equal to the price per share at which shares of Class A Common Stock are being sold in the offering, minus the exercise price for the Pre-Funded Warrants of $0.10 per share. Investors purchasing shares of Class A Common Stock or Pre-Funded Warrants will also receive a pro rata allocation of Common Warrants based on the number of shares of Class A Common Stock or Pre-Funded Warrants purchased by that investor. The closing of the offering is expected to occur on or about September 11, 2026, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. The Pre-Funded Warrants will be immediately exercisable upon issuance for an aggregate of 2,005,513 shares of Class A Common Stock at a nominal exercise price of $0.10 per share. The Common Warrants will be immediately exercisable from the date of issuance for an aggregate of 6,992,382 shares of Class A Common Stock. The Common Warrants will be issued in four series, each with an aggregate exercise price of approximately $500 million. The exercise price for each series will equal $226.8625, $272.2350, $317.6075, and $362.9800 per share of the Class A Common Stock, respectively. Each series will be divided into two equal tranches. The first tranche will expire on the second, third, fourth or fifth anniversary of September 10, 2026, as applicable, and the second tranche will expire on the date that is nine weeks after each such anniversary. The gross proceeds from the offering are expected to be approximately $500 million, before deducting the underwriting discount and other estimated offering expenses payable by Centrus. The gross proceeds from the offering do not include any proceeds that may be received upon exercise of the Common Warrants. The Company intends to use the net proceeds from the offering for general working capital and corporate purposes, which may include investment in technology development and deployment, repayment or repurchase of outstanding debt, capital expenditures, potential acquisitions and other business opportunities and purposes.
