Exxon’s Oil Boom Could Keep Guyana’s Gas at Home

No summary available

Guyana has turned into something of an oil celebrity with billions of barrels discovered by Exxon off the coast of the tiny South American country. With the oil riches came gas, too, and there were plans to add LNG to Guyana's export goods. Yet now the government is considering keeping the gas for t...

Guyana has turned into something of an oil celebrity with billions of barrels discovered by Exxon off the coast of the tiny South American country. With the oil riches came gas, too, and there were plans to add LNG to Guyana's export goods. Yet now the government is considering keeping the gas for the domestic market. Guyana's crude oil exports are about to end the year on a high note and a daily rate of over 1 million barrels, according to a recent report by Bloomberg. It only took the country 10 years to go from no oil production to that rate of exports, after Exxon and its partners in the Stabroek Block—Hess Corp and CNOOC—made a string of discoveries with reserves estimated at over 11 billion barrels. Production ramped up fast, with Exxon and partners bringing in a total of four floating production, storage, and offloading vessels to the Stabroek Block. As a result of this fast development, by September this year, wells in the block had yielded a cumulative 1 billion barrels of oil. Exxon and CNOOC, plus new partner Chevron, are not stopping, either. By 2030, Exxon eyes production capacity of 1.7 million barrels daily from eight offshore projects. This is what is interfering with natural gas plans. Two years ago, the government of Guyana launched a tender for companies interested in developing its gas reserves. It would have been faster and probably easier to just bet on the Exxon-led consortium again, but the authorities in Georgetown made it clear at the time they would like some diversification. The tender, however, ended in a somewhat odd way. Of the 17 companies that submitted proposals, Guyana's government picked one called Fulcrum LNG—set up by a former Exxon executive just a year earlier. Fulcrum was selected by the government of Guyana to develop an LNG export project, whose price tag was at the time calculated at up to $30 billion. The choice of LNG developer was considered odd, as Fulcrum competed with established LNG market players. Since that tender, Guyana's LNG plans have not exactly advanced much—and one big reason for this is the availability of natural gas for liquefaction. Exxon needs some 2 billion cu ft of natural gas daily to inject into its wells to stimulate production, Reuters reported this week, citing unnamed sources, who also said the company had informed the Guyanese government about this. The gas injection is necessary so Exxon can meet oil production targets set for its existing projects in Guyana. In other words, there does not seem to be enough natural gas getting produced in Guyana at this point to make an LNG export project feasible.

Their dividends have held up anyway. TotalEnergies raised its interim dividend 5.9% on April 29, from €0.85 to €0.90 a share, and Exxon declared another $1.03-a-share quarterly dividend with its second-quarter results on July 31. So if you put $10,000 into one of them today, which pays you more over the next 10 years? Exxon's growth is coming from two places. A strong second quarter of 2026, with $17.2 billion of free cash flow against $4.3 billion of dividends, helped bring the ratio back to a comfortable 56% over the twelve months to June 30. The main risk is the Middle East. On its May call, management laid out a three-to-five-year repair timeline for a damaged Qatar LNG train. TotalEnergies took a bigger hit from the same conflict. On its April call, management said shut-in production in Qatar, Iraq and offshore UAE made up approximately 15% of its oil and gas output. By July, it put the impact closer to 8% to 9%. Its growth is in LNG and power, with Mozambique LNG back under construction, plus Namibia, which CEO Patrick Pouyanné called "a very important hub for future growth."

The company has secured exploration rights to a massive deepwater block near Guyana, where Exxon and its partners have already discovered roughly 11 billion barrels of recoverable oil resources. Exxon's head of global exploration, John Ardill, recently told the Financial Times that the company sees Trinidad as a geological extension of its successful Guyana operations. But there's a difference between identifying promising geology and discovering billions of barrels of oil. So the question is: Should you buy Exxon now or wait until the company drills its first exploration well? Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Exxon's Trinidad exploration block, known as TTUD-1, covers approximately 7,165 square kilometers, an area larger than Trinidad and Tobago's entire landmass. The block lies in waters roughly 2,000 to 3,000 meters deep, making exploration technically challenging and expensive. But Exxon has a lot of experience operating in similar conditions. In 2015, the company made its landmark Liza discovery offshore Guyana. Since then, Exxon and its partners have made more than 30 discoveries, transforming Guyana into one of the world's fastest-growing oil-producing countries. By late 2025, production had reached approximately 900,000 barrels per day. Exxon and its partners have committed more than $60 billion to developing Guyana's offshore resources, with plans that could eventually lift production capacity to approximately 1.7 million barrels per day by 2030. Now the company wants to apply that same development strategy to Trinidad. Exxon actually negotiated its Trinidad production-sharing agreement in just seven months, which is significantly faster than the usual process. It now expects to select its first drilling location by mid-2027, with an initial exploration well potentially following in late 2027 or early 2028. If the well produces encouraging results, the company could move toward additional exploration and eventual development. Of course, there's no guarantee Trinidad contains anything close to Guyana's enormous resources. But that wouldn't be the end of the world.

HOUSTON, October 13, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Port Houston will honor ExxonMobil with the 4th Annual Lone Star Award during the Houston International Maritime Conference (HIMC), taking place November 2–5 at the Hilton Americas in downtown Houston. The award recognizes ExxonMobil's exceptional partnership with Port Houston and its longstanding role in the energy industry that is integral to the Houston Ship Channel. Michael Mustian, President, Supply Chain, ExxonMobil, will accept the award on behalf of the company on November 3 and deliver the luncheon keynote address. The presentation will be a highlight of HIMC, which brings together leaders from across the maritime, energy, and petrochemical sectors for industry insight, discussion, and networking. "The Houston Ship Channel's success is built on strong partnerships, and ExxonMobil has long been an important part of the energy and maritime community we serve," said Charlie Jenkins, CEO of Port Houston. "We are pleased to recognize that relationship with this year's Lone Star Award and celebrate the company's longstanding contributions to our region." As advocate and strategic leader for the Houston Ship Channel, Port Houston plays a vital role in a trade gateway that is the busiest waterway in the nation, the number one gateway for energy products, number one in steel, number one in resins, and home to the fifth-ranked container port in the U.S. ExxonMobil's deep connection to Houston's energy industry and the economic vitality of the Houston Ship Channel make the company a fitting recipient of this year's Lone Star Award. The ExxonMobil Baytown Complex is one of the world's largest and most advanced refining and petrochemical facilities. Since opening in 1920, it has expanded to four manufacturing sites, including a plastics plant in nearby Mont Belvieu, as well as a global technology center—spanning 3,400 acres along the Houston Ship Channel. The Lone Star Award presentation will be among the highlights of this year's HIMC program, which will explore the issues and opportunities shaping world trade and maritime operations. Sessions will address Panama Canal developments, the impact of geopolitics on global trade, import and export perspectives, the ocean carrier market, and innovations in resins trade. Beyond the program, HIMC provides an opportunity for executives, policymakers, and industry leaders from around the world to connect and exchange perspectives on the future of global trade. Register for $575 per ticket and explore sponsorship opportunities designed to increase brand visibility and engagement throughout the conference by visiting www.porthouston.com/himc.

Over the past three years, NuScale Power's (NYSE: SMR) stock price has ranged from $2 to $53 per share. Today, it sits at a little under $8. Owning it has been a roller-coaster ride, with five drawdowns of 50% or more over that span. The current drawdown is the worst of them, at roughly 85%. That said, there's a clear event that could prompt investors to rethink their views of NuScale Power. The interesting thing about NuScale Power's huge price swings is that they aren't really driven by its business. That 85% decline didn't happen because of some terrible corporate disaster; it happened because investors got overly enthusiastic about nuclear power stocks, and then moved on to other things. NuScale Power, a nuclear power start-up at the leading edge of nuclear technology, simply went along for the ride. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The technology NuScale Power is working on is small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs). It could be a game changer for the nuclear industry, as factory-built SMRs could be less costly, safer, and easier to place near where they are needed than current large-scale reactors. But the hard truth is that NuScale Power hasn't even built its first commercial SMR yet. It has an approved reactor design, which is a very big deal, but it still needs to find the first customer willing to sign on the dotted line. To the company's credit, it is working hard to ink that first sale. It has been working with the Romanian power company RoPower for quite some time and is seeing material success. RoPower has approved a project that would use six NuScale Power SMRs. But RoPower still needs to nail down project financing, so there's no agreement yet. NuScale Power is also working closely with ENTRA1 Energy and the Tennessee Valley Authority in hopes of being part of what could be "the largest nuclear power deployment program in U.S. history." But, like RoPower, there is still no deal yet. So, what the market is likely waiting for is NuScale Power's first SMR sale. That could be the event that pushes the stock back toward $20. However, it is important to remember that a signed contract is really just the start of the next stage of the company's development. Once it has that contract, it still needs to prove it can build an SMR and that the SMRs it builds are reliable and safe. In other words, NuScale Power is a high-risk start-up, and that isn't likely to change for quite some time.

Google Signed a Deal for Existing Reactors. So Why Did Oklo and NuScale Jump on the Constellation Energy News? The Read-Through Investors Are Missing.

No summary available

The technology sector's commitment to nuclear energy continues to strengthen. Just last week, Google's parent company Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) agreed to purchase nuclear-generated electricity from utility company Constellation Energy's (NASDAQ: CEG) existing nuclear power plants for 1...

The technology sector's commitment to nuclear energy continues to strengthen. Just last week, Google's parent company Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) agreed to purchase nuclear-generated electricity from utility company Constellation Energy's (NASDAQ: CEG) existing nuclear power plants for 15 years, in addition to making a 20-year agreement to purchase 890 megawatts' worth of power from nuclear power production facilities that Constellation will build in the future. Alphabet's long-term commitment will enable Constellation Energy to confidently invest $4.3 billion in new nuclear energy capacity, adding to its already-extensive nuclear power portfolio. Constellation shares jumped on the news, of course. But so did shares of small modular reactor (SMR) developers Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale (NYSE: SMR), despite having no involvement in Constellation's agreement with Google. What gives? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » NuScale and Oklo may be positioned to enter the nuclear energy business. However, they're not like Constellation. Constellation Energy's typical nuclear power facility is built to serve hundreds of thousands of utility customers. NuScale and Oklo, on the other hand, are working on small-scale reactors designed to power facilities such as refineries, smelters, and desalination plants, built where the electricity is consumed. The two approaches to providing power are obviously very different -- different enough that investors seemingly shouldn't conflate the two. Yet, they did. Why? Because there's a more philosophical message being delivered here. That's the general recognition that nuclear energy is a far more practical solution to the growing power shortage that renewables were expected to shore up by now. Alphabet's management may not be interested in small modular nuclear reactors (yet). Other companies could be, given the broader reacceptance of this once-waning energy source. Investors are simply connecting the dots, and reasonably so. SMRs will never account for the lion's share of the planet's nuclear power generation, to be clear. Their fiscal math just doesn't make sense at scale. Nevertheless, when grid independence is necessary and desirable, and the need is modest, they do have their place. That's why there are now over 70 small modular reactors already planned, if not already being built, according to estimates from the World Nuclear Association, compared to none in true commercial operation.

NuScale Power (SMR) reported revenue of $0.1 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared with $8.1 million a year earlier. That number matters because NuScale is still spending to get its nuclear power modules ready to sell. The company recorded an operating loss of about $0.7 billion over the last twelve months, but most of it was a one-time payment of about $507 million to partner ENTRA1. In the latest quarter, the operating loss was about $64 million and operations used about $58 million of cash. So where did NuScale's revenue go? Why Did NuScale's Revenue Almost Disappear? Management attributed the revenue drop to the conclusion of a single piece of work. On an August 5, 2026 call, the company noted that Fluor engineering design work for the RoPower project in Romania finished in late 2025. Nothing comparable took its place in the latest quarter. The drop is not new, either. Revenue has fallen by more than 90% from a year earlier in each of the last three quarters, ending with a 99% contraction in the latest period. Over the last twelve months, revenue fell 81%. This compares with a 305% increase in the twelve months before that. NuScale's revenue appears to have depended on one specific project rather than a steady run of orders. NuScale Has About Two Years Of Cash NuScale ended June with about $1.9 billion in cash and investments, compared to a market value of about $2.5 billion today. Its debt sits at 0.0% of its market value, but its operations consumed about $0.8 billion in cash over the last twelve months. At that pace, the cash would last a little over two years. The stock fell 84% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 17.3%. NuScale still sells for 228.5 times revenue, against 3.1 for the index. The current valuation likely assumes that a contract is coming. What Could Bring NuScale's Revenue Back? Management points to a signed customer contract as the solution. NuScale partner ENTRA1 is negotiating a definitive power purchase agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority. Management stated its understanding is that those talks are active and progressing. It identified the commercial contract as the main catalyst but offered no timeline on the August 5 call. NuScale has some things in its favor while it waits. Management noted it remains the only company in its field holding design certification from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Furthermore, the company's forgings, the components that take the longest to manufacture, have been in production for two years. The RoPower project in Romania plans to deploy six NuScale power modules. NuScale stated on the August 5 call that it is waiting for a new government to approve the final contracts.

So how far has NuScale stock fallen in past market sell-offs? NuScale Stock Dropped 72% When Bond Yields Hit 5% That decline occurred between July and December 2023, a period when the S&P 500 fell 9.5%. It ranks as the deepest fall NuScale has taken in a market shock. The stock has only traded publicly since 2020, yet it has already been through five such shocks. Across those five periods, NuScale fell 40.2% on average, compared with 13.4% for the S&P 500. That represents roughly three times the market's loss. The company lost 40% in the 2025 tariff shock, landing right near that historical average. Over a longer stretch, the damage has been even steeper. From its 2022 peak to its 2024 low, the stock lost 87%. Recovery times have varied. NuScale ultimately returned to its pre-shock high after all five falls, with a median wait from the low of 4.2 months. The longest wait came after the 2022 inflation shock, stretching to 21.0 months. Can NuScale Afford To Wait For A Contract? For now, the answer is yes. NuScale held about $1.9 billion in cash, cash equivalents and investments at the end of June, management said on the August 5, 2026 call. Here's how long the company has before it needs more cash. NuScale Power is attempting to build and sell small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs). It has an approved design and is already starting to set up its manufacturing capabilities. The company has achieved a lot, but it is still missing one crucial piece: a first customer. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. And NuScale is working with ENTRA1 Energy and the Tennessee Valley Authority on a project that could lead to a sale, but it just isn't there yet. This is why NuScale's cash burn is so important to monitor. When you add in research and development spending and selling, general, and administrative costs, the company's loss from operations totaled $64 million in the second quarter. That's actually not so bad when you compare it to the $1.1 billion in cash the company has, suggesting NuScale could muddle along for another four years before cash would become a problem. In other words, investors have two different issues to watch. NuScale appears to have plenty of cash on hand to support the business as it works toward its first sale. But once it makes its first sale, spending will likely accelerate quickly, and its cash burn will increase materially. Even there, however, the company appears prepared, as evidenced by the at-the-money stock program it has implemented. Essentially, even though you should continue to watch the company's cash hoard, it looks like NuScale is positioned fairly well from a cash perspective right now.

NuScale Power Corporation's SMR Energy Exploration Centers, or E2 Centers, are designed to make small modular reactor ("SMR") technology easier to grasp through simulation and direct interaction. Instead of relying only on classroom theory, the centers let students, researchers and future operators experience how an SMR plant behaves. That practical setup helps users understand control-room activity, operating decisions and reactor responses in a setting that mirrors real plant conditions. At the heart of each E2 Center is an advanced simulator modeled on the control room of a 12-module NuScale plant. Users can act as operators, change settings, test different situations and watch how the modules respond. Each workstation can monitor and control any of the 12 units, giving participants a broader view of multi-module plant management. This matters as future SMR facilities are expected to depend heavily on digital systems, automation and coordinated reactor operations. The E2 Centers also provide exposure to tools that are likely to play a major role in advanced nuclear plants. The simulator includes digital procedures, automated controls, system notifications and emergency-response functions. Students and future operators can therefore practice monitoring and decision-making without the risks of an operating reactor. For NuScale, the centers also help build familiarity with its technology while supporting workforce development as the advanced nuclear industry moves closer to wider commercial use. NuScale's approach centers on training and operational familiarity, but other advanced nuclear developers are taking different paths. Their reactor concepts focus more on compact size, fuel flexibility and deployment in a wider range of locations. Oklo Inc.'s OKLO technology uses liquid-metal-cooled, metal-fueled fast reactors. OKLO says this reactor type has more than 400 reactor-years of global operating experience. OKLO emphasizes inherent safety, fuel recycling and compact deployment. In simple terms, the company aims to use fast-reactor systems to supply clean electricity, advanced nuclear fuel and radioisotopes. Meanwhile, NANO Nuclear Energy NNE is developing small reactor systems for both stationary and portable use. NNE's lineup includes the KRONOS Micro Modular Reactor, ZEUS solid-core battery reactor and LOKI MMR. NNE is targeting applications such as power, heat, microgrids, remote sites and space-related uses, with an emphasis on modular designs that can be deployed more flexibly than traditional reactors.

Cameco Acknowledges United States and Republic of Korea Announcement of Framework for the Deployment of Nuclear Power

All amounts in Canadian dollars unless specified otherwise This news release constitutes a "designated news release" for the purposes of Cameco's prospectus supplement dated November 12, 2024, to its short form base shelf prospectus dated November 12, 2024. SASKATOON, Saskatchewan, September 30, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Cameco Corporation (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) acknowledges that the United States of America ("USG") and the Republic of Korea ("Korea"), under a previously entered Memorandum of Understanding (the "MOU"), today announced a framework that anticipates the investment by Korea of US$120 billion to help finance the buildout of Westinghouse reactor technology in the US using expertise and companies from both nations (the "Framework"). The Framework, which is separate and unrelated to the Department of Energy's American Nuclear Supply Chain Loans conditional commitment, contemplates the construction of up to eight large nuclear reactors in the United States, including six Westinghouse AP1000® reactors and up to two Korean APR1400 reactors that are built on Westinghouse technology. If successfully concluded, both technologies are expected to be deployed on federal sites designated by the USG, beginning with the deployment of two AP1000 reactors, contributing to the expansion of clean, reliable and domestically produced nuclear energy generation capacity. Building upon the strategic partnership announcement between Cameco, Brookfield Asset Management and the United States Department of Commerce in October 2025 (the "Partnership"), this Framework outlines a potential funding and execution pathway for the construction of new nuclear reactors in the United States under the Partnership. The Framework is subject to the negotiation and execution of definitive agreements, identification of planning of specific sites, regulatory approvals, financing arrangements, other customary conditions, and the finalization of definitive agreements under the Partnership. The Framework contemplates a waiver under the 2025 settlement agreement reached by Westinghouse in its intellectual property dispute with Korea Electric Power Corporation and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co., Ltd. The one-time waiver would allow for the construction of up to two APR1400 reactors in the United States, generating enhanced value for Westinghouse. The associated compensation package is expected to recognize the use of Westinghouse intellectual property and technology, providing approximately US$2 billion of value per APR1400 reactor through a combination of intellectual property licensing, engineering and procurement services, subcontracting opportunities and the long-term supply of fuel fabrication services, highlighting the strategic role that Westinghouse is expected to play across the contemplated reactor projects in the US.

Cameco (NYSE: CCJ), a Canada-based company, mined about 15% of the world's uranium in 2025. That makes it the second-largest uranium miner after Kazakhstan's Kazatomprom. It's also a bellwether and linchpin of the nuclear energy market. Cameco, like its industry peers, struggled for about a decade after the 2011 Fukushima disaster prompted many countries to throttle or halt their nuclear projects. But over the past few years, the nuclear energy industry recovered -- thanks to new decarbonization initiatives, safer nuclear technologies, and the growth of the power-hungry cloud infrastructure and AI markets. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The spot price of uranium sank from a record high of $136 per pound in June 2007 to just $18 per pound in Nov. 2016. But by the end of this August, it had risen back to $89.68 per pound. Cameco's stock also reached a record high of $134.09 per share on Jan. 28, 2026. Today, Cameco's stock trades at about $87. Let's see why it retreated from its record highs, and if that pullback represents a good long-term play on the resurgent nuclear energy market. Cameco operates uranium mines and mills in Canada, the U.S., and Kazakhstan. Instead of selling its uranium on the open market at its current spot prices (which would expose it to more volatility), Cameco locks most of its clients into long-term, partly fixed-price contracts. Most of those contracts were signed when uranium prices were lower. Therefore, Cameco doesn't benefit as much from rising uranium prices as its spot-price competitors do. But when uranium prices decline, the price floors from those contracts limit its losses. To further reduce its exposure to the volatile uranium mining market, Cameco doubled its stake in Global Laser Enrichment (GLE) -- its uranium enrichment joint venture with Silex (OTC: SILXY) -- from 24% to 49% in 2021. By integrating GLE's laser-based uranium enrichment capabilities into its core mining business, Cameco could gradually become a "one-stop shop" for mining, converting, and selling enriched uranium. In 2023, Cameco partnered with Brookfield Asset Management (NYSE: BAM) to acquire Westinghouse Electric, one of the world's leading nuclear technology companies. That 49% stake makes it a more diversified play on building and powering nuclear power plants.

Continue » Cameco is one of the world's largest uranium miners and the largest in North America. What sets it apart is its investment in high-grade uranium deposits at McArthur River/Key Lake and Cigar Lake, both in Saskatchewan, Canada. These deposits have low production costs of roughly $21.72 and $23.94 per pound of uranium extracted and processed, respectively, among the lowest for conventional mines worldwide. In comparison, Uranium Energy relies heavily on in-situ recovery (ISR). Using ISR, Uranium Energy pumps oxygenated water into underground sandstone aquifers to dissolve uranium, then pumps the uranium-rich liquid back to the surface. Unlike conventional underground or open-pit mines, ISR is less disruptive to the environment and has significantly lower reclamation costs. In the third quarter, Uranium Energy produced 32,195 lbs of concentrate at a total cash cost of $46.69 per pound. Since commissioning, its cumulative average cash cost per pound is around $32.40. One stark difference between Cameco and Uranium Energy is their business models and exposure to the nuclear value chain. Cameco is a massive miner, but it also has exposure across nuclear fuel and nuclear equipment sales. Cameco operates the world's largest commercial uranium refinery in Ontario. Cameco also owns 49% of Westinghouse Electric, one of the world's largest nuclear reactor developers, which plans to go public soon. Westinghouse develops the AP1000 reactor, and the U.S. intends to have at least 10 of these under construction by 2030. Uranium Energy doesn't have similar investments across the value chain. Instead, it is focused on mining projects in the U.S. and Canada. For Uranium Energy investors, its U.S. footprint could prove a competitive advantage as policymakers move aggressively to reshore the domestic nuclear fuel supply chain and eliminate reliance on adversarial foreign suppliers.

The steady drip of Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) merger talk is increasing, and this time it's coming from a Wall Street bank. In a note to clients on Wednesday, Barclays analyst Dan Levy said a tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." He pointed to media reports and to Elon Musk's own public hints. For now, though, it's still speculation. Tesla and SpaceX stock were both higher in Friday's premarket trading. Timing was the most notable part of Levy's note. Tesla must hold its annual general meeting [AGM] by Dec. 6, per SEC rules, and Levy and Barclays believe that this would be the appropriate avenue for shareholders to vote on a proposal. Levy said a merger announcement that slips later into October or early November "may increasingly challenge merger approval as part of the AGM." In that case, a deal wouldn't be dead, but may come instead in the next six to 12 months, since investors see an advantage in closing any deal under the Trump administration's friendly M&A environment. Levy argues AI vertical integration would be a key component of the merger. Tesla's physical AI, such as Robotaxi and Optimus, would be paired with SpaceX's virtual AI, such as Grok, all supplied by the companies' planned Terafab chip plant. Right now, Terafab decisions need approval from both boards, a process Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said would take "a while." Musk's shareholding in the two companies illustrates how a merger would unfold. Musk owns around 20% of Tesla, compared with about 48% of SpaceX. SpaceX super-voting Class B shares give him around 82% of the vote. SpaceX is worth about $2.1 trillion and Tesla about $1.5 trillion. If SpaceX bought Tesla at those values, Musk would own about 37% of the combined company and control 56% of the vote, Levy said. That's well above the 25% Tesla stake he has long said he wants. That's why Barclays expects SpaceX to be the buyer in an all-stock deal. At current values, each Tesla share would be worth about 0.7 SpaceX shares before any takeover premium. But the biggest factor weighing in favor of a merger happening is that Musk himself has heavily hinted at a tie-up of his two biggest companies. On Tesla's latest earnings call, Musk noted that there's "more and more overlap" between his two companies, whether it's operations, technology, or even SpaceX buying Tesla Cybertrucks. There are also Musk's own remarks at the All-In Summit last month. "With all this collaboration, on so many levels, who can imagine what action one might take when there's so much close collaboration in so many areas," he said.

Early on Wednesday, Ukraine claimed that SpaceX (SPCX) was restricting speed for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing invasion of the country, the Wall Street Journal reported. "I confirm that SpaceX implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals operating in motion last night," said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, according to WSJ. "Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions." Starlink, essentially a global broadband internet service delivered from space, is a core part of SpaceX's business. There are more than 10 million Starlink subscribers worldwide, and SpaceX is now moving to challenge legacy wireless carriers. Ukrainian military drone crews and logistics operations regularly leverage Starlink to provide video feeds and precise targeting. WSJ reported that "Ukraine's access to SpaceX's StarShield — a Starlink subscription designed for government and military use — is provided under a contract handled by the Defense Department." Ukrainian troops use both Starlink and Starshield terminals. On Wednesday afternoon, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk stated that SpaceX was not involved in the latest decision to restrict those services. A senior US official then told Barik Ravid of Axios that the Trump administration had nothing to do with any Starlink service constraints. On Thursday evening, citing official familiar with the matter, Reuters reported that "the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House." This is not the first time Ukraine has experienced Starlink throttling, though it is the first since SpaceX became a public company this summer. In 2022, as Ukraine retook territory from Russia, Musk reportedly ordered SpaceX engineers to cut some Starlink coverage in contested areas of Ukraine. In 2023, the company acknowledged efforts to throttle Starlink usage during the war. "There are things that we can do to limit their ability to [leverage Starlink]," Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, said at the time. "There are things that we can do, and have done." Musk is an ally of President Trump, who has recently ramped up criticism of Zelensky. Ukraine also bombed Russian data centers recently, disrupting bot traffic on Musk-owned X and other social media platforms. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is not running for reelection and supports the US backing Ukraine's defense, posted on X — which Musk owns — seeking clarification on SpaceX's policy related to Starlink services. This post has been updated with new details. The car uses cold-gas thrusters built with SpaceX (SPCX), whose shares rose about 2%, and in the demo it lifted off, flipped and landed. "Turns out the future does have flying cars," Elon Musk said at the event, per Fox Business. With production not planned until 2028, the bigger story for shareholders is the company behind the thrusters. Barclays analyst Dan Levy sees a possible merger announcement before Tesla's shareholder meeting, which he expects by December 6, and envisions an all-stock deal with SpaceX acquiring Tesla. The mean of 38 analyst price targets is $397.83, only about 6% above Friday's early price. The spread around it stands out: the low target is $128.11 and the high is $600, a range from roughly 66% downside to 59% upside. The ratings are just as split. Tesla has 15 buys and 4 outperforms, against 21 holds, 3 no opinions, 2 underperforms and 2 sells. Sells have dropped from 7 at the end of 2025, but holds have climbed from 17 a year ago. Fewer bears, more fence-sitters. In an all-stock deal, Tesla holders would swap a carmaker's shares for a stake in a rocket and satellite company. The argument over whether Tesla deserves $128 or $600 would turn into an argument over the exchange ratio. The hurdles are real: regulatory approvals (China especially) and governance questions, since Musk holds a larger voting stake in SpaceX. Gene Munster also called the Roadster demo an engineering showcase with little direct commercial value for Tesla. Everything hinges on whether talks exist. The 21 hold ratings alone do not establish whether analysts are waiting for a merger. Without a deal, Tesla goes back to being judged on its car business when it reports third-quarter results on October 21. On those numbers, the Roadster is a rounding error for a stock trading at 186x earnings. That's the likelier near-term test. Merger speculation may have contributed to Friday's pop, but I believe that the rally does not establish that talks are underway. The stocks of Tesla and SpaceX are little changed on Friday after the former introduced its latest Roadster model, which is equipped with thrusters from the latter. Tesla shares climbed 0.65% at 10:46 a.m. ET, while those of SpaceX dropped 1.11% at the same time. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," Elon Musk, CEO of both companies, said on Thursday at Waco, Texas when introducing the car. The car is performed a stunt during the night in which it managed to stabilize itself when falling from a curved ramp. CNBC noted that the model is expected to be high-end and low-volume. It is set to enter production in 2028, and the price has not been specified. However, the company has opened reservations for the car and is accepting $50,000 deposits from potential buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. The event also fueled speculation about the possibility that both companies will merge eventually. Their collaboration increased throughout this year, and SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said that such a move "might make Elon's life a little easier." Tesla also beat delivery expectations in the third quarter of this year as the electric vehicle maker showed a sharp improvement from earlier this year despite intensifying global competition. The company produced 464,391 vehicles during the quarter, meaning deliveries exceeded production by more than 22,000 vehicles. Wall Street analysts had expected roughly 461,100 deliveries, according to StreetAccount consensus cited by CNBC. Tesla's own company-compiled consensus, released earlier this week and based on estimates from 24 sell-side analysts, called for 461,974 deliveries. That means Tesla exceeded its company-compiled consensus by nearly 25,000 vehicles, or about 5.3%. The result, however, was still below last year's record third quarter. Tesla delivered 497,099 vehicles in the third quarter of 2025, making the latest figure a decline of about 2.1% year over year. Last year's quarter remains Tesla's delivery record. Tesla's Model 3 sedan and Model Y SUV continued to dominate its automotive business. The company delivered 478,237 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles during the quarter, compared with 8,295 vehicles across its other models. Together, the Model 3 and Model Y accounted for roughly 98% of total deliveries. Tesla produced 457,387 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles during the period. The stronger-than-expected quarter comes at a crucial time for Tesla. The company is facing increasingly aggressive competition from Chinese EV manufacturers including BYD and Xiaomi, while attempting to reverse consecutive annual declines in vehicle sales. Tesla has also dealt with consumer backlash surrounding Musk and changes to U.S. EV incentives.

His company owns a 1.25% stake in the space exploration and AI giant, an investment he says is worth about $25 billion as of June. So it wasn't all that surprising when he made the forecast that the company would be worth between $20 trillion and $50 trillion within 10 years. Elon Musk, though, said Baron was way off in his prediction. "Unless there is a major world war, SpaceX probably gets to >$100T in <10 years," Musk wrote in an Oct. 14 post on X. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP It's the latest in a long string of bombastic predictions from Musk about one of his companies. This one, though, could raise more eyebrows than previous ones. Baron, an avowed Musk bull, insisted the fundamentals of SpaceX were strong. But some investors still view SpaceX with a cautious eye. The company's $1.77 trillion valuation at the time of its debut on the Nasdaq meant it traded at a very steep multiple of its sales, even as it continued to post giant quarterly losses. And S&P Global Ratings is projecting the company won't have positive cash flow until at least 2029. Several notable analysts warned investors prior to the IPO about the company's boasts versus real-world risk. For instance, Aswath Damodaran, a professor at NYU's Stern School of Business who is best known as the "dean of valuation" said he believed SpaceX's value at the IPO to be $1.3 trillion, nearly half a trillion dollars less than the company was claiming. The company, in its IPO paperwork, said the AI division could see revenue opportunities of $26 trillion. The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has created some unlikely winners over the last few years. But lately, one of its biggest beneficiaries has suddenly become a major headache. CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV), a leading provider of AI computing infrastructure, has seen its stock plummet as investors question whether the company is borrowing too much to capitalize on surging AI demand. Meanwhile, Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) is quietly building a competing business. While SpaceX is best known for rockets and Starlink satellites, the company is becoming a serious player in AI infrastructure following its acquisitions of xAI and Cursor earlier this year. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » With several multibillion-dollar capacity agreements beginning to generate revenue, CoreWeave's troubles could create a golden opportunity for SpaceX. CoreWeave is known as a neocloud. Rather than developing AI models itself, the company operates data centers filled with Nvidia chips and rents that compute capacity to hyperscalers. It's a savvy business model but an extraordinarily expensive business to build at scale. CoreWeave has accumulated more than $50 billion in debt and operating leases as it races to build AI factories for customers including Microsoft, OpenAI, and Meta Platforms. On Oct. 14, CoreWeave stock plunged more than 15% after investors began questioning the sustainability of its borrowing strategy. The warning signs were particularly evident in the bond market. CoreWeave's senior notes maturing in 2032 briefly traded at yields near 15% -- substantially above their original 9.625% coupon. This doesn't mean CoreWeave is paying 15% interest on this debt. Rather, declining bond prices simply mean bond investors are demanding greater compensation for the company's credit risk. The bigger issue at hand here is free cash flow. According to estimates from Visible Alpha, CoreWeave is expected to generate negative free cash flow of $25 billion this year, followed by deficits of $28 billion in 2027 and $18 billion in 2028. Much of the company's spending will continue going toward infrastructure build-outs. But given the expected cash burn over the next few years, CoreWeave will depend on outside financing to continue its expansion. If lenders become less confident about the payoffs from AI data centers, CoreWeave's growth strategy becomes more vulnerable.

JPMorgan upgraded the stock to 'Overweight' from 'Underweight.' Coca-Cola (KO) rose 0.7% in premarket trading. Barclays raised its price target and maintained an Overweight rating. SpaceX (SPCX), EchoStar (ECHO) and Coca-Cola (KO) shares moved higher in premarket trading on Friday as analysts updated their price targets and outlooks for the companies. Evercore ISI raised its target on SpaceX ahead of its third-quarter results, JPMorgan upgraded EchoStar, and Barclays raised its target on Coca-Cola. SPCX shares were up about 2.35% in premarket trading at the time of writing after Evercore ISI raised the firm's price target for Elon Musk's company to $275 from $230 and maintained an 'Outperform' rating. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox Evercore expects SpaceX's third-quarter results to draw attention to developments that could shape estimates and investor sentiment through the end of the year and into 2027. The firm said major milestones may be closer than some investors expect. ECHO stock gained nearly 2.7% in premarket trading after JPMorgan upgraded the stock to 'Overweight' from 'Underweight' and set a $144 price target. "EchoStar shares trade at a 40% discount to JPMorgan's estimated net asset value, which is unwarranted and creates a 'compelling near-term opportunity,," the firm told investors in a research note, according to TheFly. It also said ECHO's $43-billion spectrum sale to AT&T and SpaceX has reduced balance-sheet risk and created further opportunities to unlock value. Potential catalysts include "upside" in the value of SpaceX shares, "additional spectrum monetization" and the possibility of share repurchases beginning sooner than expected. KO shares rose 0.8% in premarket trading after Barclays raised its price target to $98 from $93 and maintained an 'Overweight' rating. The adjustment came as part of the firm's third-quarter earnings preview for consumer staples. Barclays said relatively few companies in the sector offer both a dependable defensive outlook and an attractive valuation, leaving investors with a narrow range of options. At the time of writing, retail sentiment toward SpaceX was 'bearish,' unchanged in the past 24 hours, while message volume was 'normal.' SPCX shares have lost about 0.9% since the company went public in June.

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) are two monstrous companies. Nvidia is valued at about $5.5 trillion, while SpaceX is a $2 trillion company. The world's first trillion-dollar company didn't appear until 2018, showing how far the market has come in just a short period of time. A lot of that growth is thanks to a bullish outlook on the artificial intelligence build-out, and these two often come up as top AI options. But which is the best pick? Let's take a look. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Nvidia and SpaceX are two completely different investments in the AI field. Nvidia is more of a hardware play, while SpaceX is an application play. Nvidia makes graphics processing units (GPUs), which are the computing muscle behind many AI workloads today. Although it has rising competitors, Nvidia's products still sit atop the AI computing unit food chain. In fact, SpaceX Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk had this to say about Nvidia's computing units during its Q2 conference call: And going forward, we've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture. We think it's the best AI computer, and we greatly value our close cooperation and partnership on many levels with Nvidia. So, we're exclusive to Nvidia. This is a pretty definitive statement that SpaceX will be a solely Nvidia-powered business. The architecture Musk is talking about is Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture, which is entering production right now. This promises a 10-fold reduction in inference costs and a fourfold reduction in training costs compared to prior-generation Blackwell GPUs. That's a huge gain and will keep Nvidia at the top. SpaceX is a bit of a different AI play. Before going public in June, SpaceX purchased xAI, which produces the Grok AI model. The Grok model is a fairly popular large language model family, although it may not have the same status as ChatGPT or Claude. Still, it's a rapidly growing part of SpaceX's business, with xAI's revenue soaring 213% in Q2. xAI will be a profitable and successful business unit for SpaceX if it can continue expanding its reach and integrate into various applications. This token usage will drive a strong recurring revenue stream for xAI.
